ranges.en: Mishnaic rule: certain women permanently exempt their co-wives from levirate marriage and ḥalitza, the exemption passing along the chain of rivals.
Introduces the list of forbidden kin, starting with the yavam's daughter, her daughters and son, and his wife's daughter.
Continues the list with the daughter of the wife's son and the daughter of the wife's daughter.
Lists the yevama's relations by marriage: the mother-in-law, her mother, and the yavam's father-in-law's mother.
Closes the list with maternal half-sisters, aunts and sisters-in-law, and the wife of a maternal half-brother.

2b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishnah continues the list with a brother's wife from before his birth and a daughter-in-law, all exempting their rivals forever.
Exception: if these women die, refuse, get divorced, or prove barren, their rival wives are permitted to marry.
Mishnah notes the wording is imprecise, since mother-in-law and her mothers cannot be found barren or refusing.
Example: if the daughter was married to the brother, her rival is exempt, and the same holds for the other forbidden kin.
Chain: the rival of the daughter's rival, after marrying a second brother, is also exempt, following the same reasoning.
Even if there are one hundred brothers, the same exemption principle applies down the chain of rivals.
Example: if the forbidden relative died or divorced before the brother, her rival is permitted to him.
If the forbidden relative was a minor who could refuse, her rival performs ḥalitza and may not enter levirate marriage.
Gemara asks why the mishnah does not teach the wife's sister first, since all these cases are derived from her.
Proposed answer: the tanna listed the cases by order of severity of their punishments.
Supports the proposed answer by citing Rabbi Shimon's view that burning is a more severe penalty than stoning.
Objection: if ordering by severity is the reason, the mishnah should have started with the mother-in-law.
Burning is the penalty written in the Torah specifically for the mother-in-law case, showing she should come first.
Further objection: the daughter-in-law should follow the mother-in-law, since stoning is the most severe after burning.
Resolution: the daughter is listed first because that prohibition is derived by midrash, which the tanna particularly values.

3a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objection: all the listed exemptions also come from a midrashic derivation, not explicit text, so the mishna's presentation seems unfounded.
Reply: granted for levirate exemptions, the core prohibitions are explicit, except the daughter from rape, whose prohibition is midrashic.
Rava's teaching from Rav Yitzḥak bar Avdimi: a verbal analogy of 'hena' in Leviticus 18 extends the prohibition to a daughter from rape.
A second analogy on 'zimah' from Leviticus 18:17 and 20:14 makes the rape-born daughter liable to burning.
Given that midrashic matters are favored, why not teach the wife's sister last, since her prohibition is the source?
The tanna was discussing prohibitions on sisters, so he included the wife's sister alongside them.
If so, why not place this whole sisters section at the end, when the wife's sister is mentioned?
Alternative: the mishna orders relations by closeness, beginning with his own blood relatives: daughter, daughter's daughter, son's daughter.
The same three-generation pattern applies to the wife's line, both descending and ascending, explaining the structure of the list.
Next come his sister and mother's sister, blood relatives less close than his daughter, followed by the wife's sister.
The daughter-in-law should logically precede the brother's wife, but since the topic is sibling prohibitions, the brother's wife comes first.
Why does the mishna say they exempt their rivals rather than saying they forbid them?
Had it said forbidden, one might think levirate is banned but ḥalitza is required, so 'exempt' teaches full exemption.
Proposed wording 'forbidden to perform ḥalitza' is objected to, since ḥalitza by itself accomplishes nothing for the woman.
Why not, then? Is there a real prohibition involved in the ḥalitza wording?
If ḥalitza were allowed, one might infer that the rival may also marry the yavam, so the wording must avoid this.
The rival is forbidden only where levirate applies and permitted elsewhere, so the mishna uses exemption rather than prohibition.
Why does the mishna list ḥalitza and levirate together, rather than saying only levirate?
Mentioning only levirate would suggest ḥalitza is required; the principle is that ḥalitza applies exactly where levirate applies.
Why not teach levirate first then ḥalitza, or ḥalitza alone, as alternative orderings?
The order follows Abba Shaul, who holds that the mitzva of ḥalitza takes precedence over levirate marriage.
What do the enumeration of fifteen women in the first clause and the word 'these' in the second exclude?

3b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The enumerations exclude the two additions proposed by Rav and by Rav Asi, that is, their respective cases of extra rivals.
Asks what the mishna's enumeration excludes according to the opinions of Rav and Rav Asi.
If each agrees with the other's view, one enumeration excludes the rival of a refusing wife, the other the rival of a remarried divorcee.
If they do not share each other's view, one enumeration excludes the other's case, and the other excludes one of the two cases.
If so, why did the tanna not teach the additional cases that Rav and Rav Asi hold should be included?
Those cases were omitted because they do not involve a rival of a rival, which is the mishna's concern.
From where is this halakha derived, that a forbidden relative bars both her and her rival from levirate marriage?
Leviticus 18:18 prohibits taking a wife's sister as a rival, which is the scriptural basis for the rule.
What does the apparently superfluous phrase 'with her' in that verse add?
Deuteronomy 25:5 would otherwise suggest levirate applies to all forbidden kin, so the verbal analogy from 'with her' limits it.
The analogy shows that the prohibition on forbidden kin remains in force even where levirate is a mitzva.
Having derived only that she is exempt, from where is it derived that her rival is also exempt?
The word 'to be a rival' (litzror) teaches that the rival of the forbidden woman is exempt as well.
The full spelling of 'litzror' with double reish indicates several successive rivals, so the rival of a rival is exempt too.
Having derived only the wife's sister, from where is it derived that other forbidden relatives are also exempt?
Analogy: the wife's sister is forbidden with karet and sin-offering liability, so every such forbidden woman is likewise prohibited to the yavam.
Having derived only these cases, from where is it derived that their rival wives are also exempt?
Analogy: the wife's sister's rival is prohibited, so every forbidden woman's rival is likewise prohibited to the yavam.
The Sages therefore stated that fifteen women exempt their rivals and rivals of rivals from ḥalitza and levirate marriage forever.
Could one include the six more severe forbidden relatives, whose rivals would then be prohibited to the yavam?
Reply: the wife's sister is permitted to the brothers yet prohibited to the yavam, so the six excluded cases do not match this pattern.
The six more severe relatives are excluded, since they can never marry any brother, so no levirate bond and no rival exemption arises.
We have learned the warning against this prohibition; from where is the punishment derived?
Leviticus 18:29 says those who commit these abominations shall be cut off from their people, which supplies the punishment.
The word 'with her' is written to exclude the case where a wife's sister would perform levirate with her sister's husband.
What is the reason one would have assumed that a wife's sister performs levirate?
The reason is the principle that a positive commandment overrides a prohibition, here the mitzva of levirate overriding the prohibition.
Challenges the principle: perhaps a positive commandment overrides only certain negative commandments, not every one.
Does a positive commandment override a negative one carrying karet, and from where is it derived that it overrides an ordinary negative?

ranges.en: Deuteronomy 22:11-12 forbids mixed wool and linen yet commands fringes, showing the positive mitzva overrides the prohibition.
Where in the Torah is it derived that verses juxtaposed to one another may be interpreted homiletically?
Psalm 111 describes God's commandments as juxtaposed forever, supporting inference from juxtaposed verses.
Teaching transmitted from Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya: a yevama before a yavam with boils may not be forced into levirate marriage.
Deuteronomy 25:4 forbids muzzling an ox, juxtaposed to 25:5, teaching that the yevama's refusal must not be overridden.
Rav Yosef: even Rabbi Yehuda, who generally does not derive from juxtaposition, does so in Deuteronomy.
From where do we know that Rabbi Yehuda generally does not derive interpretations from juxtaposed verses?
Ben Azzai's baraita: juxtaposed verses on sorcery and bestiality show that sorceresses are stoned like those who lie with beasts.
Rabbi Yehuda objects: juxtaposition alone should not send someone to the most severe death penalty of stoning.
Rabbi Yehuda's own source: mediums and wizards are singled out for stoning, and this analogy extends it to sorceresses.
From where do we know that Rabbi Yehuda does derive interpretations in Deuteronomy?
Mishna: a man may marry a woman raped or seduced by his father, but Rabbi Yehuda prohibits marrying those women.
Rav Giddel, citing Rav: what is the reason behind Rabbi Yehuda's opinion?
Deuteronomy 23:1: 'shall not uncover his father's skirt' refers to any woman his father has been with, including one raped by him.
From where is it known that this verse is written about a woman raped by the father?
The preceding verse about rape, Deuteronomy 22:29, is juxtaposed to 23:1, showing Rabbi Yehuda derives from juxtaposition in Deuteronomy.
How do the Rabbis, who disagree with Rabbi Yehuda, respond to this juxtaposition argument?
The juxtaposition is broken by the intervening verse about the yavam's wife, so the verse concerns a yevama and two prohibitions.
But if Rabbi Yehuda does not generally derive from juxtaposition, what is his reason for deriving it in Deuteronomy?
Alternative: the derivation holds because the context makes the meaning evident, since otherwise it would be written with the forbidden relations in Leviticus.
Alternative: the verse is superfluous, since the phrase 'shall not uncover his father's skirt' has no other purpose, so it teaches by juxtaposition.

4b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Concludes the verse is free for a juxtaposition inference, offering two explanations: either the context is evident, or the verse is superfluous.
Objects: if the verse were free, the fringes passage would have been the natural place for it, so its placement here must teach something.
Alternative: the verse is free, since the context itself makes clear that the juxtaposition is meant to teach a further halakha.
Since the verse on mixed garments already appears, why is the separate prohibition on wearing wool and linen mixed also needed?
Conclusion: the surplus phrase is free to support homiletic inference from juxtaposed verses.
Both verses are needed: 'shall not come upon you' covers placing garments on others, while 'shall not wear' limits the prohibition to wearing.
Had only 'shall not wear' been written, one might limit the prohibition to wearing, so the phrase 'shall not come upon you' is needed too.
Objects: part of the verse is superfluous, since 'wool and linen' seems unnecessary once the general prohibition is stated.
Rabbi Yishmael's school: the general term garments is specified as wool or linen by Leviticus 13:47, so the phrase 'wool and linen' teaches juxtaposition.
Objects: the phrase is still needed, since wearing, not merely placing, involves a benefit prohibited for any two kinds of material.
Reply: let the verse omit wool and linen and derive the prohibition by verbal analogy, so the repetition must be teaching juxtaposition.
If Rabbi Yishmael's school holds wool and linen are superfluous, why would fringes be exempt from mixed kinds, given Numbers 15:38 about fringes?
Rabbi Yishmael's school: the sky-blue thread is wool, since the priestly garments specify linen shesh, showing diverse kinds are permitted in fringes.
Explains the necessity of the phrase: otherwise Rava would find a contradiction, so it must be read to resolve that contradiction.
Rava's contradiction: 'the corners' requires same-material fringes, yet 'wool and linen' seems to limit fringes to those materials.
Resolution: wool and linen fringes fulfill the obligation regardless of garment material, while other materials must match the garment.
But Rabbi Yishmael's school does not hold Rava's view, since it limits fringes to garments of wool or linen, so why is the phrase needed?
The phrase is needed to teach that wool fringes on linen, or linen on wool, still fulfill the obligation, so the sky-blue thread applies only to matching garments.

5a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If the principle works for Rabbi Yishmael's school, from where do the Rabbis, who reject that reading, derive that a positive mitzva overrides?
They derive it from the leper's 'his head' in Leviticus 14:9, which a baraita contrasts with the prohibition on rounding the head's corners.
The tanna holds that shaving the whole head still counts as rounding the corners, so the leper's shaving violates the prohibition.
Objects that the rounding prohibition does not apply to women, so it cannot prove a mitzva overrides a prohibition binding everyone.
Rather, the principle is derived from the leper's 'his beard', which the baraita treats as a separate source.
What does 'his beard' add, since a beard is already included in 'all his hair'?
Leviticus 21:5 forbids priests to shave their beard corners, so the leper's 'his beard' is needed to include lepers in that prohibition.
The beard prohibition also does not bind women, so the inference must be applied to a prohibition binding all people.
Rejects this: 'his beard' is needed to teach that priests, held to stricter duties, still have a mitzva overriding a non-universal prohibition.
Rather, the principle is derived from a different tanna's reading of 'his head', as taught in a baraita.
'His head' is needed because a nazirite's 'no razor shall come upon his head' would otherwise bar the leper's shaving, so the mitzva overrides.
Refutes the nazirite proof: a leprous nazirite may have his vow annulled, so his prohibition is not severe enough to prove anything.
Why not derive the opposite conclusion from the nazirite case, where the mitzva of shaving overrides the nazirite's growth mitzva?
Because the nazirite case is equally refutable, since his vow can be annulled upon request, the nazirite argument fails in either direction.
Concludes the Gemara must seek a different basis for the principle, introducing a further explanation.

5b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Upholds the view that the phrase is free by arguing the verse would otherwise say only to make fringes.
Objects that twisted fringes is not superfluous; it teaches the number of strings required.
Replies that if the fringe measure is the phrase's purpose, the wool-and-linen phrase remains free for derivation.
Argues wool-and-linen together is needed to teach that two stitches, not one, make attachment.
Replies that the diverse-kinds phrase is then superfluous, so the phrase must be free.
Argues diverse kinds is needed for the acronym defining shoa, tavui and noz.
Replies that the whole interpretation is derived from the term sha'atnez itself.
States that a positive mitzva overrides a plain negative prohibition.
Asks where a positive mitzva is found overriding a prohibition punishable by karet.
Suggests deriving the principle by analogy from the mitzva of circumcision.
Rejects the circumcision analogy because circumcision is a severe mitzva with thirteen covenants.
Suggests deriving the principle by analogy from the Paschal lamb.
Rejects the Paschal analogy because its neglect carries karet, unlike other mitzvot.
Suggests deriving the principle from the daily offering, which overrides Shabbat.
Rejects the daily-offering analogy because it is frequent, unlike occasional mitzvot.
Concludes the principle cannot come from one case, but may come from two combined.
Asks which two cases the principle can be derived from.
Explains that the pairs share severity, or that both serve the altar rather than personal benefit.
Suggests deriving the principle from circumcision and the daily offering together.
Rejects this because both were known before revelation at Sinai, on one opinion about the desert offering.
Asserts the opinion that the desert burnt-offering was the daily offering.
Rejects deriving from all three together because all were known before the revelation.
Explains the inference from with her is needed, since one might derive levirate from honoring parents.
Cites a baraita and verse showing honoring parents does not override Shabbat, since all owe honor to God.
Proposes that the baraita concerns a father ordering labor on Shabbat, which would not be a proof.
Explains that the verse's keep My Shabbatot warns against that case, implying otherwise the mitzva would override.
Rejects the inference by saying the positive mitzva would not override in that case.

6a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The case concerns driving a laden animal, a regular prohibition, which the mitzva of honoring parents does not override.
Asks why we do not instead infer that positive mitzvot never override even regular prohibitions, based on the parents case.
Proposes that Shabbat prohibitions are more severe, so the parents case proves nothing about regular prohibitions.
Rejects that defense: the tanna speaks generally and raises no such distinction.
Cites a baraita: honoring parents does not override even priestly impurity or returning lost property, since all owe honor to God.
Explains the baraita is refuted: the parents case is mere preparation for a mitzva, not a mitzva itself.
Suggests the principle that a mitzva overrides even karet prohibitions derives from the Temple building, citing a baraita.
Asks whether the baraita actually concerns building or demolishing on Shabbat, which would carry karet.
Explains the verse Keep My Shabbatot implies that otherwise the positive mitzva would override Shabbat, and so all karet prohibitions.
Replies that the case is driving a laden animal, and even then the Temple-building mitzva does not override it.
Repeats the objection: a mitzva might override all prohibitions, so derive from here that it overrides none.
Repeats the defense that Shabbat prohibitions are more severe than regular ones.
Rejects the defense again, since the tanna speaks generally without raising that difficulty.
Repeats the baraita on a priest's impurity and lost property, concluding that all owe honor to God.
Explains there is no proof for all prohibitions, since driving an animal is preparation rather than a mitzva.
Asks why the preparation rule should not be derived from the parents case, making the Temple derivation redundant.
Confirms that this is indeed so, the Gemara accepting the objection's premise.
Asks why the verse about Shabbat and reverence for the Sanctuary is needed if the parents case already proves the point.
Explains the verse is needed for a baraita: revere the Temple but do not worship it, since keeping applies to Shabbat and reverence to the Temple.

6b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Baraita continuation: one fears the One who commanded Shabbat and the Temple, and the Temple reverence means not entering with staff or shoes.
Derives from the verse keep My Shabbatot and revere My Sanctuary that Temple reverence applies even after the Temple is destroyed.
Suggests deriving the karet principle from the prohibition on kindling fire, taught in the school of Rabbi Yishmael.
Asks what the verse adds by repeating the word meaning additional clause in the kindling prohibition.
Explains the question depends on whether the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei, where kindling is a regular prohibition, or Rabbi Natan, where it divides labors.
Baraita: Rabbi Yosei says kindling is singled out as a regular prohibition, while Rabbi Natan says it divides the labors; Rava explains the difficulty.
Asks what the term habitations adds, since it might limit Shabbat observance to certain places.
Explains habitations cannot limit Shabbat, because obligations of the body apply both in the Land of Israel and outside it.
Cites Rabbi Yishmael's student: the verse on capital punishment implies execution occurs on weekdays, not Shabbat, as the verse says.
Suggests that the death penalty might be administered on both weekdays and Shabbat, per the general reading.
Asks how to establish the verse about profaning Shabbat if it applies only to other labors excluding court execution.
Alternative reading: court execution is included among prohibited labors, so it would fall under the same general prohibition.
Asks how to establish the verse on execution if it is to be carried out on a weekday and not on Shabbat.
Reverts to the possibility that capital punishments may be carried out even on Shabbat.
Verbal analogy from habitations and the kindling verse concludes that court-imposed executions do not override Shabbat.
Proposes that the tanna follows Rabbi Natan, so the verse teaches an inference that otherwise the execution would override Shabbat.
Rejects this proof: the tanna may follow Rabbi Yosei, so no inference from this verse follows.
Retorts that even under Rabbi Yosei, the kindling that is singled out refers only to ordinary kindling, not to court executions.
Explains that court kindling for burning is actually cooking a leaden wick, a labor distinct from kindling fire.
Rav Sheshet argues cooking a wick incurs karet, which suggests without a special verse a mitzva would override a karet prohibition.
Rav Shimi bar Ashi rejects this: the tanna raises the option not because a mitzva overrides a prohibition, but by a fortiori reasoning.
Rav Shimi explains that the tanna derives the point by an a fortiori inference, which he now states.
A fortiori argument: the labor prohibition excludes court execution, yet court execution may override Shabbat by a fortiori reasoning.

7a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A fortiori: if Temple service overrides Shabbat and murder overrides Temple service, murder should override Shabbat too.
Asks what the tanna means by the or perhaps clause that reverts to the earlier suggestion.
Explains the a fortiori can be refuted: burying a met mitzva overrides Temple service but not Shabbat.
The tanna retracts and says burial of a met mitzva does override Shabbat, by a fortiori reasoning.
Repeats the a fortiori argument, citing the nazirite verse on burying a met mitzva, and the verse about not kindling fire.
Asks how the baraita should be read if the tanna's assumption rests on a positive mitzva overriding a prohibition.
Explains the tanna's reading: the verse on profaning Shabbat excludes court execution, which overrides Shabbat.
Tanna retracts: a positive mitzva overrides only a regular prohibition, not one carrying karet.
Asks whether the tanna heard that a positive mitzva overrides a prohibition that carries karet.
Counter-claim: the prohibition is more stringent than the mitzva, since courts punish it with lashes, yet the mitzva overrides it.
Proposes that the brother's wife case is a generalization exemplar, and cites a baraita on a matter included in a generalization.
Cites the verse on eating peace-offerings in ritual impurity, to show a singled-out item teaches about its whole category.
Asks why peace-offerings were singled out if they were already included among consecrated offerings.
Explains they were singled out to compare to all consecrated altar offerings, excluding Temple maintenance property.
Argues the brother's wife was singled out from all forbidden relations to teach that all such women are permitted.
Objects that the cases differ: the general and specific both fall under one prohibition there, but not here.
Proposes the case fits a different principle: a matter singled out from a generalization cannot return to it unless the Torah says so, as a baraita teaches.
Cites the verse on the leper guilt-offering being slaughtered where the sin and burnt offerings are slaughtered, as the sin offering is the priest's.
Asks what the comparison as the sin-offering is the guilt-offering adds, since guilt-offering laws are stated elsewhere.
Explains it is needed because the leper guilt-offering was singled out for a new matter, so one might think blood placement is not required.

7b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Cites the verse as the sin-offering so is the guilt-offering, requiring the guilt-offering blood and parts to be placed on the altar.
Explains that without this verse, the excluded case would be treated separately, so no proof follows that other forbidden women are permitted.
Proposes a verbal analogy: as a brother's wife enters levirate marriage, so should a wife's sister.
Asks whether the cases are comparable, since one has a single prohibition and the other two, and why Since it is permitted, it is permitted applies.
Cites a baraita: a leper who had a seminal emission on the eighth day may enter the Temple to bring the Paschal lamb.
Explains the baraita's reason: a positive mitzva carrying karet overrides one without karet.
Rabbi Yochanan holds that by Torah law even a positive mitzva does not override this prohibition.
Cites the verse in Chronicles about Jehoshaphat standing before the new courtyard as support.
Asks what the new courtyard refers to in that verse.
Rabbi Yochanan explains it is where new rulings were issued: a ritually impure person may not enter the Levites' camp.
Ulla argues the leper may sacrifice because he is permitted to enter for his leprosy, so one prohibition permitted means two are permitted.
Objects: is this assumption comparable to the case of Ulla at all?

8a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If the deceased brother married first and the survivor later married the sister, the first prohibition is lifted and so is the second.
In the reverse order, the wife's sister prohibition comes first and so it persists even after the brother's wife prohibition lapses.
Even when the deceased married first, the sister is permitted only if she was fit for the survivor in between, not during the lifetime.
Ulla's ruling on a leper with a seminal emission the night before shows no permitted moment exists, so the principle cannot apply.
Explains that with her is needed for the case where the brother's wife was permitted for a period, so the wife's sister is still forbidden.
Rabbi Yona's juxtaposition of Leviticus 18:29 with the brother's wife case: all forbidden women are juxtaposed, so all are permitted in levirate marriage.
Rav Aha of Difti objects that the juxtaposition could equally link them to a wife's sister, so the opposite conclusion follows.
Answers that a stringent juxtaposition is preferred, and that two-prohibition cases derive only from other two-prohibition cases, not single ones.
Rava holds that a forbidden relation needs no verse, since a mitzva does not override karet, so with her is needed for a rival wife.
Asks whether the tanna really holds that a forbidden relation needs no verse, since the baraita states she is exempt.
Replies that the baraita mentions her only to introduce the case of the rival wife.
Raises another difficulty that the sisters' exemption suggests a verse-based derivation for all, which is rejected as stated due to rival wives.
Cites a baraita of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: the repeated with her phrases in Deuteronomy 25:5 prohibit rival wives and forbidden relations.
Suggests amending the baraita to say it prohibits rival wives of forbidden relations, not the forbidden relations themselves.
Asks whether two verse phrases are needed for two cases, one for the forbidden relation and one for the rival wife.
Rejects that suggestion: both phrases are needed, one prohibiting rival wives where levirate applies and one permitting them where it does not.
Explains the rival wife is forbidden only where levirate marriage applies, and permitted where it does not apply.
Rav Ashi argues the mishna's wording, that fifteen women exempt their rival wives, supports Rava's view.
Asks why a rival wife would need a verse if a forbidden relation does not, since a mitzva does not override karet in either case.
Rav Aha relays Rava's view: a rival wife, like the forbidden relation, does not need a verse, since the prohibition carries karet.

8b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks the reason for permitting a rival wife where levirate marriage does not apply.
Cites the verse with her to show the rival wife is permitted only where levirate marriage does not apply.
Rami bar Chama objects that a forbidden relative should also be permitted, by a fortiori reasoning.
Rami rejects Rava's fortiori reply, since the rival wife case already refutes it.
Rava replies that the verse itself settles the matter against Rami's claim.
Quotes the phrase in her lifetime, applying the prohibition in every case during her life.
Asks why in her lifetime is needed if it only excludes the time after death.
Derives the permission after death from the verse about a woman to her sister.
If the rule comes from a woman to her sister, a divorced sister should be permitted.
Quotes in her lifetime to show that divorce does not permit the sister.
Introduces a second interpretation, transmitted in Rava's name, of the two prohibitions.
Cites two verses: one prohibits rival wives, the other's singular nakedness implies one woman.
Asks how the two verses can be reconciled.
Both are prohibited where levirate applies; only the sister is forbidden where it does not.
Objects that the reverse reading is equally possible.
If so, the verse need not say with her at all, so the phrase must be limiting.
Rav Ashi asks how we know the extra phrase restricts rather than permits.
Explains the verse as permitting both sisters where levirate applies and forbidding them otherwise.
Rav Kahana objects that under these readings one sister could never be forbidden alone.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi teaches that the levirate verses prohibit rival wives and forbidden relations.
Objects that rival wives are not written here and are derived from a different verse.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi derives rival wives from litzror, following Rabbi Shimon's view.
Restates the verse so it need only say have intercourse, with the extra phrase limiting the case.
Asks what the words and take and and take her are meant to teach.
If either sister may be chosen, each is permitted; if one is forced, both are prohibited.
Rabbi Yehuda derives that a rival wife is forbidden only where levirate marriage applies.
Asks how the Rabbis interpret the emphatic with her phrase.
Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina: a levirate wife is divorced by a bill of divorce and may be forced into levirate marriage.
Asks from where Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi derives these accepted halakhot.
Derives the wife status from and take her to him, and forced levirate from her brother-in-law will have intercourse.
Asks what Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi does with the superfluous with her phrase.
A baraita: the court and the anointed High Priest bring a sin-offering only for erroneous rulings on karet matters.

ranges.en: Restates that idolatry offerings apply only to matters liable to karet intentionally and a sin-offering unwittingly.
Cites the mishna listing which offerings individuals, Nasi, High Priest, court and community bring for sins.
Asks from where the offering rules for idolatry are derived.
Quotes the verse about the sin by which they sinned, with its aleha wording.
