Objects that Rami bar Yeḥezkel taught one does not accept converts from the Karduyin, contradicting Haggai.
Rav Ashi: the stated term is Kartuyim, which is a different group from the Karduyin.
Gives the alternate version of the baraita and questions whether Kartuyim and Karduyim are the same category.
Objects to Rabbi Yoḥanan's ruling on Tarmodim converts, citing a mishna on blood stains from Rekem.
Rabbi Yehuda deems Rekem stains impure because its residents are converts who erred, so gentile stains are pure.

16b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A tanna teaches that stains from gentiles are pure, even those from Tarmod, implying no concern in gentile-populated places.
Rabbi Yohanan draws the inference that converts from Tarmod are accepted without concern for mamzer status.
A proposed resolution: perhaps Rabbi Yohanan only meant this as a logical inference and did not personally hold it.
Objection: Rabbi Yohanan himself ruled that halakha follows an anonymous mishna, so this inference should bind him.
Reply: the amoraim disagree, and the opposing rulings about Tarmod are each attributed to Rabbi Yohanan.
Why do the Sages reject converts from Tarmod, and what is the reason behind their disagreement on this?
Two explanations are given: the servants of Solomon who intermarried, or the daughters of Jerusalem taken captive.
Explaining the Solomon-servants view: a gentile or slave who has relations with a Jewish woman produces a mamzer child.
On the daughters-of-Jerusalem view, what is the reason the concern applies to Tarmod and not to other cities?
Rav Yosef and the Rabbis disagree on this point, and both opinions are cited in the name of Rabba bar bar Hana.
One version holds that twelve thousand men and six thousand archers came from Tarmod.
The other version holds that there were twelve thousand men, of whom six thousand were archers.
During the sack of the Temple, the gentiles seized the gold and silver while the Tarmod soldiers pursued Jewish women.
Proof from Lamentations 5:11 about women violated in Zion and maidens in the cities of Judah.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nahmani reports Rabbi Yonatan's teaching that the verse in Psalms was spoken by the ministering angel.
Psalms 37:25 is cited: I have been young and now am old, yet I have not seen the righteous forsaken.
Who said this verse? If God said it, can God speak of old age before Himself?
If David said it about himself, the objection is that David was not old enough to make such a statement.
Conclusion: the ministering angel appointed over the world said the verse, since he speaks of both youth and age.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nahmani further reports Rabbi Yonatan's explanation of a verse in Lamentations.
What is the meaning of the verse written in Lamentations about the adversary spreading his hand over her treasures?
Lamentations 1:10 is quoted: the adversary spread his hand over all her treasured things.
This verse refers to Ammon and Moab, who acted during the sack of the Temple.
Narrative: the gentiles seized gold and silver, while the Ammonite and Moabite soldiers went after the Torah scrolls.
The soldiers spoke, identifying a particular scroll as the one containing a prohibition against Ammonites and Moabites.
Deuteronomy 23:4 is cited: an Ammonite or Moabite shall not enter the assembly of the Lord.
The soldiers declared that the scroll should be burned by fire.
Lamentations 1:17 is cited: the Lord commanded that Jacob's neighbors should be his adversaries.
Rav illustrates the verse with Homanya and Pum Nahara, where Ammonite descendants harass the Jews of Pum Nahara.
Rav Yehuda, in the name of Rav Asi, holds that a gentile's betrothal nowadays may be valid, out of concern for lost tribes.
Objection: the principle that a separated item is presumed to come from the majority undermines that concern.
Reply: the concern applies only to those from the dwelling places of the ten tribes, as Rabbi Abba bar Kahana taught.
II Kings 18:11 is cited about the exiles from Samaria placed in Halah, Habor, and the cities of the Medes.
Glosses identify the places named in the verse, such as Halah being the place called Halzon.

17a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Glosses identify the rivers and cities of the Medes and their surroundings, including an alternative identification of the region.
Who said the list of surrounding towns of Hamadan?
Shmuel names Kerakh, Mushkhei, Hidkei, and Domakya as the surroundings of Hamadan.
Rabbi Yohanan rules that all of these places are disqualified because their residents may be of mixed lineage.
Rav Yehuda reports Shmuel's ruling that a son from a Jewish woman counts as the father's son, while a son from a gentile woman does not.
Are there not Jewish girls captured by gentiles whose children are considered Jews?
Ravina infers from a similar case that the son of your daughter by a gentile is also called your son.
Reply: it is a received tradition that the captured Jewish girls of that generation were barren and bore no children.
An alternative report of Shmuel's ruling: the exiles of the ten tribes became fully gentile and never returned.
Hosea 5:7 is cited: they have dealt treacherously against the Lord and begotten strange children.
Rav Yosef, Rav Kahana, and Rav Yehuda transmit the tradition that Israel will establish a festival when Tarmod is destroyed.
But Tarmod has already been destroyed, so how can the festival be awaited?
Reply: the city that was destroyed was Tamud, not Tarmod.
Rav Ashi holds that Tarmod and Tamud are the same city, which is repeatedly destroyed and resettled.
Explanation: the city is doubled, so when it is destroyed on one side it is rebuilt on the other, and it is never fully destroyed.
Narrative: Rav Hamnuna studies halakha before Ulla.
Ulla praises Rav Hamnuna, but notes that Harpanya is his city and its residents have flawed lineage, so Rav Hamnuna is embarrassed.
Ulla asks where Rav Hamnuna pays his poll tax.
Rav Hamnuna replies that he pays it to Pum Nahara, which is the city that taxes his place.
Ulla concludes that Rav Hamnuna is from Pum Nahara, not Harpanya, so his lineage is unflawed.
What is the meaning of the name Harpanya?
Rabbi Zeira explains that Harpanya is the mountain toward which everyone turns, since many without known family gather there.
A baraita teaches that anyone who does not know his family or tribe turns to that place.
Rava says that this flaw is deeper than the netherworld.
Hosea 13:14 is cited to show that one can be redeemed from the netherworld but their disqualification cannot be rectified.
The disqualification of those people has no remedy.
The disqualification of Harpanya traces back to Meishon, Meishon to Tarmod, and Tarmod to the servants of Solomon.
A folk saying describes an inaccurate measure rolling from the netherworld to Tarmod and onward to Harpanya, followed by the end of the chapter.
Mishna opening: the case of a brother's wife where the brother did not coexist with the deceased is explained.
Example: two brothers die, a third brother is born afterward, and the second brother takes the first brother's widow in levirate marriage.
Ruling: the first widow goes out without levirate obligation because her brother-in-law did not coexist, and the second widow performs halitza only.
Rav Naḥman says that the version reading first widow and the version reading second widow are both correct, since both may refer to the same woman.

17b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Naḥman's continuation: the version reading first widow is not mistaken.
What is the meaning of first in the mishna?
First means the first to fall to her yavam for levirate marriage.
The version reading second widow is likewise not mistaken.
The reading of second widow is not mistaken.
What is the meaning of second?
Second means the second to enter marriage, since the deceased brother had already married once.
Are we not dealing with a yavam who married after levirate marriage, so the wife was taken second?
Rather, what is the meaning of second?
Second refers to the wife who had married a second time, in contrast with the other who married once.
Where is it written that levirate marriage does not apply to the wife of a brother with whom one did not coexist?
Rav Yehuda reports Rav's statement that the verse itself contains the exclusion.
Deuteronomy 25:5 is expounded: dwelling together excludes such a wife, and together in inheritance excludes a maternal half brother.
Rabba derives that brotherhood means brothers from the same father by analogy to the sons of Jacob.
The analogy: just as the sons of Jacob were brothers through the father and not the mother, so too in levirate marriage.
Objection: derive brotherhood from the forbidden-relations verses, where maternal brothers count; and what difference does this make?
The school of Rabbi Yishmael uses a verbal analogy between veshav and uva in the leprosy laws to show a minor difference does not block analogy.
Reply: this applies only when nothing more similar exists, but where a more similar word exists we learn from it.
Objection: derive brotherhood from Lot, where Abraham says we are brothers.
Genesis 13:8 is cited: for we are brothers, showing relatives may be called brothers.
Reply: learning from the sons of Jacob is preferable, since Scripture could have written they were children of one father but wrote brothers, rendering the word free.
Both words are needed: brothers and together, since each alone would allow a different inference from Lot or from Jacob.
Had the Torah written together alone, one might require both the same father and mother, so brothers is also written.
But from where would one derive maternal brotherhood, when levirate marriage depends on inheritance from the father?
Rav Huna reports Rav's ruling that the yavam may marry the mother of a yevama who died before levirate marriage, implying the bond is not substantial.
Then why not conclude the halakha follows the opinion that the levirate bond is not substantial?
Reply: that ruling applies only to two brothers, but with a single brother the bond is substantial.
Then why not state the halakha follows that opinion even in the case of a single brother?
Reply: the ruling would then allow marrying the mother of a living yevama, which is forbidden because one may not nullify the mitzva of levirate marriage.
Objection from a mishna: if a yevama dies, one may marry her sister, but not her mother.
Reply: no proof, since the mishna's second clause is loosely worded, and the mother is also permitted after the death.
Rav Yehuda rules that one may not marry the mother of a yevama who died while awaiting levirate marriage, implying the bond is substantial.
Then why not state the halakha follows the opinion that the levirate bond is substantial?
Reply: that would apply to a single brother only, since with two brothers the bond is not substantial.
Objection: the tanna'im disagree in the case of two brothers, so Rav Yehuda cannot be speaking only of a single brother.
Rather, if he had said the conclusive halakha is that the bond is substantial, then what?

18a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The levirate bond is not terminated by death without an actual act such as halitza or levirate marriage.
Proposed support for Rav Yehuda from a baraita: a yevama who died leaves her sister permitted, but not her mother.
Rejection: the mother is also permitted, and the baraita's wording was precise only because the first clause is about the sister.
Rav Huna bar Ḥiyya objects from a mishna: the second widow requires halitza only if levirate betrothal was performed, which would be pointless if the bond were substantial.
Rabba corrects the reading, and the mishna's wording excludes Beit Shammai, who hold levirate betrothal is a full acquisition.
Abaye objects from a baraita about brothers where the second brother's betrothal creates a rival wife under a substantial bond.
The baraita follows Rabbi Meir, who holds that the levirate bond is not substantial.
Does Rabbi Meir indeed hold that the levirate bond is not substantial, given that unattributed mishnayot follow him?
A mishna is cited: with four brothers and two married sisters, the widowed sisters perform halitza and may not enter levirate marriage.
If Rabbi Meir held the bond is not substantial, these sisters came from different houses and should be allotted separately.
Reply: Rabbi Meir holds the bond is not substantial, but forbids nullifying the mitzva, since one brother's death could nullify it.
If the bond is not substantial then the mitzva could be nullified, which Rabban Gamliel expressly permits.
A mishna is cited: Rabban Gamliel rules that a minor refusing or waiting until adulthood resolves the sister question.
Rabba asks whether Abaye means to raise a contradiction between Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Meir.
Abaye rejects this: each tanna's concern about nullifying the mitzva differs depending on certainty and uncertainty, and the views need reconciling.
Abaye tells Rav Yosef that Rav Yehuda's ruling derives from Shmuel, and cites a mishna as evidence.

18b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira says the brother who betrothed the sister must wait until the yavam performs ḥalitza or levirate marriage, and Shmuel rules accordingly.
Rav Yosef asks what the difficulty would be if this were Rav's opinion.
Abaye replies that it is difficult, because it contradicts another statement of Rav reported by Rav Huna.
Rav Yosef suggests the two reports of Rav may be amoraic disagreements about his opinion.
Reply: since Shmuel's view is stated explicitly, we will not reinterpret it as an amoraic dispute about Rav's view.
Rav Kahana reports the teaching before Rav Zevid, and the explicit statement of Rav Yehuda in Shmuel's name that the levirate bond is substantial.
Explanation: Shmuel follows Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira, and both teachings are needed to show the bond applies to two yevamin and persists after death.

Mishna: the second brother's levirate marriage with a wife of a brother with whom the third brother coexisted; Rabbi Shimon allows choice. Rav Oshaya says Rabbi Shimon disagreed even in the first mishna.
From where is it derived that Rabbi Shimon disagreed in the first mishna, and to whose opinion is that mishna attributed?
Reasoning: the first mishna is needed for Rabbi Shimon's view, while the second conveys the Rabbis' stringency, and the mishna's author delayed noting the disagreement.
But according to Rabbi Shimon, how can the case of a wife of a brother with whom he did not coexist arise?
Reply: it arises with a single brother who died and was followed by a newborn brother, or with two brothers where the bond survives.
Why does Rabbi Shimon permit the woman when the third brother was born after the second brother's levirate marriage was already completed?
Reply: Rabbi Shimon holds the levirate bond is substantial and creates kinship, so the bonded woman is like a married woman.
Rav Yosef objects: if Rabbi Shimon is uncertain whether levirate betrothal plus bond makes her like a married woman, the bond alone cannot do so.
What is the proof that this is Rabbi Shimon's opinion?
A mishna on three brothers and three women is cited, with Deuteronomy 25:5, to show that the woman bonded to two yevamin requires halitza.
Rabbi Shimon says the third brother may take either woman in levirate marriage and perform halitza with the other, since perhaps the bond is substantial.

19a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Only one widow from each household may be taken, and taking one while exempting the other would imply Rabbi Shimon is uncertain whether the bond is substantial.
Rejecting that hypothesis: the rabbinic-decree reading is wrong, since Rabbi Shimon's reason is stated in the baraita as a matter of the bond's strength.
A baraita quotes Rabbi Shimon's argument: if the second brother's betrothal counts as marriage, the third brother would be with the second brother's wife.
Abaye objects that the proof does not show Rabbi Shimon's view, since he may hold the bond is substantial only with one yavam, not two.
A baraita quotes Rabbi Shimon's principle: when the third brother is born before the levirate marriage, she is a wife of a brother with whom he did not coexist.
Objection: perhaps that baraita refers only to a single yavam, where she would be forbidden as a non-coexisting brother's wife.
If the baraita addressed the single-yavam case, why does Rabbi Shimon not simply specify the case of two yevamin?
Reply: the entire baraita concerns two yevamin, distinguishing cases of birth before or after the marriage.
Rather, what is the governing principle in this matter?
Rav Oshaya objects from a mishna about two women bound to one yavam, where Rabbi Shimon exempts them, which would be impossible if the bond were substantial.
Rav Amram explains that only the second woman is exempt.
Objection: a baraita states that Rabbi Shimon exempts both women.
Rava explains that the baraita refers to three brothers, with the pairs of relatives among the women.
The Gemara rejects Rava's reading as mistaken, citing the mishna's use of or and the baraita's wording about all four.
Leviticus 18:18 is cited to show Rabbi Shimon exempts both women, so Rava's explanation is rejected.
Rav Ashi's reply: the women fall at once because both brothers die together, and Rabbi Shimon follows Rabbi Yosei HaGelili that exact timing is possible.
Rav Pappa holds that Rabbi Shimon disagrees only when the second brother performed levirate marriage before the third brother's birth.
Rav Pappa's view explains the earlier difficulty about redundancy: the mishna uses the style of teaching not only this but also that.
A baraita in accordance with Rav Pappa refutes Rav Oshaya: the first widow is exempt as a non-coexisting brother's wife, and the second needs halitza or levirate marriage.

19b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A baraita records Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon: the two women are exempt from halitza and levirate marriage, but Rabbi Shimon lets the third brother choose between them.
To whom is the latter clause of the baraita attributed? It cannot be Rabbi Meir, since he makes no distinction between birth before or after the marriage.
The latter clause must reflect Rabbi Shimon's opinion, which disagrees only when the marriage precedes the birth, as Rav Pappa explained.
The Master taught the baraita: the second brother was about to perform levirate betrothal but did not manage to before the third brother was born.
What is the meaning of was about to and did not manage in the baraita, given that the actual act is what counts?
The words refer to consent: the betrothal was with her consent, or against her will, which follows Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's dispute with the Rabbis.
What is the reason for Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's view?
He derives levirate betrothal from intercourse with a yevama, which needs no consent, while the Rabbis derive it from ordinary betrothal, which needs consent.
With regard to what principle do Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and the Rabbis disagree?
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi infers yevama matters from yevama matters, while the Rabbis infer levirate betrothal from general betrothal law.
The baraita's other case: the second brother performed levirate betrothal, a brother was born, and Rabbi Shimon says intercourse or halitza with one exempts her rival.
To which case does Rabbi Shimon's statement refer, given that he was not disputed where the marriage followed the birth?
If the third brother performs halitza with the widow of the first brother, the rival is not exempt, since the obligation of the betrothed widow is uncertain and certainty must be addressed first.
Rav Menashe bar Zevid sits before Rav Huna and raises the reason for Rabbi Shimon's position.
What is the reason for Rabbi Shimon's position?
He permits the third brother's levirate marriage since she was never prohibited to him, having been in a permitted state when he was born.
Rather, what is the reason for the Rabbis' opinion?
Deuteronomy 25:5 is cited: the first levirate bond still attaches to her after she is taken as a wife by the second brother.
Objection from a mishna: once a yavam takes his yevama as a wife she is his wife in every respect, which seems to contradict that reading.

20a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Gemara asks why the case of a divorced yevama should not also require halitza, given the first levirate bond continues to attach to her.
Reply: the case differs because the verse makes her a wife once taken, but the verse of veyibbema shows the bond continues for later-born brothers.
What led you to distinguish the two cases in this way?
It stands to reason that the permitted status is absolute, while the prohibition on a non-coexisting brother's wife continues for later-born brothers.
Objection to Rabbi Shimon: why should a maternal half-sister not likewise be permitted to a later-born half brother, given that she was in a permitted state?
Reply: the prohibition on a sister has no permitted case, while the prohibition on a brother's wife does, so it is canceled by levirate marriage.
Mishna: a yevama forbidden for forbidden relations is fully exempt; a yevama forbidden by a mitzva or by sanctity performs halitza. Two sisters case and the categories are explained.
What did the mishna add, since the list of forbidden relations was already given in the first chapter?
Rafram bar Pappa says it includes the rival wife of an aylonit, following the view of Rav Asi.
Others say Rafram's statement was made in another context, excluding the rival wife of an aylonit, contrary to Rav Asi.
Whose sister is meant by the mishna's sister who is her yevama, and does it refer to a forbidden relation?
The mishna's categories of prohibitions resulting from a mitzva and from sanctity are restated.
Why is a prohibition from a mitzva called that?
Abaye says because it is a mitzva to obey the words of the Sages.
Mishna: a prohibition stemming from sanctity covers a widow to a High Priest, and a divorcée or halutza to a common priest.
Leviticus 21:6 is cited: the priests shall be holy to their God, which explains why these are called prohibitions of sanctity.
A baraita: Rabbi Yehuda switches the terms, calling the widow-to-High-Priest case a prohibition of a mitzva.
Leviticus 27:34 is cited: these are the mitzvot the Lord commanded Moses, explaining why the term is a mitzva.
A prohibition of sanctity refers to secondary relationships forbidden by rabbinic law.
Why is that called a prohibition of sanctity?
Abaye says whoever fulfills the words of the Sages is called sacred.
Rava objects: then one who does not fulfill them would not be called wicked, which is untrue.
Rava explains that sanctity means separation, so one must sanctify oneself by refraining from what the Torah permits, and the Sages decreed against secondary relations.
Mishna: a widow may not enter levirate marriage with a High Priest, whether a widow from marriage or from betrothal alone.
Granted for a widow from marriage, but for a widow from betrothal, why does the positive mitzva of levirate marriage not override the prohibition?
Rav Giddel, citing Rav, explains the word his yevama in Deuteronomy 25:7 teaches that some yevamot go to halitza but not levirate marriage.
Is this referring to women liable for karet, who also may not enter levirate marriage?
Reply: the verse states if the man does not wish, which implies levirate marriage depends on his choice, so karet cases require no halitza.
If so, why should those liable for ordinary prohibitions not also be exempt from halitza?

20b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Gemara resolves the question: betrothal takes effect with forbidden women who incur a prohibition violation but not with those liable to karet.
Rava objects to Rav with a baraita: if women liable for prohibitions needed only halitza, the rival wife would not be exempt after intercourse.
Rava resolves the objection by reading the baraita disjunctively: one case is intercourse from a mitzva, the other is halitza from sanctity.
Rava objects from a Tosefta on infertile men whose brothers' levirate acts take effect, implying the prohibition does not block validity.
The prohibition on maintaining such unions rests on the verse in Deuteronomy barring the crushed or severed from the assembly.
If prohibited women needed only halitza, why would intercourse acquire them, since no levirate mitzva would apply?
Rava offers an alternative: a priest's betrothed widow is excluded because that union breaks a positive and a negative commandment together.
Leviticus says the priests shall be holy, which teaches that priestly prohibitions carry an added positive mitzva of sanctity.
What is the explanation for mamzerot and Gibeonites, who are also barred from the congregation for reasons of sanctity?
All commandments carry a positive mitzva of sanctity, derived from the verse in Leviticus 11 commanding holiness.
If so, every prohibition in the Torah would also contain a positive mitzva, an untenable consequence.
Rava gives a new reason: a rabbinic decree bars a betrothed widow from the High Priest, because of the case of a married widow.
Why would a rabbinic decree apply to a mamzeret or Gibeonite, where no such decree seems to have any basis?
The decree forbids intercourse with a mamzeret even where levirate applies, lest people think she is permitted where levirate does not apply.
If so, the wife of a paternal brother should be barred by decree due to the wife of a maternal brother, who is always prohibited?
The Torah made levirate depend on inheritance, which is known to all to be patrilineal, so no confusion arises.
Likewise a childless woman should be barred by decree due to a woman who has children, by the same logic.
The Torah made levirate depend on the presence of children, which is well known, so no confusion arises.
Similarly, the wife of a brother who lived with him should be barred due to the wife of a brother who did not live with him.
The Torah made levirate depend on brothers dwelling together, which is explicit in Scripture and well known to all.
No woman should enter levirate, so all women should be barred by decree due to the case of an aylonit who cannot bear children.
The aylonit case is not common, and the Sages did not decree on matters that are not common.
Mamzerot and Gibeonites are also uncommon, so why would the same reasoning not apply to them?
Rava proposes the first act is prohibited by decree lest a second act of intercourse follow once the mitzva was already fulfilled.
A baraita teaches that the first intercourse acquires her, but it is prohibited to retain her for a second act.
Rava retracts his explanation as not correct, rejecting his own earlier rationale (some attribute the retraction to Rav Ashi).
Reish Lakish's principle: when a positive and a negative commandment conflict, one should fulfill both if possible, otherwise the positive overrides.
Here too it is possible to fulfill both by halitza, so the positive mitzva does not override the prohibition.
A baraita says the yevama is acquired by intercourse even when halitza was possible, which refutes Rava's final explanation.
Regarding a High Priest's intercourse with a widow who is his yevama, Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar disagreed.
One Amora held that such intercourse does not exempt the rival wife, since the act was prohibited.
The other Amora held that such intercourse does exempt the rival wife, since it is a valid levirate enactment.

21a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: All agree a widow from marriage does not exempt her rival wife, since the positive mitzva does not override the prohibition here.
The disagreement concerns a widow from betrothal; one view holds the positive mitzva of levirate marriage overrides the prohibition.
The other view holds a positive mitzva does not override the prohibition, since halitza is possible and fulfills the mitzva.
The Gemara objects from the baraita: intercourse acquires the yevama even when forbidden, so the rival wife should be exempt, refuting that view.
Shall we say this also refutes Reish Lakish's principle?
Reish Lakish could reply that his principle applies only when the mitzva is properly fulfilled, and halitza in place of levirate is not a proper fulfillment.
Rava asks where in the Torah the prohibition of secondary forbidden relations is hinted.
Leviticus 18:27 says these abominations the people of the land did; the word these implies harshness, so softer transgressions must exist.
Rava explains the inference: there are lesser, soft transgressions, and these are the secondary forbidden relations.
From where does the inference that the word ha-el means harsh derive?
Ezekiel 17:13 uses the word eilei for mighty, showing that the similar word ha-el also connotes harshness.
Does this statement contradict the view of Rabbi Levi?
Rabbi Levi taught that the punishment for dishonest measures is harsher than the punishment for forbidden relations.
Deuteronomy uses el regarding forbidden relations and eleh regarding dishonest measures, indicating the latter is harsher.
El connotes harshness, but eleh is harsher than el, so there is no contradiction.
Eleh is also written regarding forbidden relations, so why is deception in measures considered harsher?
In the forbidden relations verse, eleh serves to exclude one who deceives in measures from karet, not to indicate severity.
In what respect is deception in measures more severe than forbidden relations?
Forbidden relations can be rectified through repentance, but deceiving many customers cannot be fully repaired since they cannot be tracked down.
Rav Yehuda says the prohibition of secondary forbidden relations is learned from Solomon's work in arranging proverbs.
Ecclesiastes 12:9 describes Solomon weighing and setting in order many proverbs, which supports that derivation.
Ulla cites Rabbi Elazar's analogy: before Solomon the Torah was like a basket without handles, and Solomon gave it handles for understanding.
Rabbi Oshaya says the prohibition of secondary forbidden relations is learned from here.
Proverbs 4:15 says avoid it, do not pass by it, turn away and pass on, meaning one must distance oneself from prohibited acts.
Rav Ashi's parable: guarding an orchard from outside protects all of it, while guarding from inside protects only what lies in front.
The parable is called inaccurate: in the orchard the front is protected, but without the decree one would eventually transgress the biblical prohibition itself.
Rav Kahana says the prohibition is alluded to from the verse concluding the forbidden relations passage.
Leviticus 18:30 says to guard my charge, which Rav Kahana reads as establishing a safeguard for My prized possession.
Abaye asks Rav Yosef: if learned from here it would be Torah law, yet the prohibition is rabbinic.
Rav Yosef replies that the requirement to add a safeguard is itself Torah law, and the Sages defined where and when it applies.
Abaye objects: the Sages interpret all of the Torah too, yet those laws have Torah force, so this answer does not resolve the issue.
Rather, the prohibition is rabbinic, and the verse is merely a support and does not indicate a Torah law.
A baraita lists secondary forbidden relations: grandmothers, grandfathers' wives, wives of half-brothers on either side, and daughters-in-law of sons and daughters.
A man may marry his father-in-law's former wife and his stepson's former wife, but not his stepdaughter; a stepson may marry his stepfather's wife or daughter.
Example: a stepson's wife tells the stepfather she is permitted to him, but her daughter is forbidden to him as his stepdaughter.
The Gemara challenges: the stepson's daughter is forbidden by Torah law, so she should not be listed as a rabbinic secondary relation.
Leviticus 18:17 forbids a woman's son's daughter and daughter's daughter, showing the stepson's daughter is biblically forbidden.
The baraita included her in the first clause only because it wanted to teach the latter clause about the stepson's wife.
The latter clause: the stepson's wife says she is permitted to him, but her daughter is forbidden to him.
Although the daughter is biblically forbidden, the Sages did not decree against the mother, so the first clause also includes the stepdaughter.
If so, the baraita should also have taught the father-in-law's wife, whose daughter is forbidden to him as his wife's sister.
The stepson's wife's case is conclusive, but the father-in-law's case is not final, since if his wife dies her sister becomes permitted.
Rav received a tradition that four women have a conclusion; he knew three: the wife of his mother's paternal half-brother, the wife of his father's maternal half-brother, and his daughter-in-law.
Ze'eiri adds a fourth: the wife of his mother's father.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak gives a mnemonic: Ze'eiri's list is Rav's list with one additional generation, the wife of the mother's father.
Why did Rav not count the category added by Ze'eiri among those that have a conclusion?
It might be confused with the wife of the father's father, which has no conclusion, since the prohibition applies to all paternal ancestors' wives.
And why is Ze'eiri not concerned that the two categories will be confused?
Ze'eiri often goes to his father's home and knows its prohibitions, while he rarely visits his mother's household, so no confusion arises.

21b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Is this not forbidden by Torah law, as the verse says? The Gemara asks this about the daughter-in-law.
Leviticus 18:15 forbids uncovering the nakedness of your daughter-in-law, which is the Torah basis raised here.
The Gemara emends the text to say the son's daughter-in-law, resolving the apparent Torah prohibition on the daughter-in-law.
Does the prohibition against a son's daughter-in-law really have a conclusion?
A baraita states the daughter-in-law is Torah-forbidden, the son's daughter-in-law is secondary, and the prohibition extends through all generations.
Rather, say the daughter's daughter-in-law, which is the case that has a conclusion.
Rav Ḥisda introduces a teaching he heard from Rabbi Ami.
Rav Ḥisda heard from Rabbi Ami that a daughter-in-law was prohibited only because of another daughter-in-law, but he did not grasp the meaning.
Rav Ḥisda reflects that he would either reason it out himself or ask the Sages who come to the synagogue.
Rav Ḥisda now understands Rabbi Ami: his daughter's daughter-in-law was prohibited only to avoid confusion with his son's daughter-in-law.
Abaye offers Rava an illustration of how confusion could arise: the daughters-in-law in the house of bar Tzitai.
Rav Pappa gives an example: the daughter-in-law of the house of Rav Pappa bar Abba.
Rav Ashi gives an example: the daughter-in-law of the house of Mari bar Isak.
The dilemma: is the wife of a mother's maternal half-brother subject to a rabbinic decree, as cases with a paternal aspect are, or not?
Rav Safra answers that she is herself a decree, and the Sages would not issue a decree to guard against violating a decree.
Rava rejects this: all of these secondary prohibitions are decrees to prevent violation of decrees, so the reasoning cannot be dismissed.
Rava gives examples: the mother's mother and the father's mother were decreed due to the house of the grandmother.
Similarly, the father's father's wife and the mother's father's wife were decreed due to the house of the grandfather.
Likewise the wife of a father's paternal half-brother and the wife of a father's maternal half-brother were decreed due to the house of the uncle.
The Gemara asks the reason and offers a source: come and hear a statement of Rav Yehuda bar Sheila.
Rav Yehuda bar Sheila states the principle from the West: for every female relative forbidden by Torah law, the wife of the equivalent male is decreed.
Rava challenges this principle with counterexamples where a female relative is forbidden but the wife of the corresponding male relative is permitted.
The Gemara asks what Rav Yehuda bar Sheila's principle came to include, if it is not universal.
The Gemara restates the principle as including the wife of the mother's maternal half-brother, since the decree applies to her by similarity.
What distinguishes the permitted cases from this prohibited case of the wife of the mother's maternal half-brother?
This case is linked by a single betrothal, while the permitted cases are linked only through two betrothals.
Rav Mesharshiyya asks about the wife of a father's father's paternal brother and the sister of the father's father, and whether generations above are decreed.
A baraita lists secondary relations without these women, which suggests they are permitted.
The Gemara replies that the baraita's list is not exhaustive: the tanna omitted some cases.
What else did the tanna omit, since an exhaustive list cannot omit only one case?
The tanna omitted the list enumerated by the school of Rabbi Ḥiyya.
Ameimar permitted the wife of the father's father's paternal brother and the sister of the father's father.
Rav Hillel challenges Ameimar, saying he personally saw a list written by Mar son of Rabbana.
That list counted sixteen forbidden women, which Rav Hillel reports from Mar son of Rabbana's written list.
The eight from the baraita, six from Rabbi Ḥiyya's school, and these two total sixteen, which Rav Hillel uses against Ameimar.
Rav Ashi defends Ameimar: by Rav Hillel's reckoning there would be seventeen, but the difficulty is not real.

22a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The two cases, the wife of a father's father's brother and the sister of a father's father, are similar and are counted as one, giving sixteen.
Rav Hillel restates his challenge: I myself saw them written as prohibited, so they should be counted as forbidden.
Rav Ashi replies: a list that permits them would not be relied on without the signature of Mar son of Rabbana, and the same holds for one that prohibits them.
A teaching from the school of Rabbi Ḥiyya lists the third generation from one's children and wife's children, and the fourth generation from in-laws.
Ravina asks Rav Ashi why the wife is counted for the generations above but not for those below.
Above, the prohibition stems from the wife, so she is counted; below, the descendants are blood relatives, so she is not counted.
The Gemara objects: the granddaughter of the wife's son and daughter is listed as forbidden due to the wife, yet the wife is not counted there.
The teacher had already counted three generations below himself, and for uniform style he described the wife's descendants the same way.
Rav Ashi asks Rav Kahana whether the secondary relations taught by Rabbi Ḥiyya's school have a conclusion, or extend to all generations above and below.
Come and hear: Rav said four women have a conclusion, which implies these four alone.
The Gemara rejects this: perhaps Rav spoke only of the relations listed in that baraita, not of all secondary relations.
Come and hear from the baraita: the third and fourth generations are forbidden, which implies that no further generations are.
The Gemara rejects this: perhaps the baraita means from the third onward and from the fourth onward, so the question is unresolved.
Rava asks Rav Naḥman whether Western sages held that decrees on secondary relations apply to converts, or do not.
Rav Naḥman says the Sages would not extend the decree to converts, since a convert is like a newborn and the decree protects Torah prohibitions that do not apply to them.
Rav Naḥman rules that maternal half-brothers who both convert may not testify together, but if they do, their testimony is valid.
Ameimar holds that even maternal half-brothers who both convert may testify together ab initio.
What is different from forbidden relations, where converts are restricted by rabbinic decree?
Forbidden relations are known to all and individuals choose their own wives, so a decree was needed; testimony goes to the court, which can distinguish born Jews from converts.
Mishna: a brother of any kind creates a levirate bond, except a brother born from a Canaanite maidservant or a gentile woman.
Mishna: a son of any kind exempts his father's wife from levirate and is liable for striking or cursing his father, except a son from a maidservant or gentile woman.
The Gemara asks what additional case the phrase brother of any kind is meant to add.
Rav Yehuda says it adds a mamzer, who is considered a brother for levirate purposes.
The Gemara objects: is that not obvious, since he is his brother?
It is needed lest one derive from the brothers of Jacob that only unflawed brothers obligate levirate; the verbal analogy is rejected by teaching that a mamzer is a brother.
The Gemara asks: say a mamzer brother does not obligate levirate, just as a mamzer son would exempt the wife from levirate.

22b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishna's claim: the husband's brother creates a levirate bond even if he is a mamzer, since he is his brother in all respects.
With regard to what halakha is it said that he is his brother in all respects?
It applies to inheritance and to a priest's obligation to defile himself for his brother at a funeral.
Isn't this obvious, since he is his brother?
One might think a priest does not defile himself for an unfit brother, as he does not for an unfit wife; the Gemara resolves the verses and distinguishes the two cases.
Say also that an unfit brother is like an unfit wife, so the same reasoning would apply?
The cases differ: an unfit wife must be divorced by Torah law, but an unfit brother remains his brother.
The mishna excludes a brother from a Canaanite maidservant or gentile woman, who do not count as brothers.
What is the reason for this halakha?
Exodus 21:4 says the wife and her children shall be her master's, so the children follow the mother's status.
Mishna: a son of any kind exempts his father's wife from levirate and is liable for striking or cursing his father, except one from a maidservant or gentile woman.
What does the phrase of any kind come to add?
Rav Yehuda says it adds a mamzer, who exempts the wife from levirate.
What is the reason that a mamzer exempts the wife?
Deuteronomy 25:5 says if a man has no child; the phrase is read as investigate him, and any child, even a mamzer, exempts.
Why is the son liable for striking or cursing his father, if the father sinned with a forbidden woman?
Exodus 22:27 forbids cursing a ruler of your people, implying the prohibition applies only to one who acts according to the deeds of your people.
Rav Pineḥas, citing Rav Pappa, says this refers to one who repents, and after repentance his son is liable for cursing him.
The Gemara objects: Shimon ben Menasya says a crooked thing cannot be made straight, so one who fathers a mamzer cannot fully repent.
At least after repentance the father acts according to the deeds of your people, so the son is liable though the repentance is not complete.
The Sages taught that one who unwittingly has relations with his sister, the daughter of his father's wife, brings two sin-offerings, one for each prohibition.
Rabbi Yosei ben Yehuda says he is liable only for the sister prohibition, not for the prohibition of the daughter of his father's wife.
What is the reason of the Rabbis, since the verses seem to make a second prohibition redundant?
Leviticus 18:9 and 18:11 both address this relation, and the Rabbis read them as establishing separate liability for each.
Why is the additional verse needed if the first already covers the case?
It concludes that he is liable separately for both the sister relation and the father's wife's daughter.
Rabbi Yosei ben Rabbi Yehuda says the verse she is your sister limits liability to the sister prohibition alone.
What do the Rabbis do with the phrase she is your sister?
It teaches that the Sages may not derive additional prohibitions by a fortiori inference beyond what the text states.
Rabbi Yosei ben Rabbi Yehuda says if the phrase was for that purpose, the verse should have said only your sister; the phrase she is limits liability.
The Rabbis say the phrase she is is needed so that one not think the Sages may derive prohibitions by a fortiori inference, and the principle applies generally.
Rabbi Yosei ben Rabbi Yehuda says if so, the phrase should be written in the other verse, about the daughter of the father, not the daughter of the father's wife.
What does Rabbi Yosei ben Rabbi Yehuda do with the verse about the daughter of the father's wife?
It teaches liability only for a half-sister whose mother could have had marital ties with the father, excluding daughters of a maidservant or gentile.
Could the verse instead exclude a half-sister born of a raped woman, so she is not considered a sister?
One cannot say that, due to the reason Rava gives.
Rava raises a contradiction: Leviticus 18:10 seems to permit a son's daughter or daughter's daughter, while another verse explicitly forbids them.
Leviticus 18:17 explicitly prohibits a woman's son's daughter and daughter's daughter.
How can these two verses be reconciled?
Verse 18:10 refers to a woman who was raped, whose daughter is permitted if not his daughter; verse 18:17 refers to a married woman, whose daughter is forbidden.

23a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Say the verse excludes women forbidden to the father, such as a mamzeret, so that a sister from such a union would not count as a sister.
Rav Pappa: betrothal takes effect with forbidden women, so the union is a marriage and she is called the wife of your father.
Deuteronomy 21:15 speaks of two wives, one beloved and one hated, which the Gemara reads as referring to marriages.
Is one wife loved by God and another hated by God?
Beloved means her marriage is permitted by halakha, and hated means it is not; both are considered married.
The Merciful One says if a man has two wives, indicating that both are considered married wives.
Say the verse excludes a forbidden union that renders both parties liable to karet, since betrothal does not take effect with them.
Rava: Leviticus 18:9 includes all daughters, even those of women forbidden to the father, and the verse calls her your sister regardless.
Say that the verse 'she is your sister' also includes a sister from a Canaanite maidservant or gentile woman.
The verse says the daughter of your father's wife, meaning one who can enter marriage with the father, which excludes a maidservant or gentile woman.
What was your reason for including the daughter of a karet-liable woman but excluding a maidservant's or gentile's daughter?
Relationships that are forbidden yet permit betrothal to other men should be included, since betrothal takes effect with them.
On the contrary, it should include a maidservant or gentile woman, since if she converts betrothal can take effect with the father himself.
When she converts she is like a different person, but as a gentile no marital relation was possible, so the verse excludes her.
And the Rabbis, who read a different meaning into the verse, from where do they exclude the sister from a maidservant or gentile?
From Exodus 21:4 about a maidservant married to a Hebrew slave: the children's lineage follows only the mother.
Why does Rabbi Yosei ben Rabbi Yehuda not derive this from the same verse?
Both cases need separate verses: a maidservant could be excluded only for lacking pedigree, while a gentile has no mitzva connection, and a maidservant does have one.
The Gemara asks: according to the Rabbis we have a source for maidservants, but from where do we derive that a gentile woman's son is excluded?
Rabbi Yoḥanan, in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai, cites Deuteronomy 7:4: your son from a gentile woman is called her son, not yours.
Ravina says the son of your daughter by a gentile father is still called your son, meaning your grandson.
Does Ravina hold that offspring of a gentile or slave with a Jewish woman has unflawed lineage?
No conclusive proof: she is not a mamzer, but she is not of unflawed lineage either; she is a Jew unfit to marry into the priesthood.
Was this verse written about the seven nations of Canaan and not about other nations?
The words he will turn away include all who would turn your grandson from God, that is, any gentile.
This works for Rabbi Shimon, who derives halakha from the rationale of the verse; but how do the Rabbis derive it without that?
The tanna who disagrees with Rabbi Yosei ben Rabbi Yehuda is Rabbi Shimon, who applies the rationale of the verse to all nations.

23b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: one who betrothed one of two sisters but does not know which must give a bill of divorce to each sister.
If the betrothing man died with one brother, that brother performs halitza with both; with two brothers, one does halitza and one may marry, and prior marriages stand.
Two unrelated men each betrothed one of two sisters without knowing which; each gives two bills of divorce, one to each woman.
If both men died and each had a brother, each brother performs halitza with both women.
If one man had one brother and the other had two, the single brother does halitza with both, and of the two, one does halitza and one may marry.
If each man had two brothers, each brother does halitza with one sister, and each may take in levirate marriage the halutza of the other man's brother.
If two brothers acted first, the other two may not both marry; one does halitza and one may marry, and marriages already made stand.
The Gemara infers from the mishna that betrothals not destined for consummation are still valid, contrary to Rava's view.
Rejection: the case is one where both sisters were first recognized and later confused, so the betrothal was valid from the start; the wording supports this.
What does the last clause of the mishna teach, since the bills of divorce case is obvious?
Restating the case: one brother performs halitza with both; with two brothers, one does halitza and the other may marry.
Specifically, halitza must come first and levirate after; levirate first would encounter the sister of his bound yevama.
The mishna then turns to the case of two men who each betrothed one of two sisters.
The Gemara again infers that such betrothals are valid, since they are not destined for consummation.
Again the case is one recognized and later confused; the wording says he does not know now, not that the matter is unknown.
What does the last clause of the second case teach, since the bills of divorce are obvious?
The last clause teaches: if one man had one brother and the other had two, the single brother does halitza with both, and one of the two does halitza while the other may marry.
Is this not obvious, identical to the first clause? Why should this case differ from the previous one?
Lest one think the Sages decreed that two brothers be treated like one; they did not, but levirate must follow the other's halitza since the woman might belong to someone else.
The mishna's other case: each man had two brothers.
Why do we need this, since it is identical to the previous halakha?
Lest one decree that levirate may occur without the other's halitza; the Sages did not issue such a decree, so one of each pair may marry.
How does this differ from the mishna about four brothers, where the married sisters perform halitza but may not undergo levirate with the remaining brothers?

24a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains the mishna by two views; here the uncertainty means each brother may have taken his own yevama, so no decree was issued.
Mishna: if they married before consulting the court, the court does not remove them from their marriage, and a baraita adds this holds even for priests.
A halutza is forbidden to a priest only by rabbinic law, akin to a divorcee, so in doubt about her status the Sages issued no decree.
Is the halutza's prohibition for priests really rabbinic, given a baraita deriving it from the verse neither shall they take a woman?
The prohibition is rabbinic, and the verse is merely a support, not the source.
Mishna: it is a mitzva for the eldest to perform levirate; if the younger brother performed it first, he acquires the yevama.
Baraita: Deuteronomy 25:6 establishes the firstborn's mitzva, excludes an aylonit, and says the levirate son is established in the dead brother's name for inheritance.
Does established in the name of his brother mean inheritance only, or that the child must be named after the dead brother?
The baraita uses a verbal analogy with Genesis 48:6, where name refers to inheritance, so the same holds here.
The baraita excludes a eunuch whose name is already blotted out; Rava says the verbal analogy takes the verse beyond its literal sense.
Without the analogy, whom does the verse address, and why say his brother rather than your brother or his father's brother?
The court is addressed: tell the yavam that the child shall be established in the name of his brother; the analogy removes the literal reading.
If the firstborn alone performs levirate, an ordinary brother may not, and if the firstborn cannot, no one may.
If only the firstborn is obligated, the separate exclusion of a brother with whom one did not coexist would be unnecessary.
Rav Aha suggests the exclusion concerns a firstborn of the mother alone; rejected, since levirate depends on inheritance, which comes from the father.
Deuteronomy 25:5 says and one of them dies, without specifying which brother.
Does the verse not cover the case of the firstborn having died, so that a younger brother then performs levirate?
Say the verse refers to a younger brother who died, so only then must the firstborn perform levirate.
The verse explicitly excludes a wife of a brother with whom one did not coexist, which can apply only to a non-firstborn.
If no firstborn exists and a younger brother consummates first, he acquires her; but if a firstborn exists, his first levirate does not acquire her.
Deuteronomy 25:5 if brothers dwell together equates the brothers' dwelling, so all brothers are equally obligated.
If the firstborn refuses, the mitzva returns to the eldest; without a firstborn, the court does not return to the eldest.
Why did Abaye the Elder teach that the mitzva returns to the eldest, implying the eldest, though not firstborn, has a greater mitzva?
The eldest takes precedence as the firstborn does: just as firstborn status gives priority, seniority gives the eldest priority.
Say that a firstborn who performs levirate inherits, while an ordinary brother who performs it does not.
The verse says the firstborn shall be established in his dead brother's name, so a younger brother performing levirate also establishes the name and earns the inheritance.
If there is no difference between firstborn and eldest, why does the Merciful One call the levirate brother the firstborn?

24b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks for what halakha the verse was written, the Gemara's opening challenge.
Explains the purpose: a successor takes only property already in hand, like a firstborn, not property owed.
Mishnah: a man suspected with a maidservant or convert may not marry her, and a married woman removed from him must be divorced even if he remarried her.
Inference from the Mishnah: a woman who converted for the suspect is still at least a convert.
Baraita contradicts this: those who converted for a woman, a king's table, or Solomon's servants are not converts, per Rabbi Nehemya.
Rabbi Nehemya's explanation: forced converts, dream converts and Esther-era converts are not converts until converting in this period.
Objects that the baraita cannot literally mean only the present time, since Mordecai and Esther's converts predate Nehemya.
Corrects the wording: the baraita means like the present time, when conversion brings no material benefit.
Cites Rav, via Rav Yitzhak bar Shmuel, that the halakha follows the view that all such converts are converts.
Asks why the suspect may not marry her even ab initio if she is a true convert.
Rav Asi's reason: a verse warns against giving substance to the earlier suspicions by marrying her.
Baraita: converts are not accepted in the Messianic era, and were not accepted in the days of David or Solomon.
Rabbi Eliezer cites Isaiah 54:15 to derive that only converts in exile, not in revealed times, are accepted.
Restates the Mishnah's case of one suspected of relations with a married woman.
Rav's ruling: the divorce requirement applies only when there were witnesses to the adultery.
Rav Sheshet rejects Rav's ruling, claiming Rav was dozing and quoting a baraita that conflicts with it.
The baraita: a suspect who married the woman after her second divorce need not divorce her again.
Asks what the baraita's circumstances are, and what difference the other man's marriage would make if witnesses existed.
Suggests the baraita implies a divorce is required even without witnesses, contradicting Rav.
Defends Rav: the same rule holds regardless of the later marriage, and the baraita only stresses the ab initio prohibition.
Objects with a baraita: with children the woman is not divorced, but witnesses of impurity require divorce even with children.
Rav reads the Mishnah as the case with children and witnesses, so divorce follows only from witnesses.
Asks why Rav forces that reading rather than the case with no children and no witnesses.
Rava: the plural they remove her refers to the court, which acts only on witnesses, not suspicion alone.
Alternative: the baraitot follow Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who requires divorce without witnesses.
Supports this with Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's cases of the peddler and the saliva, deemed distasteful enough to require divorce.

25a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi rules that reversed shoes found under the bed make the matter distasteful, so the wife must be divorced.
Challenges the case: the husband could simply check whose shoes these were.
Reframes the case: he found only reversed shoe prints under the bed he cannot identify, and Rabbi Yehuda still requires divorce.
Concludes the halakha follows Rav on witnesses and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi on distasteful matters.
Objects that the two halakhot contradict each other.
Resolves the contradiction: one ruling concerns a rumor that ceases, the other a rumor that persists.
Rules that a persistent rumor without witnesses follows Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, while a ceased rumor with witnesses follows Rav.
Asks how long a rumor must last before it counts as persistent.
Abaye's mother said a rumor in the city lasts a day and a half.
A rumor that ceased counts only if it stopped without fear, and a rumor persists when the subject has no known enemies.
Cites a Gittin mishna: a man who divorced his wife for bad reputation or a vow may not take her back, even if the cause was disproved.
Rabba bar Rav Huna asks Rabba bar Nahman whether a remarried suspect must divorce her again in such cases.
Rabba bar Nahman cites the mishna: remarrying the suspect after divorce obligates a second divorce.
Objects that the cases differ, since there the court removed her while here he divorced her voluntarily.
Rabba bar Nahman replies that his version of the mishna also reads he divorced her.
Still the cases differ: there the adulterer remarries and strengthens the rumors, while here the husband does.
Rabba bar Nahman replies that the cases are comparable, since the Sages require divorce in both.
Rejects that comparison: the suspect's remarriage confirms the rumor, whereas here the husband found the rumor baseless.
Mishna: an agent who brings a bill of divorce from overseas may not marry the divorcee, and Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes cases of a witness who killed the husband.
Explains the agent rule: the court relies on his testimony only for a bill from overseas, not from Eretz Yisrael.
Objects that a woman is exacting about a husband's death, so the witness should be permitted, yet the mishna forbids him.
Distinguishes: a death report has no document, while a bill of divorce is proven by its writing.
Restates the death-witness rule and infers that the witness himself may not marry the widow, but others may.
Cites Rav Yosef: a witness who admits a willing sexual offense is wicked and cannot testify, as Exodus 23:1 forbids.
Proposes a distinction: the Sages ruled leniently on testimony about a woman's husband's death.
Challenges the distinction by citing Rav Menashe.

25b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A robber under rabbinic law may testify that a woman's husband died, but one wicked under Torah law may not.
Asks whether Rav Menashe's ruling follows Rabbi Yehuda's opinion.
Rav Menashe could reply that he holds this even according to the Rabbis, so the ruling stands.
Supports the Rabbis' reasoning with Rava's principle that a person is a relative of himself and cannot make himself wicked.
Asks whether Rav Yosef's view also follows Rabbi Yehuda.
Rav Yosef replies he holds this even according to the Rabbis, since testimony permitting remarriage is treated leniently, and Rav Menashe follows Rabbi Yehuda.
Quotes the mishna: a witness who says I killed him or we killed him, permitting the woman to remarry.
Asks what distinguishes I killed him from we killed him.
Rav Yehuda explains: we killed him means he was merely among the murderers, not one of them.
A baraita about a bandit who confessed to killing a priest's husband, and Rabbi Yehuda's reading that he was only present, supports this.
Challenges Rabbi Yehuda's reading: the baraita says the witness was himself an armed bandit.
Replies that he was arrested on a charge of banditry.
Challenges again: the baraita says he was taken out to be executed, implying he was found guilty of murder.
Replies that a gentile court executes imprecisely, so presence in a bandit gang suffices, and Rabbi Yehuda accepts only I was with his murderers.
Mishna: a sage who forbade a woman by vow to her husband may not marry her, but a judge who sat with two others may.
Asks what the case is, and whether one judge alone could dissolve the vow.
Objects that a baraita requires three judges to dissolve vows, and that a single judge would be suspect, yet the mishna allows him to marry.
Explains the single judge was a recognized expert, since Rabbi Yohanan holds one expert may dissolve vows.
Infers from the mishna that the reason is the court of three, so with only two judges he could not marry her.
Asks why this differs from the mishna on witnesses to a field sale or divorce, where the Sages were not concerned.
Replies the mishna itself teaches that refusal must be performed before three judges, excluding the view of two.
Raises a dilemma: if one married a woman he was forbidden to marry, must he divorce her?
Gives positions: Rav Kahana says he must divorce, Rav Ashi says he need not, and a baraita follows Rav Ashi.
The Rabbis ask Rav Ashi whether his view is from tradition or from reasoning.
Rav Ashi replies that the mishna shows it: the court does not remove a woman from a suspect who remarried her.

26a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Concludes that a wife is not removed from her husband on the basis of rumor alone.
Mishna: if the wives of the judge, agent or witness die, the women they freed may marry them, and freed women may marry their sons or brothers.
Infers from the mishna that if the first wives were divorced rather than dead, the freed woman may not be married.
Rav Hillel challenges Rav Ashi with a baraita permitting marriage even after the first wives were divorced.
Resolves the conflict: the mishna covers a quarrel the man started, while the baraita covers one the wife started.
Restates the mishna that freed women may marry their rescuers once a later marriage ends.
Considers that the mishna means death after death or divorce after divorce, each validated by a single witness.
Asks whether the mishna follows Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, since a woman with two dead husbands is presumed murderous.
Restates that the freed women are permitted to the sons or brothers of those who freed them.
Asks why this differs from the Tosefta, which forbids a suspected adulterer from marrying the woman's mother, daughter and sister.
Women often stay overnight at one another's homes, creating a concern that men do not share.
