ranges.en: Abaye holds that for Beit Hillel the husband's hand is no stronger than hers, so she keeps possession and her heirs inherit.
Rava objects to Abaye: if the property came when she was under the first husband, everyone agrees his hand is stronger.
Rava offers his own resolution: the two clauses concern a widow awaiting her yavam, before or after a levirate betrothal.
Explains Rava's view: a levirate betrothal is like betrothal for nullifying a rival's bond, and like uncertain marriage for dividing property.
Notes that an interpretation attributed to Rabbi Elazar matches Rava, and one attributed to Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina matches Abaye.
Objects: did Rabbi Elazar really say that, given his statement that a betrothal acquires only for nullifying a rival's bond?
Offers two solutions: reverse the attributions, or read Rabbi Elazar's limit as applying only to divorce, leaving property acquisition intact.
Rav Pappa holds the mishna's precise wording follows Abaye, even though the case of her death is difficult for him.
Explains that the mishna's enters and leaves refers to her marriage to the first husband, consistent with Abaye, and concludes the question is unresolved.
Cites the mishna: if the yavam consummated the levirate marriage, she is his wife in every sense.
Asks what practical halakha this clause teaches.
Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina says it teaches that he may divorce her with a bill of divorce and then take her back.
Asks whether this point is not obvious.
Explains it is needed because the verse calling her a levirate wife might suggest the levirate bond survives, so only halitza would sever it.
Asks whether it is not obvious that he may take her back after divorce.
Explains it is needed because the mitzva is already fulfilled, so she might again be forbidden as a brother's wife.
Challenges: why not say she should indeed be forbidden to him?
Cites Deuteronomy 25:5, taking her as a wife, to show that once he takes her she is his wife in every respect.
Cites the mishna: her ketubah remains payable from the first husband's property, not the yavam's.
Asks what the reason for this is.
Explains that Heaven made her his wife, so he did not obligate himself, and the Sages ensured a second ketubah to deter divorce.
Mishna: the mitzva of levirate marriage belongs to the eldest brother; if he refuses, the court approaches the others, then returns to him.
Mishna: a brother who conditions his choice on a minor, an absent brother or a deaf-mute or imbecile is not heeded; the court insists on halitza or yibum.
Gemara: Rabbi Yohanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi dispute whether a minor's yibum or the eldest's halitza is preferable.
Explains each view: yibum by a minor is preferred because it is the mitzva itself, while the eldest's halitza is preferred since the minor's yibum counts for nothing in his presence.
Proves the first view from the mishna: when the eldest refuses, the others are asked to perform yibum, so a minor's yibum is preferred.
Rejects the proof: the mishna may mean the eldest refuses both halitza and yibum, so the others are approached only then.
Asks why the court should go back to the eldest if the others could be compelled instead.
Responds that the mitzva rests on the eldest ab initio, so it is he who is compelled.
Offers another proof from the mishna's ruling on a conditional brother: why not wait for a minor to mature, if his yibum were preferable?
Responds that even on the other view, waiting for an absent brother is not allowed, since no mitzva may be delayed.

39b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Some say the dispute is narrow: when yibum is possible, all agree a minor's yibum is preferred, and they differ only about a minor's halitza.
Reports the dispute between Rabbi Yohanan and Resh Lakish: one holds the eldest's halitza is preferred, the other that the two are equal.
Explains the first view: the mitzva rests on the eldest, but only for yibum, while for halitza all brothers are equal.
Proves the first view from the mishna: when the others refuse, the court returns to the eldest for halitza, so the eldest's halitza is preferred.
Rejects the proof: the others may refuse both halitza and yibum, so the court returns to the eldest only in that case.
Asks why the court should return to the eldest to compel him, rather than compelling the others.
Responds that the mitzva rests on the eldest from the start, so he is the one compelled.
Offers a second proof: a brother waiting for the eldest who is overseas is not heeded, which suggests the eldest's halitza is not preferred.
Objects: on that reasoning, the minor and overseas cases would also need waiting; the mishna shows that no mitzva may be delayed, so no proof follows.
Cites the Bekhorot mishna: yibum precedes halitza when intent is for the mitzva, but halitza precedes yibum when it is not.
Rav rules that a yavam is not compelled to perform halitza, and may choose yibum, since the verse makes it depend on his will.
Argues from Rav Yehuda's court, which enacted a halitza formula offering the yavam the choice of yibum, that he is not compelled.
Gives Rav Yehuda's formula for the bill of halitza, which allows the yavam to choose yibum before halitza is performed.
Continues the formula: the yavam extends his right foot, the yevama removes his shoe and spits before the court.
Rabbi Hiyya bar Avya adds, in Rav Yehuda's name, a closing clause that the required declarations are written in the Torah of Moses.
Explains the phrase we identified him: Rav Aha and Ravina dispute whether witnesses are needed, and the halakha is that a relative or a woman suffices.
Paraphrases the Bekhorot mishna on the order of yibum and halitza, with and without intent for the mitzva.
Rami bar Hama reports that Rabbi Yitzhak said later generations reverted to yibum taking precedence.
Rav Naham bar Yitzhak wonders whether later generations improved so as to intend yibum purely for the mitzva.
Explains that earlier generations followed Abba Shaul, while later ones followed the Rabbis, so the order changed, not their spiritual level.
Baraita: Abba Shaul holds that yibum for beauty, marriage or another motive is like forbidden relations, so the child is a mamzer.
The Rabbis hold that the verse requires yibum regardless of motive, so any such union is permitted.
Asks who the tanna is of a baraita that describes a forbidden wife becoming permitted again.
Quotes the baraita: the verse requires yibum as a mitzva, since she reverts from forbidden to permitted, and the verse prevents her full return to her original status.
Rav Yitzhak bar Avdimi identifies the tanna as Abba Shaul, and reads the baraita as requiring intent for the mitzva.
Rava says the baraita can follow the Rabbis: the yavam may choose either yibum or refusal, and the verse marks yibum as a mitzva.
Objects that this is implausible: she is bound to him by a levirate bond and cannot be released without any act.
Emends the argument: he may choose yibum or halitza, and the verse establishes yibum as a mitzva.
Suggests the first clause should be read as the sense of mitzva, citing the Leviticus 6:9 usage of mitzva for a sacrificial rite.

40a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Baraita continues the meal-offering analogy: a forbidden item reverts to permitted, and the verse makes eating it a mitzva.
On Rava's reading, the baraita means a priest is obligated to eat the offering himself, parallel to the levirate mitzva.
Proposes a rival reading: the priest may eat it or leave it, or another priest may eat it, with the same structure.
Objects with Leviticus 29:33: priests eat the offerings so owners gain atonement, so eating cannot be optional.
Resolves the reading: the verse makes it a mitzva for the officiating priest, and not another priest, to eat it.
Asks, on Rav Yitzhak bar Avdimi's view that the baraita follows Abba Shaul, what two manners of eating the first clause could mean.
Proposes two manners: eating with appetite or eating to excess when already satiated.
Objects: excessive eating is not legally eating, as Reish Lakish shows from the Yom Kippur karet exemption.
Proposes an alternative: the meal-offering may be eaten unleavened or leavened, as the baraita's two manners.
Objects with Leviticus 6:10: the offering may not be baked leavened, as Reish Lakish taught, even the priest's portion.
Proposes that the two manners are unleavened or boiled, with the verse requiring unleavened.
Asks how boiled flour is classified: if unleavened, it is valid; if not, the Torah's unleavened requirement disqualifies it.
Responds that boiled flour is unleavened yet disqualified, the verse repeating unleavened to invalidate boiled flour.
Asks what practical halakha depends on the claim that boiled flour counts as unleavened.
Says it matters for Passover: one who boiled and then baked the dough fulfills the obligation to eat bread of affliction with it.
Mishna: a yavam who performs halitza shares the estate like the brothers; if the father lives, he owns it. Rabbi Yehuda says the father inherits either way.
Asks why the mishna teaches the obvious point that halitza gives no special inheritance rights.
Explains it is needed because halitza might be thought to replace yibum, giving the halitzah brother all the property.
Asks why the mishna says he is like one of the brothers, rather than stating that he is still only one of them.
Explains the wording is needed because one might think he should be penalized for causing the loss of yibum, so he forfeits his share.
Mishna: if the father is alive, the estate belongs to the father.
Explains that the father takes precedence over all descendants of his line, so the brothers inherit nothing while he lives.
Mishna: one who performs yibum acquires his brother's property.
Asks what the reason is for this rule.
Cites Deuteronomy 25:6: he succeeds his brother by marrying the widow, so he succeeds to the property too.
Presents Rabbi Yehuda's position from the mishna: the father inherits in either case when he is alive.
Ulla and Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha rule that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda.
Gives the scriptural basis for Rabbi Yehuda: the yavam, called firstborn, like a firstborn, takes nothing during the father's life.
Asks: if the yavam is like a firstborn, why does he not take a double portion after the father dies?
Explains the verse names the brother, not the father, so the yavam has no special entitlement to the father's estate.
Asks whether, on Rabbi Yehuda's view, the yibum mitzva also applies only when the father is dead.
Rejects this: yibum is not made dependent on inheritance, so the yavam performs it in all cases and takes property only if entitled.
Rabbi Hanina Kara states in Rabbi Yannai's study hall that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda.
Rabbi Yannai rebukes him, saying the halakha is not Rabbi Yehuda and he should recite verses outside the study hall.
A tanna in Rav Nahman's presence teaches that the halakha is not in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda.
Rav Nahman replies that the halakha must then follow the Rabbis.
Asks whether this is not obvious, since the halakha follows the many against the one.
Rav Nahman rebukes the tanna for misstating the point, though his objection to the other side is well formulated.
Mishna: the yavam who performs halitza is forbidden to the wife's relatives, and she is forbidden to his relatives.

40b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: the yevama is forbidden to his close relatives, and to certain others, while the other brothers are permitted; a man may marry a rival wife's relative but not her relatives' rival wife.
Poses a dilemma: did the Sages extend the secondary forbidden relations to the halutza, or only where Torah law forbids the relative?
Proves from the mishna: it forbids the mother and mother's mother but not the mother's mother's mother, so secondary relations are not extended.
Rejects the proof: the mishna omitted it for the sake of the latter clause, but if so, why not list all of them, so the proof stands.
Second proof: she is forbidden to his father's father, which must be a rabbinic secondary relation through the halutza.
Third proof: she is forbidden to his son's son, which must be a rabbinic secondary relation through the halutza.
Rejects it: she is forbidden to the grandson because of her prior marriage to the deceased, which is Torah law, so no proof follows.
Asks: Ameimar permits marriage to the wife of a brother of one's father's father, so the mishna cannot rest on that relation.
Ameimar explains that the son's son means a grandson of the grandfather, so the mishna teaches Torah-level relations, not secondary ones.
Objects: if so, the brother and his son are already listed, so the paternal and maternal brother distinction must be the point of repetition.
Cites a baraita of Rabbi Hiyya: four relations are Torah-level and four rabbinic, including the father's father, which would show secondary relations apply.
Rejects it: the father's father is forbidden due to the prior marriage to the deceased, which is Torah law.
Further baraita proofs: the mother's father, and the son's son, are listed as rabbinic relations, and would show the same thing.
Rejects this proof as well: the son's son is forbidden due to the prior marriage, so the secondary relation is not shown.
Asks: but Ameimar permits the wife of a brother of the father's father, so why does he say the rabbinic decree applies to the son's son?
Another baraita proof: she is forbidden to his daughter's son, which would be a rabbinic secondary relation by the halutza's status.
Rejects it, saying the forbidden relation comes from the prior marriage, and challenges this with the case of secondary relations of incest.
Concludes that the Sages decreed secondary relations for the halutza, since the case shows the rabbinic decree.
Cites the mishna: a man is permitted to a relative of his halutza's rival wife.
Shmuel rules that one who has relations with a halutza's rival wife produces a mamzer, because she remains in her original prohibition.
Rav Yosef cites the same mishna as support for the permitted relation of the rival's relatives.
Objects: if the rival wife is like the halutza, why would the mishna permit the relation to the sister, the question given the decree?
Objects that this would refute Rabbi Yohanan, who held that neither the halutza nor her rival carries karet for the relations involved.
Rabbi Yohanan replies: it is not sensible that a halutza's sister is Torah-level, so the mishna's relation must be rabbinic.
Objects with Reish Lakish: Rabbi Yohanan taught the sister of a divorcee is Torah-level and of a halutza rabbinic, so why the difference?
Asks what distinguishes this case from the other, and why each differs.

41a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains the earlier distinction: a rival wife who attends court with the halutza could be mistaken for her, so she is forbidden, but the other is not.
Mishna: if a halutza's brother marries her sister and dies, the sister performs halitza but not yibum; the same applies after a divorce.
Mishna: when the yavam's brother betrothed the sister, Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira says the brother must wait until the levirate bond is resolved by halitza or yibum.
Asks what the words and similarly mean, since the two cases differ in the required act.
Emends the mishna to read however, and Reish Lakish explains the sister of a divorcee is Torah-forbidden while the sister of a halutza is rabbinic.
Restates the mishna's ruling on a yavam who betrothed the sister of his yevama.
Shmuel rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira.
Raises a dilemma: if the yavam's betrothed wife dies, may he then perform yibum with the yevama?
Rav and Rabbi Hanina hold that after the wife dies, the yavam may perform yibum with the yevama.
Shmuel and Rav Asi hold that after the wife dies, the yavam remains forbidden to the yevama.
Rava explains Rav's reasoning: the yevama reverts to her original status after the temporary prohibition ends.
Rav Hamnuna objects from a baraita: a yevama who was forbidden and then reverted should be permitted, yet the baraita forbids yibum.

Rava, silent at first, later answers that the baraita follows Rabbi Elazar, who held that a prohibition once in force is permanent, unless the yevama was eligible at the time of falling before the yavam.
Cites a baraita in which Rabbi Elazar holds that if the wife dies the yevama may not perform yibum, supporting Rava's reading.
Asks whether Shmuel and Rav Asi hold like Rabbi Elazar.
Replies that they may follow the Rabbis, who concede that a prohibition arising after the yevama fell before the yavam is permanent.
Mishna: a yevama may not perform halitza or yibum until three months have passed, and the same waiting applies to other women before betrothal or marriage.
Rabbi Yehuda holds that married women may be betrothed without waiting, except for betrothed women in Judea, due to the concern of seclusion.
Rabbi Yosei holds that all women may be betrothed within three months, except for a widow.

41b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Closes the mishna's reason for waiting: the mourning period the widow observes for her husband.
Asks why a pregnant widow may not perform halitza, since a viable child would make the levirate act a forbidden union.
Suggests the mishna refutes Rabbi Yohanan, who held that a halitza performed while pregnant is valid, from this mishna as well.
Rejects the suggestion: the mishna's concern is that a meaningless halitza would wrongly disqualify her from the priesthood.
Asks why she should not perform halitza anyway, with a public announcement if needed.
Asks, for a divorcee, what reason there is for delay, since she has no support and cannot marry during the waiting period.
Asks the same about a betrothed divorcee, who has neither sustenance nor eligibility for marriage.
Offers a reason from a baraita: Rabbi Yosei forbade halitza within three months, since a pregnant woman would be harmed.
Rabbi Yosei proves from Deuteronomy 25:7 that one eligible for yibum is eligible for halitza, and one ineligible is ineligible for halitza.
Rav Hinnana objects from a baraita that women of uncertain yevama status perform halitza but may not do yibum.
Asks what cases of uncertain yevama status are meant, and why such a woman may not perform yibum.
Explains the case: a man betrothed one of two sisters and does not know which, so the yavam may not perform yibum with either.
Rejects the proof: in the uncertain-betrothal case Elijah would resolve it, so the woman is fundamentally eligible, unlike in the three-month case.
Explains that the three-month rule applies even where pregnancy is impossible, so the yevama is fundamentally ineligible for both yibum and halitza.
Baraita: a yevama receives support from her husband's estate during the first three months; afterward she gets none, unless the yavam defied a court order.
Asks whether a yevama whose yavam is a minor receives support from the husband's estate.
Rav Aha and Ravina dispute this; the halakha is she has no right, since the husband is not responsible and Heaven penalized her.
Baraita: if the brothers performed halitza within the three months, she must still wait three months before remarrying.

42a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Baraita: if the yavam performs halitza after three months, she may remarry at once; the three months are counted from the husband's death.
Asks how this differs from a divorce, where Rav counts from delivery and Shmuel from writing of the bill.
Rava argues a fortiori that for a yevama the count runs from the husband's death, since a karet-level prohibition is already lifted after three months.
Asks why other women should wait three months, if the yevama's wait is explained by the risk of a levirate act.
Rav Nahman, citing Shmuel, explains that the waiting period distinguishes the lineage of the first husband's child from the second's, as Genesis 17:7 requires.
Rava objects from a baraita that converts also wait three months, where no question of lineage arises for them.
Explains that the converts case concerns seed sown in holiness, and offers Rava's own reason: a decree against incestuous or levirate mistakes over a child's paternity.
Rav Hananya objects that the baraita gives the three-month rule the purpose of protecting the child, not preventing forbidden relations.
Defends Rava: the offspring benefits from the rule because it prevents the child from encountering forbidden relations.
Asks why she may not wait only two months, since uncertainty about the child's age would remain.
Asks why she may not wait one month, since a child born at seven or eight months would be identifiable.
Replies that a child born at eight months could still be the second husband's, if conception came a month after remarriage.
Asks why she may not wait two and a half months, since a child born at six and a half months is not viable.
Objects that Mar Zutra's view allows a seven-month birth to be incomplete, so six and a half months is possible for the second husband.
Cites 1 Samuel 1:20: the seasons of the days indicate that Samuel was born after six months and two days.
Suggests a minimal wait, followed by an examination of her body after three months to see whether pregnancy is noticeable.
Rav Safra rejects the examination, since married women may not be checked for shame; the walk test is then suggested.
Rami bar Hama says a woman conceiving from her first husband would conceal the pregnancy in her gait, so no test is reliable; three months is required.
Asks why a pregnant or nursing woman may not remarry if pregnancy is certain; a baraita forbids it and requires divorce.
Explains the prohibition is a decree against a second pregnancy deforming the first fetus, and answers the parallel objection on contraception.
Objects that the same solutions apply to a woman pregnant with another man's child, so they do not explain the prohibition.
Suggests the reason is pressure on the fetus during intercourse, and that a husband spares his own child but not another's, which is then rejected as parallel.
Proposes the reason is that a pregnant woman is typically poised to nurse, so the pregnancy would be disrupted by the nursing.

42b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks: if a pregnant nursing woman's milk dries up, the same danger arises for a child of the husband, so why is the prohibition on the other's child only?
Explains that the husband will not fund a child that is not his, and the mother cannot easily sue the heirs, so the child is endangered.
Asks which women are virgins and which betrothed, and which non-virgins and married, since the terms seem to overlap.
Rabbi Yehuda explains the mishna states a general rule: widows and divorcees, from betrothal or marriage, both wait three months.
Rabbi Elazar reports that Rabbi Yohanan ruled the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei, allowing betrothal before three months.
Rabbi Elazar infers from Rabbi Yohanan's need to state this that an individual opinion disagrees with the mishna.
Rabbi Asi confirms from a Tosefta baraita: women certainly not pregnant, such as the barren or minor, are exempt according to Rabbi Yehuda, though Rabbi Meir requires waiting.
Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba reports that Rabbi Yohanan retracted his ruling in favor of Rabbi Yosei.
Rav Yosef challenges this: would Rabbi Yohanan retract from the baraita recording the Sages of Yavne's view?
Cites a baraita: Rabbi Yishmael heard from the Sages of Yavne that all such women must wait three months, which accords with Rabbi Yosei only if he is the halakha.
Rabbi Yirmeya raises a contradiction: Rabbi Yohanan held that an unattributed mishna ruling governs, and the mishna here is unattributed.
Rabbi Abbahu replies that this is a dispute followed by an unattributed opinion, and Rav Pappa's principle says the unattributed ruling is not necessarily the halakha.
Narrates that Rabbi Abbahu, leaning on Rabbi Nahum, taught him halakhot as they walked.
Rabbi Nahum asks a series of questions on how to decide when an unattributed mishna ruling conflicts with a dispute or a baraita, and Rabbi Abbahu answers.

43a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains that the unattributed ruling in the baraita reflects Rabbi Hiyya's acceptance of the mishna's dispute, not an independent halakha.
Rabbi Nahum objects with a mishna on a flax comb: if only two teeth remain it is a utensil, so the unattributed-ruling principle seems contradicted.
Quotes the rest of the mishna on combs for wool: which teeth remain and when a comb or a removed tooth counts as a utensil.
Rabbi Hiyya replies that the principle does not apply here, since Rabbi Yohanan and Reish Lakish both held this mishna is not authoritative.
Asks why the mishna is not authoritative, and Rav Huna bar Manoah cites an internal contradiction between its clauses about two and three teeth.
Asks whether the difficulty is real, proposing that the clauses address inner versus outer teeth, or prepared versus unprepared teeth.
Offers resolutions: base versus no base, narrow versus thick teeth, and ultimately that the mishna is the minority view of Rabbi Shimon.
Reports Rabbi Hiyya bar Avin's halakha from Eretz Yisrael that one may betroth but not marry within three months, and how the three months are counted.
Ameimar permits betrothal on the ninetieth day itself.
Rav Ashi objects that Rav and Shmuel require three full months, excluding the death day and the betrothal day.
Ameimar replies that the exclusion applies to a nursing mother, who waits twenty-four months, as Rav and Shmuel both held.
Asks about the incident in which Rava nullified a betrothal feast held on the ninetieth day, and answers that it was a marriage feast.
Summarizes the halakha: a nursing mother waits twenty-four months, and a non-nursing widow waits three months, with the exclusions noted.
Cites the mishna of Rabbi Yosei: all women may be betrothed within three months except a widow, due to mourning.
Rav Hisda objects a fortiori: if betrothal is allowed in the mourning week before Av, it should be allowed during a husband's thirty-day mourning.
Explains the mourning week before the Ninth of Av: laundering is forbidden, yet betrothal is allowed, and this is the basis of the a fortiori.
Defends Rabbi Yosei: the baraita refers to the period before that week, when betrothal is allowed, so the a fortiori base falls away.
Rava offers a stronger a fortiori: if business is forbidden yet betrothal allowed, betrothal should be allowed when business is allowed.
Concludes that Rabbi Yosei's statement must be emended: all women may marry within three months, except a widow, who may still be betrothed.

43b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether Rabbi Yosei accepts the three-month decree for distinguishing lineage, since the emendation seems to leave no case for it.
Replies that Rabbi Yosei may accept the decree and apply it to a divorced married woman, and the emendation covers women only betrothed before divorce.
Asks how this differs from Rabbi Yehuda, and answers that they dispute whether a previously married woman may be betrothed before three months.
Objects from a baraita: Rabbi Yosei permits betrothal of all women except widows, but none may marry before three months.
Asks what difficulty the baraita poses, and whether the latter clause implies betrothal is permitted while marriage is not.
Rava resolves by emending Rabbi Yosei: women only betrothed may marry within three months, except a widow, while previously married women may not be betrothed.
Asks whether a widow from betrothal must mourn at all, citing a baraita that a betrothed widow does not observe mourning.
Explains that the Ninth of Av period is disputed among tannaim, so Rabbi Yosei may hold betrothal is prohibited then, which undercuts the a fortiori.
Rav Ashi objects that the prohibition may cover only the betrothal feast; the Gemara challenges this and rejects the parallel with marriage.
Rav Ashi offers that new mourning for a relative differs from old mourning for the Temple, and public mourning from private, so no a fortiori follows.
Mishna: when four brothers married to four wives, some died childless, the eldest survivor may perform yibum with all of them.
Mishna: when a man married to two wives dies childless, yibum or halitza with one wife frees the rival from the levirate bond.

44a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: if one of the widows is fit for the priesthood and one is not, halitza is done with the unfit one and yibum with the fit one.
Asks how all four brothers could have died, since then no one would remain to perform yibum, and proposes emending the mishna.
Mishna: the eldest of the surviving brothers may choose to perform yibum with all the widows.
Asks whether the others actually leave him that choice.
Cites a baraita on Deuteronomy 25:8: the elders advise him, so if the age gap is great, he should not marry several wives, lest discord arise.
Restates the case of a man married to two women who dies childless.
Asks why he may not perform yibum with both wives.
Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba cites Rabbi Yohanan: Deuteronomy 25:9 says he may not build his brother's house, so only one house may be built.
Mar Zutra bar Toviya cites Deuteronomy 25:10: the singular house means halitza is performed with only one wife.
Deuteronomy 25:7 shows that only one eligible for yibum is eligible for halitza, so the second wife cannot be released either way.
Adds a reason: so people do not say the brother's house was partly built and partly released, and a halitza first would bar a later yibum.
Asks why the Torah's text, which speaks of one wife, would show that yibum does not apply to two.
Argues from the Torah's prohibition on a rival wife of a forbidden relation that yibum applies even when there are two wives.
Objects that the prohibition is needed to show the forbidden relation does not disregard her, so the rival is still forbidden.
Says the repeated term his yevama, his yevama, enlarges the yibum mitzva to cover multiple wives.
Rav Yosef holds that the mishna teaches not to act in a way that needlessly harms others, comparing it to not spilling water others need.
Mishna: a man who remarries a divorcee after she was married again, or who marries a halutza or her relative, must divorce her; Rabbi Akiva says the offspring is a mamzer.
Asks whether Rabbi Akiva really holds the offspring of a halutza's relative is a mamzer, since Reish Lakish holds that such a relative is forbidden only rabbinically.
Concludes the mishna should read a relative of his divorcee, since the phrase they concede makes sense only with that case.
Objects that the Rabbis concede only the karet-liable mixture; the Gemara rejects this, since the mishna later rules like Rabbi Shimon HaTimni.
Persists: perhaps the mishna records Rabbi Shimon HaTimni anonymously; the Gemara rejects this and concludes Rabbi Akiva meant that case.
Persists again: perhaps the mishna teaches the divorcee's relative only by analogy with Rabbi Akiva's other cases; the Gemara accepts this possibility.
Concludes a relative of a halutza is Torah-forbidden under Rabbi Akiva, since the verse calls her relationship a house, as Rabbi Yohanan explains.
Rav Yosef reports Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: all agree about one who remarries his divorcee.

ranges.en: The offspring, though not a mamzer, has flawed lineage and is unfit to marry into the priesthood.
Identifies who is meant by all agree: Shimon HaTimni, who holds such offspring is not a mamzer but still has flawed lineage.
Argues a fortiori from the widow of a High Priest, whose child has flawed lineage, to the child of a remarried divorcee.
Refutes the a fortiori: a widow is herself disqualified by the union, unlike a divorcee, and Leviticus calls only the woman an abomination.
Cites a baraita: Rabbi Akiva holds such a union's betrothal is void and the child unfit, while the Rabbis hold the child fit.
Asks in what sense the woman and child are unfit, whether for the congregation or the priesthood, and whether the two clauses address the same issue.
Argues by analogy that the baraita's two clauses concern different matters, as the first clause's use of unfit shows.
Asks whether the child's unfitness refers to the priesthood, and rejects it since Rabbi Akiva says the child is a mamzer.
Concludes that the child is unfit even for the congregation, and returns to the verse objection, which can be resolved differently.
Concludes that the widow objection to the a fortiori still stands, so there is no basis for flawed lineage in the divorcee's child.
Rav Yosef reports that Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi said all agree the child of a forbidden relation liable for karet has flawed lineage.
Identifies the all agree as Rabbi Yehoshua, who holds such offspring is not a mamzer but still has flawed lineage.
Repeats the a fortiori from the widow of a High Priest to the child of a karet-liable union.
Rejects the rebuttal that a widow differs: the karet-liable union also renders the woman a zona, disqualifying her from a priest.
Rabba bar bar Hana reports Rabbi Yohanan: all agree that a slave or gentile who has relations with a Jewish woman produces a mamzer.
Identifies the all agree there as Shimon HaTimni, whose view applies only to the karet-liable case.

45a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains why a gentile or slave's union differs from a forbidden relation liable to lashes: betrothal does not take effect with them, so the union is like karet.

Rav Yosef identifies the all agree as Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, citing Rav Dimi's tradition that the child of a gentile or slave is a mamzer.
Reports that Rabbi Ami ruled, in the names of Rabbi Yohanan, Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Hanina, that such an offspring is a mamzer.
Rav Yosef responds that many Sages holding a view does not make it halakha, and lists opposing authorities who hold the offspring is fit.
Rav Yosef holds the halakha is that the offspring is a mamzer, since this is Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's view, per Rav Dimi's report.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi holds that the offspring's lineage is sullied and a daughter is restricted in marriage.
Asks whether the restriction refers to the congregation, which Rabbi Yehoshua rejects, and answers it must concern the priesthood.
Argues a fortiori from the widow of a High Priest, whose child has flawed lineage, to the child of a gentile or slave.
Rejects the rebuttal that the widow differs: the gentile or slave union also disqualifies the woman from marrying a priest.
Rabbi Yohanan, citing Rabbi Shimon, derives from Leviticus 22:13 that such unions disqualify a priest's daughter from the priesthood.
Abaye challenges Rav Yosef's reliance on Rav Dimi and urges Ravin's report that Rabbi Natan and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi permit the offspring.
Shows Rav also permits the offspring, citing a questioner who was himself such a child and was told his lineage is unflawed.
Rav states that the lineage of such an offspring is unflawed, and refuses his own daughter to the questioner.
Shimi bar Hiyya tests Rav's sincerity with the camel-dancing proverb: if he really held his ruling he would give his daughter.
Rav replies that his refusal rests on other reasons, and the questioner's family would be shunned, so he still declines.
Relates that the man kept pleading and Rav's gaze caused his death.
Reports that Rav Mattana and Rav Yehuda also rule permitted, and Rava advises such a person to conceal his lineage or go into exile.
Residents of Bei Mikhsei ask Rabba about the offspring of a half-slave and a Jewish woman.
Rabba replies that if a full slave's offspring is unflawed, the question about a half-slave hardly needs asking.
Rav Yosef notes that the master responsible for disseminating this halakha is the authority on this tradition.

ranges.en: Identifies the earlier speaker as Rav Yehuda, whose ruling is cited above.
Objects: Rav Yehuda held that the offspring of a half-slave and a Jewish woman has no means of marrying in, which conflicts with Rava's view.
Resolves the objection: Rav Yehuda's ruling concerns a half-slave betrothing a Jewish woman, so the slave side engages with a married woman.
Objects with the Sages of Neharde'a in the name of Rabbi Yaakov: each side's view on a married or unmarried mother is grounded in the halakha of a father's wife.
Explains the view that renders the child unfit: as betrothal to a father's wife is void, the child of any void betrothal, including gentile or slave, is a mamzer.
Explains the lenient view: the father's wife limits the rule, so gentile or slave betrothals never take effect and the child is not a mamzer.
Offers another resolution: Rav Yehuda's ruling concerns a half-slave with a married woman, whose free side makes the child a mamzer.
Ravina reports that Rabbi Yosei bar Avin, or Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Zevida, or Ameimar, rendered such offspring fit whether the mother was married or not.
Concludes that the halakha is that the offspring of a gentile or slave and a Jewish woman is unflawed, whether she was married or not.
Rava ruled that Rav Mari bar Rahel, son of a gentile father and Jewish mother, is fit and may hold public office, since his mother is Jewish.
Rav Yosef holds that the daughter of a slave's immersion for purification from menstruation can be rendered fit, as the intention of conversion can be imputed.
Rav Yosef's ground is Rav Asi's ruling: a woman who immersed for purification from menstruation is treated as converted, and her daughter is unflawed.
Concludes that the child of a gentile or slave and a Jewish woman is unflawed, and that the convert's daughter is fit on that basis.
Cites precedents: a man called son of an Aramean woman was treated as fit when his mother's immersion was for purification, and similarly for a father's conversion.
Rav Hama bar Gurya reports Rav's ruling: a Jewish buyer's slave who immerses for conversion before the purchase is completed becomes a freeman.
Asks the reason for this ruling.

46a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A gentile owner never acquired the slave's body; the Jew only got labor rights, and immersion for freedom cancels the lien.
Rava's principle that consecration, leavened-bread prohibition and emancipation nullify liens is cited in support.
Rav Hisda objects from the Beloreya baraita, which seems to say a later immersion would not free the slaves.
Rava reconciles the baraita: the slaves go free only if their immersion was explicitly for conversion.
Rav Avya limits the labor-only acquisition to buying from a slave owner; a gentile selling himself gives the body.
Leviticus 25:45 is brought to show Jews may acquire gentile slaves but not vice versa.
To what kind of acquisition does the verse refer, given that the labor-only reading seems to limit it?
Objection from Leviticus 25:47 and the alternative reading about uprooting a stranger's family.
The verse must refer to the body, since it explicitly permits acquiring even the body of a gentile.
Rav Aha refutes Rav Avya by reading the verse as acquisition by money plus immersion, and the Gemara finds it difficult.
Shmuel rules that the owner must hold the slave under water to show dominance, so the immersion counts as for slavery.
The Minyamin incident, where the slave was held and bridled during immersion, illustrates Shmuel's ruling.
Explains the bridle actions: loosening avoids interposition, tightening prevents a claim of conversion, and the clay bucket shows he stayed a slave.
Rav Pappa asks whether those redeemed by the house of Pappa bar Abba need a bill of emancipation.
Rava replies that the owners did acquire the bodies, so a formal emancipation document is needed.
Rav Sheshet's teaching that all residents are the king's slaves, so the poll-tax buyers gain full ownership, is cited.
Rabbi Hiyya visits Gavla and sees Jewish women with converts who never immersed, Jewish wine poured by gentiles, and lupines cooked by gentiles, but says nothing.
Rabbi Yohanan orders a public declaration that their children are mamzerim, their wine forbidden, and their lupines forbidden, because they are not learned in Torah.
Rabbi Hiyya reports Rabbi Yohanan's view that a convert is not a convert until circumcised and immersed, supporting the ruling on children.
Unimmersed converts remain gentiles; a gentile or slave who has relations with a Jewish woman produces a mamzer, per Rabbi Yohanan.
The wine is forbidden by a protective decree, like a nazirite kept from vineyards, and lupines are forbidden because the people are not learned.
Does the reasoning imply that lupines are permitted for those who are learned in Torah?
Rav's rule that food eaten raw is not subject to gentile cooking is cited, and lupines are not eaten raw, so the objection seems to hold.
Rabbi Yohanan follows the other version of Rav's rule: food not served at kings' tables is exempt, so lupines are permitted to the learned.
A baraita states Rabbi Eliezer's view that one who circumcised but did not immerse is a convert.
Rabbi Eliezer's view is supported by the example of the patriarchs, who circumcised but did not immerse.
Rabbi Yehoshua holds that one who immersed but did not circumcise is a convert.
Rabbi Yehoshua's view is supported by the matriarchs, who immersed but were not circumcised.
The Sages hold that a convert must both circumcise and immerse; neither act alone suffices.
Rabbi Yehoshua derives his view from the patriarchs and Rabbi Eliezer from the matriarchs, the sources of each opinion.
Objection: if one does not derive from possibility to impossibility, the inference from the patriarchs or matriarchs fails.
A baraita derives from the Passover offering in Egypt and in later generations that only a consecrated animal from the flock may be brought.
Rabbi Akiva objects that the inference from possible to impossible is not valid.
Rabbi Eliezer replies that even if the inference is impossible, it is a strong proof and one can learn from it.

ranges.en: Everyone agrees immersion alone suffices; the dispute concerns a man who was circumcised but did not immerse.
Rabbi Eliezer derives the rule from the patriarchs, while Rabbi Yehoshua holds the patriarchs also immersed.
The Gemara asks where Rabbi Yehoshua gets the idea that immersion occurred in that case.
A proposed source from Exodus 19:10 about washing garments, read as an a fortiori argument for immersion.
Objection: the washing in that verse may mean mere cleanliness, so no a fortiori inference follows.
Exodus 24:8 is offered instead: sprinkling at Sinai requires immersion, so the forefathers must have immersed.
It is a received tradition that sprinkling is never valid without prior immersion.
The Gemara asks where the immersion of the foremothers is derived from, according to Rabbi Yehoshua.
The inference is logical: otherwise, how would the foremothers have entered under the wings of the Divine Presence?
Rabbi Yohanan rules that no one becomes a convert until he is both circumcised and immersed.
Is this not obvious, since the halakha always follows the many Sages over an individual?
The Rabbis in the baraita are identified as Rabbi Yosei, a lone Sage, so the ruling had to be stated explicitly.
A baraita supports Rabbi Yosei: a convert claiming circumcision without immersion is not immersed, and the Shabbat ramification follows.
Obviously, Rabbi Yehuda's view that one act suffices permits immersion when circumcision was witnessed by the court.
Could one think that for Rabbi Yehuda immersion is primary, so immersing on Shabbat would improve the person and be forbidden?
The Gemara teaches that this is not so, and the ruling follows Rabbi Yehuda's position.
The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Yosei's ruling that one may not immerse on Shabbat is meant in this way or that.
Since Rabbi Yosei requires both circumcision and immersion, one does not improve a convert's status on Shabbat.
Could one think that for Rabbi Yosei circumcision is primary, so one could immerse a convert on Shabbat when circumcision was witnessed?
This teaches that Rabbi Yosei requires both acts, so the immersion cannot be done on Shabbat.
Rabba relates a case in which a convert who had been circumcised but not immersed came before the Sages, as precedent for the ruling.
The Sages tell the convert to wait until the next day; from this, three lessons are drawn about conversion and night immersion.
Could one still say that experts are needed to verify, lest the converts merely happened to pass by?
Rabbi Yohanan teaches that a convert requires a court of three, as written in the verse.
A baraita about a claimant who says he is a convert and needs witnesses, supported by Leviticus 19:33 on the stranger who sojourns with you.

47a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The baraita derives from the repeated phrase with you that a convert is accepted in and outside the Land.
Rabbi Yehuda holds that in the Land a convert must bring evidence, but outside the Land his claim is accepted.
The Sages hold that evidence is required both inside and outside the Land.
Why is the verse about his witnesses needed if witnesses are always relied upon?
Rav Sheshet explains the case where witnesses only say they heard of the conversion, so the verse teaches they are relied upon.
Didn't the baraita already use the phrase with you for the earlier point, so why use it again?
The Sages restate their view: evidence of conversion is needed whether in the Land or outside it.
If the verse says in your land, how can the Sages require evidence without distinction inside and outside the Land?
The phrase in your land teaches that converts are accepted even in the Land, lest they convert only for its benefits.
Rabbi Yohanan rules that the halakha requires evidence both in and outside the Land.
Isn't this obvious since the many outweigh one? Could one think Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning is sound because verses support it?
The Gemara teaches that the Sages' ruling stands despite verses supporting Rabbi Yehuda.
A baraita cites Deuteronomy 1:16 about judging between a man, his brother and his stranger.
Rabbi Yehuda rules that a convert accepted by a court is a convert, but one who converted only privately is not.
An anecdote: a man came before Rabbi Yehuda claiming he converted privately, illustrating the ruling.
Rabbi Yehuda asks whether the man has witnesses and whether he has children.
He is believed to disqualify himself but not to disqualify his children, since he cannot testify against them.
Objection: Rabbi Yehuda seems to deny credibility, yet a baraita on Deuteronomy 21:17 supports acknowledging a son to others.
Rabbi Yehuda holds that a man is believed about his firstborn son, and by parity about a son's mamzer or chalutza status; the Sages disagree.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzhak explains that Rabbi Yehuda's words are addressed to a gentile, so his testimony is not accepted.
Ravina explains that the question concerns the man's children and grandchildren: he is believed about his children but not his grandchildren.
A baraita supports Rabbi Yehuda: a man is believed about a minor son but not about an adult son.
Rabbi Yohanan clarifies that minor means one with children, and the halakha follows Rav Nachman bar Yitzhak.
Isn't it taught like Ravina's view, which concerns only the acknowledgment case?
A baraita on a convert in this era: tell him the hardships of Israel, then inform him of light and stringent commandments and their rewards.
Inform the convert of the punishments for transgressions, and of the reward; the world to come is for the righteous, and Israel now cannot bear it.

ranges.en: The court does not overwhelm a prospective convert with the rewards or the calamities, nor scrutinize him over fine details of the mitzvot.
A male convert is circumcised at once, recircumcised if needed, immersed when healed, and then is a full Jew with two scholars instructing him.
A female convert is immersed up to her neck, with two scholars outside the bath instructing her in mitzvot, out of modesty.
The same rules apply to a convert and a freed slave, and the same interposition rules as for a menstruating woman's immersion.
The baraita on a prospective convert who is asked what he saw and told about the mitzvot is quoted as support.
Why tell him this at all? If he will withdraw, he should withdraw at this stage.
Rabbi Helbo explains that converts are as harmful to Israel as a scab, citing Isaiah 14:1 on the convert cleaving to the house of Jacob.
The baraita continues to instruct the convert about neglecting the gleanings, forgotten sheaves, corner, and poor man's tithe.
Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba reports Rabbi Yohanan's reason: a gentile is executed even for stealing less than a peruta, so these laws are specifically mentioned.
The baraita restates that one does not overwhelm the convert with mitzvot or scrutinize him over details.
Rabbi Eleazar cites Ruth's words to Naomi as the model: Ruth accepted Sabbath limits, the 613 mitzvot, idolatry's prohibition, and four death penalties.
Once the convert accepts these, he is immediately immersed.
The reason for immediate immersion: a mitzva should not be delayed.
If shreds of flesh remain that hinder circumcision, the convert is circumcised again.
A mishnah lists the shreds that invalidate circumcision, supported by Rav's explanation of the flesh covering the crown of the organ.
If the convert heals he is immersed at once; if not, the procedure is not yet complete.
The reason: a wound that has not healed is like a scab on an unhealed wound, so the procedure waits.
Two Torah scholars stand beside the convert during the procedure.
Objection: Rabbi Yohanan says a convert needs three, so two scholars cannot suffice; the answer is that the tanna taught three.
A convert who has immersed and emerged is like a born Jew in every respect.
What is the practical ruling behind this status?
If the convert retracts and marries a Jewish woman, he is an apostate Jew, and his betrothal is valid.
A convert and an emancipated slave are two cases treated alike under this rule.
Objection: one might think a convert must accept the yoke of mitzvot, but a baraita says an emancipated slave need not accept it.
Rav Sheshet resolves the contradiction: the baraita follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, while the other baraita follows the Sages.
Deuteronomy 21:13 on a captive woman mourning her father and mother is cited as the source.
The rule applies when she did not accept the mitzvot; if she accepted them, she is immersed and permitted at once.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar holds that even without her acceptance, she is compelled, immersed as a bondwoman, then immersed again to be freed.

48a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The baraita continues: the convert is immediately permitted to marry, since immersion completes the process.
What is the reason behind Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's view?
Exodus 12:44 says slave of a man, which teaches that a male slave may be circumcised against his will but a gentile's adult son may not.
The Rabbis, through Ulla, reason that an adult slave cannot be circumcised against his will, just as an adult son cannot.
If so, why does the verse say every slave of a man, if that phrase is already needed for something else?
The phrase is needed for Shmuel's ruling that a master who renounces ownership frees his slave without a bill of emancipation.
Rav Pappa objects: the Rabbis' requirement of accepting the yoke may apply only to a female captive, not to a slave who was already bound by mitzvot.
A baraita: a convert and one who buys a slave from a gentile must accept the yoke of mitzvot; buying from a Jew does not require it.
In accordance with whose opinion is this baraita, given that Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar would not require acceptance even for a gentile's slave?
It must follow the Rabbis, so the ruling is that acceptance is needed for a gentile's slave but not for one bought from a Jew.
If so, how can the baraita say that this applies to both a convert and a freed slave, when the acceptance clause is earlier?
That clause refers only to immersion, which is mentioned immediately before, and not to the acceptance of the yoke.
A baraita reads the verse about the captive woman's shaving and nails, with Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva's competing derivations, supported by the case of Mephibosheth.
The Sages teach that the verse says she shall weep for her father and mother, introducing the rules for the captive woman.

48b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Eliezer holds that her father and mother mean her actual parents.
Rabbi Akiva reads her father and mother as the idol she worshiped, which she no longer serves.
Jeremiah 2:27 is cited to show that people call idols father and mother.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar derives a ninety-day waiting period from the words month, days and after that.
Ravina objects that the same reasoning would yield a sixty-day addition, and the Gemara finds it difficult.
A baraita records a dispute: Rabbi Yishmael permits maintaining uncircumcised slaves, while Rabbi Akiva forbids it even briefly.
Rabbi Yishmael cites Exodus 23:12 about the maidservant's son being refreshed as support.
The verse refers to a slave bought at twilight who had no time to circumcise him, and everyone agrees on that case.
If all agree on that, what does the verse indicate when it refers to an uncircumcised slave?
A baraita argues from Deuteronomy 5:13 and Leviticus 25 that the verses refer to uncircumcised slaves and to resident strangers.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rules that one who buys a gentile slave who refuses circumcision must resell him to gentiles after twelve months.
The Rabbis ask Rav Pappa which view this follows, given that Rabbi Akiva would not allow the owner to maintain such a slave.
Rav Pappa replies that Rabbi Akiva's view holds only where the master did not stipulate, but where he stipulated, the stipulation governs.
Rav Kahana reports his earlier explanation to Rav Zevid, that Rabbi Akiva's reasoning rests on one of two grounds.
Rabbin relays Rabbi Ilai's teaching: an uncircumcised slave may be kept only if his master bought him on condition he not circumcise him.
The Rabbis again ask Rav Pappa which view this follows, since Rabbi Akiva would not permit maintaining such a slave.
Rav Pappa answers that Rabbi Akiva's view applies only where there was no stipulation, while a stipulated slave may be kept.
Rav Kahana repeats his explanation to Rav Zevid, and Rav Zevid replies that Rabbi Akiva gave one of several grounds.
An anecdote about a city in Eretz Yisrael whose slaves refused circumcision and were resold after twelve months.
The case matches the view of a particular tanna whose baraita is cited.
A baraita rules that one who buys a gentile slave who refuses circumcision must resell him after twelve months.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar rules that such a slave may not remain in the Land for the sake of ritual purity, nor near a scroll.
Rabbi Hanania, son of Rabban Gamliel, explains that converts now suffer because they did not keep the seven Noahide mitzvot.
Rabbi Yosei holds that a convert is like a newborn child, but converts are troubled because they lack expertise in mitzvah details.
Other views: they are troubled because they do not act out of love but fear, or because they delayed entering under the Divine Presence's wings.
Ruth 2:12 is cited, May the Lord repay your deed, to explain the reward for coming under the Divine Presence's wings.

ranges.en: Mishnah: a mamzer is the offspring of any forbidden relation of close kin, per Rabbi Akiva.
Shimon HaTimni holds that the offspring of any union carrying karet at the hand of Heaven is a mamzer, and the halakha follows him.
Rabbi Yehoshua holds that the offspring of any union punishable by court-imposed death is a mamzer.
Ben Azzai says he found a lineage scroll in Jerusalem recording a mamzer from adultery, supporting Rabbi Yehoshua.
Mishnah: the prohibition on a wife's sister or yevama's sister applies only while the wife or yevama is alive, whatever her later status.
What is the reasoning behind Rabbi Akiva's view?
Deuteronomy 23:1 is read as forbidding relations with a father's wife, and the offspring of the union is a mamzer, as Rabbi Yehuda's view allows.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Simai and Rabbi Yeshevav extend Rabbi Akiva's view to other forbidden relations, including those with positive mitzva liability.
Shimon HaTimni follows the Rabbis' reading of the verse about a yevama, with karet liability, and cites the mamzer verse as support.
Rabbi Yehoshua derives his view from the two clauses of Deuteronomy 23:1, which would otherwise be redundant.
Abaye says all tanna'im agree that the offspring of relations with a menstruating woman is not a mamzer.

49b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The offspring of a sota is also not a mamzer, continuing Abaye's point about forbidden relations.
Leviticus 15:24 shows betrothal takes effect even during a menstruating woman's impurity, so the child is not a mamzer.
The same reasoning applies to a sota, since betrothal can take effect with her.
A baraita confirms Abaye: all agree the offspring of relations with a menstruating woman, a sota, or a yavam's widow is not a mamzer.
Abaye omits the yavam's widow because he is unsure whether a non-yavam betrothal takes effect, a question between Rav and Shmuel.
The Gemara cites Ben Azzai's statement from the mishna about the lineage scroll.
A baraita gives the expanded contents of the lineage scroll: a mamzer from adultery, Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's teachings, and Manasseh's killing of Isaiah.
Rava says Manasseh judged Isaiah a false witness for teachings contradicting the Torah, and then killed him.
Manasseh challenges Isaiah with apparent contradictions between Moses' words and Isaiah's prophecies about seeing God and the length of life.
Isaiah foresees Manasseh's response, hides in a cedar, and dies when the saw reaches his mouth, punished for his words about an unclean people.
How can the contradictory verses be reconciled?
All prophets saw through an obscure looking glass, while Moses saw clearly, which resolves the first contradiction about seeing God.
Seek God while He may be found applies to the individual, while nearness to the community is constant; the individual's time is the Ten Days of Repentance.
A baraita records a dispute among tanna'im about how the verse I will fulfill the number of your days should be read.

50a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Akiva holds that the years of a person's lifespan are fixed, and the Sages hold that a deserving person gets years added.
The Sages object to Rabbi Akiva from Isaiah's promise to Hezekiah of fifteen added years; he answers they came from his own allotted lifespan.
Rabbi Akiva cites a prophecy about Josiah, born before Manasseh, to show Hezekiah's allotted years were not yet complete.
The Sages rebut that the prophecy only says House of David, so Josiah need not descend from Hezekiah.
The mishna's wife's sister rule is cited, and Rav Yosef says Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi taught an unneeded mishna, since the rule is in the Torah.
Mishna: Rabban Gamliel holds that a second get, intercourse, or halitza is ineffective after an earlier one, while the Sages allow a second get and betrothal.
The mishna gives practical examples of how the sequence of get, betrothal, intercourse, and halitza affects the levirate bond.

50b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishna's principles apply to one yavam with one or two yevamot, illustrated by cases of betrothal, divorce, intercourse and halitza.
More cases follow, showing which later acts are void after halitza or intercourse, with Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Nehemya's differing views.
The Gemara concludes that Rabban Gamliel and the Rabbis disagree only about repeating divorce or betrothal, not about a single act.
What is the reason the Sages hold that a divorce is effective for a yevama?
Divorce is effective generally for married women; denying it for yevamot would wrongly suggest halitza is also ineffective.
What is the reason the Sages hold that betrothal is effective for a yevama?
Betrothal is generally effective; denying it would wrongly suggest intercourse is also ineffective, leading to remarriage after halitza.
What is the reason the Sages hold that intercourse is void after a defective intercourse?
The Sages decree that intercourse after a get or a betrothal is a preventive measure, so a defective act cannot be followed by another.
The Sages ask why they should decree, and explain that halitza after betrothal or intercourse is treated like the earlier cases.
An argument that intercourse, like betrothal, requires a get to undo, so the parallel holds.
Rava's remark begins the next point of the discussion.

51a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: What is the reason for Rabban Gamliel's ruling that a second divorce is ineffective after a first?
Rabban Gamliel is uncertain whether a divorce or betrothal acts at all, so a later act of either would have no effect after the first.
Abaye objects from a baraita that Rabban Gamliel concedes later divorce and betrothal are effective, and the consistent reading makes his ruling difficult.
Abaye explains that Rabban Gamliel is certain, but each act reaches its limit, so the second divorce or betrothal does nothing after the first.
The Rabbis instituted both divorce and betrothal as each effective for a yevama.
The Gemara explains the Rabbis' view by comparing intercourse with divorce and betrothal, since intercourse has a different effect on the rival wife.

Analyzes Rabbi Yehuda's view: whether the convert's daughter stays in her betrothal, she does not eat, since a convert's offspring are like a disqualified one.
Analyzes Rabbi Yossi's view: whether or not she stays in her betrothal, the daughter of a priest's convert wife eats.
Analyzes Rabbi Yossi's view on converts: the convert who married a convert's daughter is fit, and the assembly of converts is not called an assembly except by this Tanna.
Cites the Mishnah: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says a convert's daughter may not marry a priest until her mother is Israelite; the question is whether she eats.
Brings a proof: come and hear what Rabbi Achai bar Chinnana brought from the south.
A baraita from the south: a priest who married a convert's daughter feeds her terumah, from the verse on the priest's purchased property.
Asks for whom the baraita is meant: shall we say Rabbi Yehuda.
Rejects Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yossi as the source, since the verse would be unnecessary on Rabbi Yossi's view.
Concludes the source is Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, so the convert's daughter is fit and she eats.
States that Rav said the matter, in the form of a ruling.

ranges.en: Asserts that there is a marriage canopy for disqualified women.
Shmuel says there is no canopy for disqualified women, and says Abba agrees with him.
Abba's point concerns a girl under three years and a day.
Since such a girl has no intercourse, she has no canopy either.
Rava cites our Mishnah: a girl of three years and a day is betrothed by intercourse.
Mishnah continues: if a yavam has intercourse with her he acquires her, and both are liable as adultery, and a priest's wife eats terumah.
If she is married to a priest, she eats terumah.
If she has intercourse with any disqualified man, she is disqualified.
Infers that if intercourse disqualifies a girl at three years and a day, so does the canopy, and a younger girl is affected by neither.
Rami bar Chama says a canopy does apply to disqualified women, and the Tanna of this view is Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Elazar, and Rabbi Shimon.

58a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Sets out the positions: Rabbi Meir says betrothal disqualifies and so does canopy, while Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon say neither does.
Asks from where we know this: perhaps Rabbi Meir spoke only of betrothal that acquires her, not canopy that does not.
Offers an alternative reading: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon spoke only of betrothal not near intercourse, whereas canopy is near intercourse and disqualifies.
Asks whether the dispute can be read as one between these two tannaim.
A baraita: if couples married or entered the canopy without intercourse, they eat from their own property and eat terumah.
Asks whether entered implies married in the full sense, or means entered the canopy without intercourse.
Explains the baraita as the case of entering the canopy without intercourse, where the woman eats from her own property and terumah.
Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka: where intercourse feeds her, the canopy feeds her too, and where intercourse does not, the canopy does not.
Asks whether Rabbi Yishmael agrees with Rabbi Meir, who holds betrothal does not feed her, so the statement needs clarifying.
Rav Amram says he heard this matter, and that Rav Sheshet told it.
Rav Sheshet reports the same matter to us.
Illuminate the point from the Mishnah: there is a canopy for disqualified women.
The Tanna taught the cases: a betrothed woman, a married woman, a woman guarded by a yavam, and one brought into the canopy.
Asks what a betrothed woman case looks like.
Objects: if he acquired her while betrothed and gives her drink while betrothed, the Mishnah teaches betrothed women do not drink.
The Mishnah: a betrothed woman and a yavam-guarded woman do not drink the water and do not take the ketubah.
Rather: he acquired her while betrothed, she hid, and he gave her drink as a married woman, so can she be tested by water?
Objects with a baraita on the water test: only if the husband is clear of guilt is the wife tested; the case of betrothal then canopy without intercourse shows canopy disqualifies.
Rava objects: does that make sense, since she is willing and does not object?
Rabbi Achai bar Chanina came from the south with a Mishnah in hand.
Cites the verse Num 5:20 except your husband: the husband's prior intercourse matters, not the adulterer's.
Rami bar Chama: such a case can be found, when he had intercourse with her while betrothed in her father's house, and similarly the yavam's case in his father-in-law's house.

58b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A yavam-guarded woman is fine here, since Rav said so.
Rav holds acquisition applies to all cases, unlike Shmuel, who limits it to the matters in the passage.
Asks whether this is really the reason for the difference between Rav and Shmuel.
Asks what case is being dealt with here, given Rav's view that acquisition applies to all.
Explains: the case is one where he performed a betrothal act with her, which Beit Shammai treat as a full acquisition, so this is a betrothed woman.
By your reasoning the married woman and the entered canopy are different cases, so the betrothed and yavam-guarded cases should differ too.
Rav Pappa says this is a tanna's baraita: one may not give a betrothed woman drink, but may give a married woman drink.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says Rav Chanina sent in Rabbi Yochanan's name that a betrothal act with a yevama disqualifies her from terumah, even for a priest.
Asks whether this follows Rabbi Meir, who holds one guarded for intercourse is disqualified by Torah law and so does not eat.
Objects: on the view of Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon, one guarded for intercourse is disqualified by Torah law but eats by Rabbinic law, so the question remains.
Ravin reports that all agree she eats where a yavam acts with her, and where another brother is a disqualified man she does not eat; they disagree only where he gave her a divorce.
Rabbi Yochanan holds she eats, and Resh Lakish holds she does not eat.
Rabbi Yochanan holds she eats even on Rabbi Meir's view, since the rule of disqualification is Torah law only in the guarded case, while Rabbinic law allows eating.
Resh Lakish holds she does not eat even on Rabbi Elazar's view, and Rabbi Shimon agrees she eats only where he can feed her elsewhere, not here.
Objects: here too he can feed her with one who returns, but if the earlier link ended and she is near to another, the bond is no longer attached.
Quotes the Mishnah: whether widowed or divorced.
Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef asks Shmuel about a high priest who betrothed a minor who matured under him.

59a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether the law follows the marriage or the betrothal as the reference point.
Replies that we learned: those widowed or divorced from marriage are disqualified, while those from betrothal are fit.
Clarifies that the question is not whether intercourse makes her a disqualified woman.
Asks which taking the verse on a virgin wife requires: the taking of betrothal, or the taking of marriage.
Notes a widow betrothed to a high priest may marry, since that verse differs: here too one wife is written, not two.
Objects: what did you see? Here her body has changed, but in the other case it has not changed.
Quotes the Mishnah: a High Priest may not marry a widow, from betrothal or marriage, or a bogeret; Rabbis Elazar and Shimon permit a bogeret.
A baraita: the verse says a widow he shall not take, from betrothal or from marriage, which is obvious.
Asks what the apparent question is: one might learn widow from Tamar, so only marriage counts.
Proposes the widow rule is like the divorcee, which applies from both betrothal and marriage.
Restates the Mishnah: he may not marry a bogeret.
A baraita: the verse on a virgin excludes a bogeret whose virginity has gone, per Rabbi Meir, while Rabbis Elazar and Shimon permit it.
Asks what the dispute between them is about.
Rabbi Meir holds virginity means even part of the virginity remains, so that the act must be in the normal manner.
Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon hold virginity means full virginity, and all of it must remain, whether in the normal manner or not.
Rav Yehuda states Rav's view: if she was had in an unnatural way, she is disqualified from priesthood.
Rava objects with the verse on the wife, which excludes the widow for a High Priest and the divorcee and chalutza for an ordinary priest.
Asks what the case is: if normal, why mention the widow; it should be the baalah case, and the widow is not the issue.

59b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whose view this is, whether Rabbi Meir's, and whether Rav holds like Rabbi Elazar.
Objects: why mention a ba'ulah at all, since she is already a harlot, as Rabbi Elazar taught about an unmarried man and woman.
Rav Yosef: take the case of one who was had by an animal, where there is the ba'ulah issue but not the harlot issue.
Abaye's dilemma: if ba'ulah makes her a harlot too, and if not a harlot, then not ba'ulah either.
Objects: if so, no woman would be fit for priesthood unless made stick-wounded by a stone, so the point needs another reading.
Rabbi Zeira says the case is a refusing woman; Rav Shimi bar Chiya says one had by an animal is fit for priesthood.
A baraita agrees: one had by a non-man is fit for priesthood, even if she is liable to stoning.
Rav Dimi reports a case of a woman had by a dog, whom Rabbi declared fit for priesthood.
Shmuel says a High Priest in Rabbi's time was not the point, since she is fit for a High Priest.
Rava asks Rav Ashi from where the Sages derive that there is no harlotry with an animal.
Cites the verse: do not bring the hire of a harlot or the price of a dog, and the Mishnah's two cases are permitted only as two, not four.
A baraita: one who was forced or seduced by himself may not marry, and if he did, the child is a chalal, while the Sages say it is fit.
Rav Huna, citing Rav, says he must divorce with a bill of divorce.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov explains what the case of one who married, while married, is meant to teach.

60a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Narrates that one who seduced a woman pays no fine, and that Rav Ashi responded to a ruling he was given.
Objects that Rav and Rabbi Yochanan both hold a bogeret or stick-wounded woman may not marry, so the rule about her later status is difficult.
Quotes the baraita: a man who forced or seduced another's wife may not marry her, and if he did the child is a chalal per Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov, but fit per the Sages.
Rav Huna and Rav Giddel each report Rav's ruling that the halakha follows Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov.
Asks what Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov's reasoning is, and whether he holds like Rabbi Elazar, since the Mishnah follows him on a kav and a clean matter.
Rav Amram reports Rav's ruling that the halakha does not follow Rabbi Elazar, which is difficult.
Rav Ashi: the dispute is whether a chalal violates a positive commandment, with Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov holding yes and the Sages no.
Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov's reasoning from the verse: the list of forbidden women is included in the prohibition on profaning one's seed, while the Sages read these as interrupting the matter.
Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov reads these to exclude a niddah, and his view is followed here.
A baraita: one makes a chalal from these, but not from a niddah, which accords with Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov's view of the verse.
Objects that the Sages' teaching is difficult.
A baraita on a sister betrothed: Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda say she defiles him, while Rabbi Yossi and Rabbi Shimon say she does not.
Rabbi Shimon's view: if she is fit for a High Priest, a man defiles her; if not, he does not.
A bogeret, by the view of all, defiles her for any man.
Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda derive from the verse on the virgin sister: the verse excludes the seduced and forced woman, and a stick-wounded one is included by another verse.
Continues the derivation: the verse on a woman with no husband excludes one with one, includes the betrothed and the bogeret, and asks why a verse is needed.
Objects: Rabbi Meir holds virgin means even part of a virgin, so why does the verse need to say it?
It might be thought to learn virgin from virgin there, but the verse teaches that here too na'arah applies there.
Rabbi Yossi and Rabbi Shimon's reasoning: the verse on the virgin sister excludes the forced, the seduced, and the stick-wounded, and includes a betrothed woman who was divorced.

60b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objects: Rabbi Shimon said a woman fit for a High Priest defiles him, and one not fit does not, which seems to contradict the earlier ruling.
Replies that the case there differs, since the Merciful One made her a near relative, and the stick-wounded woman is also near, but only one such case, not two.
Objects: what did you see? Here an act was done with her, but there none was done.
Rabbi Yossi's reasoning implies he holds like Rabbi Meir about the stick-wounded woman, since the verse covers the woman who was not to a man.
Rabbi Shimon's view that virgin means a complete virgin, and his reason from the verse that includes the bogeret.
A baraita of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai: a convert's daughter under three years and a day is fit for priesthood, from the verse on the girls who did not know a man.
The Rabbis apply the same reasoning to slaves and maidservants, so a girl under three years and a day would likewise be included.
Rav Huna raises a contradiction: one verse says a woman who knew a man is killed, implying one who did not know survives, and the other says the girls who did not know survive.
Resolves it: the verse speaks of a woman fit to be had, not one who has been had.
A baraita repeats the point: the verse speaks of a woman fit to be had, and so the girls who did not know a man are fit.
Asks from where they know who is fit to be had.
Rav Huna son of Bizna reports Rabbi Shimon Chasida: they were passed before the tzitz; a woman whose face shines is known to be fit, and one whose face does not is not.
Rav Nachman: the sign of a forbidden woman is the drukan, cited from the verse on the virgins in Gilead who did not know a man.
Rav Kahana: they were made to sit on a barrel of wine, and a ba'ulah's scent wafts, while a virgin's does not.
Rav Kahana son of Rav Nathan says they should be passed before the tzitz as well.
Cites the verse on the tzitz being for their favor: if so, then in the Midianite case too.
Rav Ashi: the verse says for them, for their favor and not for harm, while idolaters may be harmed.
Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi reports Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai.
Rabbi Zeira asks whether Rabbi Yaakov heard it explicitly or by implication, and what the implicit rule is.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi reports: Rabbi sent Rabbi Romanus to examine a city, found a convert's daughter under three years and a day, and declared her fit for priesthood.
Rabbi Yaakov replies that he heard it explicitly, and asks whether the implicit case differs.
Objects: since the marriage was made, it stands, as Rav and Rabbi Yochanan both say a bogeret or stick-wounded woman may not marry, and if she did, it is a marriage.
Objects that there her end is to become a bogeret or a ba'ulah, but here her end is to become a harlot.
Rav Sefra taught it implicitly, found it difficult, and answered as a priest who married a convert's daughter under three years and a day.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak asks what this is.
Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi replies that he reported the halakha from Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, and tells him to go and bring it or he will prove it.
A baraita states that Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai held this way.
