ranges.en: Graves of gentiles do not convey tent impurity.
Ezekiel 34:31 shows only Jews are called adam, so the tent rule excludes gentiles.
Objection: Numbers 31:40 calls the captives nefesh adam, so gentiles count as adam.
Second objection from Jonah 4:11 calling the Ninevites adam.
Reply: gentiles get the title adam only to distinguish them from animals.
Numbers 31:19 implies gentile corpses convey impurity, contradicting the ruling.
Reply: perhaps a Jew was killed, so the impurity came from his corpse.
Rabbis cite Numbers 31:49 that no Jew fell, refuting that reply.
Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai reads the verse as meaning none sinned, upholding his view.
Ravina grants that the verse excludes gentiles from tent impurity.
Citing Numbers 19:14 with the word adam as the source of that exclusion.
Ravina asks whether the verse also excludes gentiles from touching and carrying impurity.
Mishnah: a priest who betrothed a widow, then became High Priest, may marry her, with the Yehoshua ben Gamla precedent.
The reverse case: a widow awaiting yavam whose yavam became High Priest may not be married.
Baraita asserts a High Priest may marry a widow he had betrothed as a common priest.
Leviticus 21:14 take a wife is inclusive, so it also covers a yavam's widow.
Refers back to the Yehoshua ben Gamla incident as a precedent.
Did the king actually appoint him, or was he not appointed?
Rav Yosef says he sees a difficulty in this case.
Rav Asi explains Marta bribed King Yannai, so he was appointed among the great priests.
Mishnah: a High Priest whose brother died performs chalitza and does not perform levirate marriage.
Gemara notes the Mishnah teaches no difference between betrothal and marriage.
Explains the marriage case: a positive command cannot override the prohibition there, but from betrothal one might expect it to.
Resolution: a decree that the first intercourse is treated as a precedent for the second.
Mishnah: a common priest may not marry an eunuch woman unless he already has a wife and children.
Rabbi Yehuda: even with a wife and children, he may not marry an eunuch, since she is the zonah of the Torah.
The Sages: zonah means only a convert, freed slave, or one with forbidden intercourse.
Resh Galuta asks Rav Huna the reason, suggesting it is because of be fruitful and multiply.
Objection: only priests are commanded, so that cannot be the reason.
Rav Huna replies that the Mishnah wishes to teach its latter clause.
Rabbi Yehuda's position restated: even with a wife and children, he may not marry an eunuch.

61b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains why the Mishnah teaches the rule about priests, since it applies equally to all Israelites.
Rav Huna asks the reason for Rabbi Yehuda's view.
Hosea 4:10 expounded: intercourse that cannot lead to children is merely licentious.
Baraita: Rabbi Eliezer says a priest may not marry a minor girl.
Rav Hisda asks Rabba to investigate the reason for Rabbi Eliezer's ruling.
Rabba's finding: Rabbi Eliezer follows both Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda.
Rabba explains: Rabbi Meir's concern for the minority, and Rabbi Yehuda's view that an underdeveloped woman is a zona.
Challenge: does Rabbi Eliezer follow Rabbi Meir, when a baraita says minors may not perform chalitza or yibum?
The Rabbis concede Rabbi Meir's chalitza ruling, citing the word man in the verse.
If woman is compared to man, what is the reason they may not perform yibum?
Rabbi Meir replies: a minor boy may become a saris, a minor girl an eunuch, so they might meet in forbidden relations.
Does Rabbi Eliezer really follow Rabbi Yehuda, given a baraita on minor girls doing yibum but not chalitza?
Baraita lists opinions on the meaning of zona: Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Matya ben Harash.
Rabbi Yehuda: zona here refers to an eunuch.
The Sages: zona means only a convert, a freed slave, or one who had forbidden intercourse.
Rabbi Eliezer: a single man who has intercourse with an unmarried woman, not for marriage, makes her a zona.
Rav Adda bar Ahava resolves the contradiction: the case concerns a High Priest.
When did he acquire her, and was she already married when she grew up?
Rava: if her father betrothed her, he acquires her from that moment; a self-betrothal follows Rabbi Eliezer, not the Rabbis.
Rava's resolution: a common priest, and we fear she may be seduced, since seduction of a minor is rape for Israelites too.
Rav Papa says the case concerns a High Priest.
The baraita on Leviticus 21:3: virgin excludes a minor, and the word woman includes a grown girl only if not a minor.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: this is the teaching of that tanna.
Virgin means a na'ara, supported by Genesis 24:16 describing Rivka.
Rabbi Elazar: a single man who has intercourse with an unmarried woman, not for marriage, makes her a zona.
Rav Amram: the halakha is not like Rabbi Elazar.
Mishnah: a man may not forgo procreation unless he has children; Beit Shammai say two sons, Beit Hillel a son and a daughter, citing Genesis 5:2.
The Mishnah's latter clause supports Rav Nachman: having children exempts from procreation, not from marriage.
Shmuel: even with many children, a man may not remain without a wife.
Shmuel's proof: Genesis 2:18, it is not good for man to be alone.
Some say: if children exempt from procreation and also from marriage, this refutes Rav Nachman.
Shmuel's distinction: without children one must marry; with children, one may marry a woman who cannot bear, with a difference for selling a Torah scroll.
Beit Shammai: two sons.
What is the reasoning of Beit Shammai?
Beit Shammai derive it from Moses, whose sons were Gershom and Eliezer, in 1 Chronicles 23:15.
Beit Hillel derive it from the creation of the world, male and female.
Beit Shammai should also learn from creation; the derivation from creation cannot decide the matter.

62a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objection: Beit Hillel should learn from Moses, who separated from his wife.
Beit Hillel reply: Moses acted on his own perception, so it does not excuse neglecting procreation.
Baraita: Moses did three things on his own perception that God agreed with, including separating from his wife.
What did Moses expound to justify separating from his wife?
Moses's a fortiori argument from Exodus 19:15: if Israel was told not to approach a woman, all the more so he.
Deuteronomy 5:30 supports that God agreed with Moses's decision to separate.
What did Moses expound about breaking the tablets?
A fortiori from the Passover rule, supporting that God agreed with Moses breaking the tablets because of Israel's sin.
Reish Lakish: God told Moses well done for breaking the tablets and adding a day on his own.
What did Moses expound about adding a day to the separation?
Exodus 19:10-11 sanctify them today and tomorrow shows two days of preparation, and the Shechina did not rest until Shabbat.
Baraita: Rabbi Nathan says Beit Shammai hold two males and two females, and Beit Hillel one male and one female.
What is the reason for Rabbi Nathan's view according to Beit Shammai?
Genesis 4:2 and 4:25 on Cain, Abel and Seth's sisters support Beit Shammai's position.
The Sages merely acknowledge what the verses show, not a halakhic conclusion.
Another baraita: Rabbi Nathan says Beit Shammai hold a male and female, or a male or female.
Rava: Isaiah 45:18 says God formed the world to be inhabited, supporting Beit Hillel's reading.
Dispute on a convert who had children as a gentile: Rabbi Yochanan says he fulfilled procreation.
Reish Lakish says he did not fulfill procreation.
Rabbi Yochanan's reason: since he already had children, they count toward procreation.
Reish Lakish's reason: a convert is treated like a minor born at the time of conversion.
Restates the same dispute about whether a child born before conversion counts as firstborn for inheritance.
Rabbi Yochanan: no firstborn share, since the child was his first-fruit; Reish Lakish: a firstborn share, since a convert is like a newborn.
Gemara: both cases are needed; for procreation such children count, but for inheritance they are not heirs.
Gemara reconciles the two rulings: each sage may have spoken only about a specific case.
Rabbi Yochanan objects to Reish Lakish from II Kings 20:12, where Berodach-Baladan sent to Hezekiah.
Reish Lakish replies: as gentiles they had family feeling, but after conversion they lack it.
Rav: all agree about a slave who lacks compassion.
Genesis 22:5, sit here with the donkey, the one like a donkey, is the proof for Rav's statement.
Objection from II Samuel 9:10: Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants, challenging Rav's rule.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov: there the sons are attributed by name and their father's name, unlike here.
Alternatively, the sons are attributed to another place by their father and grandfather.
I Kings 15:18 shows genealogy traced through father and grandfather, as in the example of Ben-Hadad.
If children were born and died, Rav Huna says he fulfilled procreation.
Rabbi Yochanan says he did not fulfill procreation.
Rav Huna's basis: Rav Asi's teaching that the son of David does not come until all souls in bodies are finished.
Rav Asi's teaching is supported by Isaiah 57:16, for the spirit before Me would be enwrapped.
Rabbi Yochanan: not fulfilled, since we require the world formed to be inhabited, as Isaiah 45:18 says.
Gemara objects that the supporting case is absent and raises a counter-objection.

62b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Baraita: grandchildren are considered like children.
Gemara: that baraita is taught to complete the required number of children.
Objection from another baraita: if one of the children dies or is a eunuch, the father has not fulfilled procreation, refuting Rav Huna.
The baraita restated as the key line of the refutation.
Abaye's suggested reading: a grandson through a son or daughter suffices, but a granddaughter through a son does not.
Rava rejects Abaye: the requirement is merely that the earth be inhabited, and that is fulfilled here.
Everyone agrees that two grandchildren from one child do not suffice.
Objection: the Rabbis told Rav Sheshet to marry and father sons, although he had none.
Rav Sheshet: my daughter's sons are considered my sons.
Background to Rav Sheshet's case, where he was displaced from his position and Rav Huna responded.
Rabba asks Rava from where the Rabbis' principle derives.
Repeats the baraita: grandchildren are considered like children.
Is the source Genesis 31:43, the daughters are my daughters and the sons are my sons?
If so, then the flock is my flock would also count, which is absurd.
Rather, the sense is that the children were acquired from me, and here too the grandchildren are acquired from me.
I Chronicles 2:21-22: Hezron came to the daughter of Machir, who bore him Segub, as a source for grandchildren.
Judges 5:14 and Psalms 60:9 use Machir and Judah as lawgivers, showing grandchildren's standing.
The Mishnah does not follow the view of Rabbi Yehoshua.
Baraita: Rabbi Yehoshua says a man marries a wife in his youth, and if he has children in youth, they will have children in old age.
Ecclesiastes 11:6 in the morning sow your seed, and by evening do not rest your hand, proves the principle.
Rabbi Akiva: one should learn Torah in youth and continue in old age.
Rabbi Akiva's proof from Ecclesiastes 11:6, in the morning sow your seed.
Rabbi Akiva had twelve thousand pairs of students from Gevat to Antipatris, and all died in one period for not honoring each other.
The world was desolate until Rabbi Akiva came to the teachers in the south.
Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yosi, Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua were the ones who established the Torah at that time.
A Tanna: all of them died between Passover and Shavuot.
What was the bad death that struck them?
Rav Nachman: it was diphtheria.
Rav Mattana: the halakha follows Rabbi Yehoshua.
Rabbi Chanilai: every man without a wife lives without joy, blessing, goodness or happiness.
Deuteronomy 14:26, and you shall rejoice, you and your house, shows a man without a wife lacks blessing.
Ezekiel 44:30, to cause a blessing to rest on your house, shows a man without a wife lacks goodness.
Genesis 2:18, it is not good for man to be alone.
In the West they say: without Torah, without a wall.
Job 6:13 is not my help within me, and wisdom is driven from me, as a source for lacking a wall.
Jeremiah 31:21-22: a woman will encompass a man, as a source for lacking protection.
Raba bar Ulla: a man without a wife lives without peace.
Job 5:24: you will know that your tent is at peace, and you will visit your home and not sin.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: anyone who knows his wife to be God-fearing and does not visit her is called a sinner.
Job 5:24 quoted as the basis for that ruling.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: a man must visit his wife before leaving on a journey.
Job 5:24 again, and you will know that your tent is at peace.
The same lesson derives from here, and it also derives from there.
Genesis 3:16, your desire is toward your husband, teaches that a wife longs for her husband when he leaves on a journey.
Rav Yosef: this is needed only close to her period.
Rava: the frequency is set for a voluntary matter, but for a mitzva one is distracted.
Baraita: one who loves his wife as himself, honors her more than himself, and guides his children in a straight path is blessed with peace.
Baraita: one who loves his neighbours, brings close his relatives, and marries his sister's daughter is also praised.

ranges.en: Isaiah 58:9 about one who lends to a poor man in his time of need, promising an answer.

ranges.en: Mishna opens: pregnancy by an Israelite disqualifies a priest's daughter, a miscarriage restores her, and a priest's child can enable her when a slave's child cannot

Rava's proof from a mishna in which a priest's child enables the mother, showing the child is attributed to the rumored father

Abaye objects: where she is rumored with others, Rav holds the child a mamzer even if rumored with him; the mishna concerns no rumors at all
Mishna: a slave disqualifies a woman through intercourse but not through being her offspring
Exodus 21:4: a maidservant's children belong to her master, so they are not their father's offspring for disqualification
Baraita: the word zera in Leviticus 22:13 shows that a grandchild and an unfit child both disqualify a woman from teruma

Grandchildren count as children, so the verse is needed only for the unfit child
Reish Lakish asks: whose opinion holds that a child of a Jewess and a slave or gentile is a mamzer, only Rabbi Akiva's or also the Rabbis'?

Mishna restated: a High Priest may sometimes disqualify his own grandmother from teruma
Baraita: the grandmother would atone for her mamzer grandson, the small jug, who enables her, but not for the High Priest grandson, who disqualifies her
Chapter-closing formula that ends the previous chapter and opens the next mishna
Mishna: an uncircumcised priest or one who is impure may not eat teruma, but their wives and slaves may
Mishna defines crushed testicles and a severed penis; a priest's wife is disqualified if relations occurred after the injury, while the priest may still eat

Which instance of sojourner and hired servant is superfluous and available for the analogy?

Two superfluous phrases exist, one applied to teruma and one to the Paschal lamb, making a two-sided analogy that cannot be refuted
A half analogy is impossible, so the same analogy should bar an acute mourner from teruma, which is not the halakha
Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina: a verse bars the foreigner from teruma but not the mourner, while the sojourner analogy bars the uncircumcised priest
What led to including the uncircumcised priest but excluding the mourner? Perhaps the opposite is true
The lack of circumcision carries several stringencies, such as karet and its precedence before Sinai, so it is included
Counter: acute mourning is also stringent, since it applies at any time, to men and women, and can be fixed only after burial
Rava: the mourner cannot be included, since his bar from the Paschal lamb is learned only from tithe law
If the analogy holds, uncircumcised male children and slaves should also bar a priest from teruma, which is not the halakha
Rejection: the verse then he shall eat from it shows that uncircumcised household members bar only the Paschal lamb, not teruma
Difficulty: if from it excludes other cases, an uncircumcised man should be allowed teruma
Sojourner and hired servant appear for both teruma and Passover, so by analogy an uncircumcised priest may not eat teruma
What led to including one's own uncircumcision but not that of household members?
One's own lack of circumcision is an act on one's body punishable by karet, so it precludes eating teruma
Counter: household uncircumcision is relevant at any time and the priest is commanded to fix it, so it should bar teruma too
The analogy teaches that the priest's own lack bars teruma, while his household's lack does not
Since from it is already used for exclusion in the Paschal law, why is the other from it needed?
Exodus 12:43, no son of a foreigner eats of it, shows the exclusion applies only to the Paschal lamb itself

71a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Apostasy disqualifies from the Paschal lamb, since the stranger there means one estranged from God, but not from tithe

From it bars the uncircumcised only from the lamb, but he eats matza and bitter herbs like any Jew
The uncircumcised and the stranger each need a separate prohibition, since each is excluded for a different reason
Why is the other from it needed in the verses on not leaving the lamb raw or until morning?
These exclusions are needed for a teaching of Rabba citing Rabbi Yitzhak, explained later
Rabbi Akiva says the verbal analogy is unnecessary, since the verse itself shows the teaching
The repeated word man includes the uncircumcised priest in the teruma prohibition
Perhaps the repetition instead includes the acute mourner in the teruma prohibition?
Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina: no foreigner bars from teruma the foreigner, but not the mourner, so the repetition covers the uncircumcised

Let us say the dispute over a retracted foreskin is parallel to a tannaitic dispute?

ranges.en: Quoted rule that circumcision is done by day, or day and night when it was delayed.

Replies that this baraita follows Rabbi Akiva's school, which treats the uncircumcised like the ritually impure.

Asks which of the phrases of it is not needed in its own context.
Rava cites Rabbi Yitzchak: of it appears three times regarding the Passover offering, each with a separate purpose.
Explains how each of the three Passover phrases serves a different teaching, one for a prohibition and one for a mitzva.
The phrase of it likewise appears three times for second tithe, each expounded separately.
Reish Lakish cites Deuteronomy 26:14 and Rabbi Samya to permit anointing the body with impure second tithe.
Mar Zutra objects that the verse may mean buying a coffin and shrouds for the dead with tithe money.
Rav Huna and Rav Ashi reply that of it limits benefit to the tithe itself, so the three phrases still have distinct uses.
Raises the difficulty that the analogy is available from only one side, and asks what can be said if analogies can be refuted.
Answers that Rabbi Abbahu's ruling on burning impure teruma oil derives from Rav Nahman's report of Rabba bar Avuh.
Numbers 18:8 speaks of two terumot, one pure and one impure, permitting burning impure teruma beneath a cooked dish.
Quotes the mishna that all who are impure may not eat teruma.
Asks from where these matters are derived.
Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yishmael derives it from Leviticus 22:4, any man of Aaron's seed who is a leper or a zav.

ranges.en: The phrase all the seed of Aaron refers to teruma, which both male and female priests may eat.
Suggests the verse may instead mean the breast and thigh, which a returning priest's daughter may not eat.
If so, teruma would also be barred from a halala, but a halala is not considered the seed of Aaron.
Challenges the baraita's claim that a man lacking atonement may eat teruma after sunset, since the verse may require atonement first.
A Yishmael-school tanna shows the verse concerns a zav with two sightings and a quarantined leper, who need no offering and are pure at sunset.
Asks whether the sunset rule holds only for one who needs no offering, not for one who must bring an atonement offering.
Asks from where the different waiting periods for second tithe, teruma, and sacrifices in the mishna are derived.
Rav Hisda cites three verses on purity for sacred food and assigns each to tithe, teruma, or sacrificial food.
Asks why the stricter condition should not instead apply to tithe, and answers that teruma has the mem-het-peh-zayin stringencies.
Counters that second tithe has its own stringencies, such as bringing to Jerusalem, declaration, and removal.
Responds that the death penalty is a greater stringency, so teruma appropriately requires waiting until sunset.
Rava argues from the verse the soul that touches it that the first verse must refer to tithe, since teruma is for priests only.
Objects that a confirmed leper who must bring an atonement offering might not eat teruma until he brings it.
Abaye cites two verses on a woman after childbirth and resolves them by assigning one to teruma and one to sacrificial food.
Asks why the stricter condition should not apply to teruma, and answers that sacrificial food has the peh-nun-kuf stringencies.
Counters that teruma is stricter, with its own mem-het-peh-zayin stringencies, and then says sacrificial food is still more numerous.
Rava argues that the sunset verse cannot refer to sacrificial food, citing Leviticus 7:19 on impure flesh, so it must mean teruma.
Rav Sheisha objects that the childbirth verse cannot be about teruma, since teruma is not written there.
A baraita shows a convert and an emancipated maidservant are included in the childbirth law, which excludes teruma eligibility.
Rava asks whether the verse is also referring to teruma.

75a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objects that the childbirth verse in Leviticus 12:4 already includes teruma under touching any consecrated food.
Replies that the Torah treats several distinct matters separately, so not every verse refers to teruma.
Asks why three verses are needed to teach the purity rules for teruma.
Each verse is necessary: without the sunset verse one would not know whether immersion alone suffices.
Leviticus 12:4 and the until he be pure phrase show that teruma follows the day of purification and immersion, not a sacrifice.
Asks why two verses are needed for sacred food if the other tanna reads until he be pure as requiring the atonement offering.
Both verses are necessary, since a rule stated only for the childbirth case or only for the zav could be limited to that case.
Asks why the vessel verse in Leviticus 11:32 is needed at all.
Rabbi Zeira says the verse teaches that touching teruma by an impure vessel or person still makes it impure until nightfall.
A baraita shows the apparent contradiction is resolved: second tithe needs only immersion, teruma needs sunset.
Asks whether the stringency should be reversed, and answers that teruma's touching is stricter like its eating.
Offers an alternative: the touching prohibition is derived from the Sanctuary verse, which warns against entering while impure.
Juxtaposes consecrated food to the Sanctuary, so touching consecrated food must carry a life-taking penalty like eating.
Explains that the verse speaks of touching but means eating, since touching and eating are both forbidden until sunset.
Quotes the mishna on a priest's wife whose husband has crushed testicles or a severed organ.
Asks which tanna teaches that a woman awaiting intercourse that disqualifies her may still eat teruma.
Rabbi Elazar says the halakha is disputed, and the mishna follows Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon on a betrothed widow of a High Priest.
Rabbi Yohanan explains it can follow Rabbi Meir, because she had already eaten teruma before the injury.
Rabbi Elazar counters that otherwise an Israelite woman widowed after marrying a priest would keep eating teruma.
Rabbi Yohanan replies the cases differ: death lapses the acquisition, but an injury leaves the marriage intact.
Asks who is deemed a man with crushed testicles.
A baraita says anyone with a wounded, punctured, or decayed testicle counts as crushed, and Rabbi Yishmael limits it.
Rabbi Yishmael says one with only one testicle is a eunuch by nature and is fit, though the wording is disputed.
Asks whether he could be a eunuch by nature, since that term refers to one born without testicles.
Rather, he resembles a eunuch by nature, and so is fit.
Asks whether a punctured testicle also makes one incapable of children, citing a man who climbed a palm tree.

ranges.en: Narrates a man punctured by a thorn who still had children, and Rav's instruction to investigate where the children came from.
Shmuel rules that a man with crushed testicles from Heaven, such as from birth or illness, may marry a born Jewish woman.
Rava reads the wording a wounded man, not the man wounded, to show the injury must come from an outside cause.
A baraita compares Deuteronomy 23:2 and 23:3 and concludes the mutilation must be inflicted by man, as with a mamzer.
Rava explains that wounded, crushed, and severed each apply to the member, the testicles, or the spermatic cords.
A Sage asks Rava how one knows that crushing refers to an injury in the genitals rather than the head.
Rava says the verse omits the generations of descendants, which implies the blemish prevents fathering children.
Asks whether the omission of generations could instead be a halakhic reason, applying only to the man himself.
Derives the meaning of crushed from the adjacent case of severed, which is also an injury to that place.
Asks how one knows that the severed emission refers to the genitals rather than the lips.
Asks whether the nose could be the source, since the verse does not say what the emission comes from.
Says the verse speaks of a place that pours out only when an organ has been severed, which excludes the nose.
A baraita again compares the mamzer verse, saying the injury must be in that place and connected to cohabitation.
Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba considers rendering fit a man whose member was punctured below the corona on one side only.
Rabbi Asi objects, citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, that any puncture in the corona impedes fitness.
Quotes the mishna that a remaining hairsbreadth of the corona keeps the man fit.
Ravina asks whether the hairsbreadth must surround the whole member or only most of it.
Rava Tosfa'a answers that it must surround a majority of the member, toward its head.
Rav Huna rules that a member cut like a quill is fit, but one cut like a gutter is unfit, because air penetrates.
Rava upholds Rav Huna's view over Rav Hisda's, reasoning that air penetration is the operative concern.
Compares the rubbing contact of the upper end to a barrel stopper that closes the hole despite its tapered end.
Mar Zutra in the name of Rav Pappa rules that a quill or gutter cut is fit, though a dilemma about the location remains.
Raises the question whether the cut is below the corona or above it.
It is obvious the cut is above the corona, since a cut below it would make fitness absurd.
Argues that if it were below the corona, even a fully severed member would be fit, which is absurd.
Ravina raised the dilemma only to test Mereimar's understanding, not out of real doubt.
Reports that Mar bar Rav Ashi trimmed a gutter-shaped member to a quill and rendered the man fit.
Reports a Pumbedita case of a blocked seminal duct, where Rav Beivai bar Abaye intended to render the man fit.
Rav Pappi objects that the case was rendered fit only because of the trimming, so the reasoning does not transfer.

76a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rebukes the speaker's claim that semen which misses its place cannot fertilize, calling it truncated and unsound.
Shmuel rules that a punctured member that heals shut is unfit if it would tear open again, and otherwise fit.
Rava asks where the puncture is, since a puncture below the corona would not make the man unfit.
The ruling concerns a puncture in the corona itself, as Shmuel is quoted saying the same in that location.
Rava son of Rabba asks Rav Yosef how to verify whether the perforation has closed adequately.
Rav Yosef says to place warm barley bread on the man's anus so he emits semen and the closure can be observed.
Abaye's remark is objected to: not everyone is like Jacob, who never had an emission, so the method is needed.
Abaye proposes instead passing colorful women's garments before the man to bring him to arousal.
Rava objects that not everyone is like Barzilai the Gileadite, so the garments proposal does not work for all.
A baraita: a punctured man is unfit because his semen dribbles and does not fertilize, but fit once the hole closes.
Explains the baraita's wording that this is an unfit man returning to fitness.
Asks what the word this comes to exclude in the baraita.
It excludes a membrane formed on an animal's lung after a wound, which is not a proper membrane and does not restore kosher status.
Rav Idi bar Avin asks Abaye how to expedite healing of such a perforation.
Abaye describes barley-grain cutting, fat, and a biting ant to promote scarring, with iron forbidden and only small holes sufficient.
Rabba bar Rav Huna rules that one who passes water from two places is unfit, like a man with crushed testicles.
Rava rules that the halakha follows neither the son nor the father in this dispute.
Explains the father's view: women who rub against each other sexually are unfit to marry into the priesthood.
Rava limits Rabbi Elazar's rule to intercourse with a man, so lewd conduct between women does not make a woman a zona.
Quotes the mishna: a man with crushed testicles or a severed penis may marry a convert or emancipated woman but not a born Jewish woman.
Rav Sheshet is asked whether a priest with crushed testicles keeps his sanctity for the purposes of marrying converts.
Rav Sheshet cites a baraita permitting Gibeonite women to an Israelite with crushed testicles, and Deuteronomy 7:3 implies loss of sanctity.
Rava says this is no proof, since the concern with Canaanites is about children who might turn to idolatry, not sanctity.
Explains the reason: a Canaanite's child may worship idols, so the ban covers only those who can father, not the crushed.
Objects that by the same logic a mamzer who can father should also be barred from marrying a convert.
Objects with a mishna that mamzerim and Gibeonites may marry each other, so the decree does not reach the unfit.
Rava retracts his earlier view that the prohibition applies only to gentiles, since converts can validly marry.
Rav Yosef cites Solomon's marriage to Pharaoh's daughter as proof that valid marriage with gentiles is possible.
Converts were not accepted under David and Solomon only out of concern for those seeking the king's table.

76b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Pharaoh's daughter did not need such proof, since as a royal daughter her sincerity of conversion was not in doubt.
Asks why Solomon's marriage is not explained by her being a first-generation Egyptian convert, who is forbidden.
A baraita from Rabbi Yehuda tells of a first- and second-generation Egyptian convert, showing they were barred in the Mishnaic period.
Rav Pappa replies that Solomon never validly married these women but only loved them, so no objection arises.
Because of Solomon's great love, the verse credits him as if he had married her legally.
Ravina objects that the mishna permits crushed men to marry converts, which conflicts with the baraita on Gibeonites.
Rav Ashi says the mishna's other clause cannot yield a contrary inference, so one relies on the expressly taught halakha.
Quotes the mishna: Ammonite and Moabite converts are barred eternally, but their women are permitted immediately.
Quotes the mishna: Egyptian and Edomite converts are barred only three generations, and Rabbi Shimon permits the women at once.
Rabbi Shimon argues a fortiori: if the women of the eternally barred nations are permitted at once, so should be these.
Rabbi Shimon's colleagues object that the a fortiori argument can be refuted, unless he received it from his teachers.
Asks from where it follows that the women of Ammonites and Moabites are permitted at once.
Rabbi Yohanan cites Samuel 17:55, where Saul asks whose son David is, to suggest Saul was asking about David's father.
Objects that Saul had already made David his armor-bearer, so he could not have failed to recognize him.
Rav, or perhaps Rabbi Abba, says Jesse was a prominent man known to all, entering and leaving among crowds.
Explains Saul's question: a king may breach a way for himself, so Saul asked if David descends from Perez, the royal line.
Asks why Saul told Abner to inquire about David.
Saul clothed David in his own garments that fit him, and Saul was tall, so Saul feared David for the throne.
Doeg the Edomite asks whether David is even fit for the congregation, since he descends from Ruth the Moabite.
Abner replies that the mishna bars Ammonite and Moabite men but not women, so there is no concern.
Doeg objects that by the same logic a mamzer should be barred only if male.
Abner answers that mamzer means a defect of forbidden union, which applies to both sexes.
Doeg objects that an Egyptian man alone should then be barred, not an Egyptian woman.
Abner says the Ammonite case differs, since the verse gives a reason tied to men going out to meet travelers.
Doeg counters that men should have met men and women met women, and Abner has no reply.
The Gemara notes that Saul calls David a lad here, and says Saul told Doeg the halakha was hidden from him.
The study hall answers: an Ammonite or Moabite man is barred, but not the woman.

ranges.en: Doeg raised objections against David based on the disqualified nations, and the Sages were silent, so Doeg wanted to proclaim it.
Samuel 17:25 and Chronicles name Amasa's father differently, once Israelite and once Ishmaelite, answering Doeg's objection.
Rava teaches that Amasa girded on a sword like an Ishmaelite and received the tradition that Ammonite and Moabite women are permitted.
Asks whether Amasa is trusted to testify, since he had a personal stake in the halakha.
Here it is different, because Samuel and his court were still alive, so the report could be checked.
Asks that Doeg's unanswered objection still stands as a difficulty.
Babylonians explain the matter from Psalms that the king's daughter is glorious within, and Eretz Yisrael from Genesis 18:9.
Presents the tanna'im dispute: Rabbi Yehuda derives the rule from the masculine forms, and Rabbi Shimon from Deuteronomy 23:5.
Rava reads Psalms 116:16 as David thanking God for the loosened bands of Ruth the Moabite and Naamah the Ammonite.
Rava reads Psalms 40:6 as saying upon us, meaning Rehoboam, son of Naamah the Ammonite, sat on David's lap.
Rava reads Psalms 40:8 and 89:21 as showing that David descends from the daughters of Lot, mothers of Ammon and Moab.
Ulla, citing Rabbi Yohanan, rules that the daughter of an Ammonite convert is fit even to marry into the priesthood.
Rava bar Ulla asks in whose opinion Ulla spoke, since Rabbi Yehuda would disqualify such a daughter.
Shows that Rabbi Yehuda equates a convert's daughter with a halal's daughter, while Rabbi Yosei makes her fit.
Asks whether Rabbi Yosei spoke only of converts fit for the congregation, and from where the distinction is derived.
Derives it from a High Priest who married a widow, whose daughter is disqualified, a stringent case involving transgression.
Objects that a halal has no transgression in intercourse yet his children are barred, so the analogy may fail.
A High Priest who married a widow was not the product of a forbidden union, so the derivation goes back and forth.
Combines both sources: the common factor is that the man is not in the majority of the congregation, so his daughter is disqualified.
Objects that the common factor shared by the High Priest and halal is transgression, which an Ammonite convert lacks.
Explains that Rabbi Yohanan spoke of an Ammonite convert who married a Jewish woman, where the intercourse is a transgression yet the daughter is fit.
Ravin reports from Eretz Yisrael that Rabbi Yohanan rules fit both the Ammonite and second-generation Egyptian convert's daughters.
Reish Lakish disqualifies her by deriving from the High Priest who married a widow that any daughter of a forbidden union is unfit.
Rabbi Yohanan holds that she is fit to marry into the priesthood.

ranges.en: A baraita from Rabbi Zakkai cites Leviticus 21:14 to show an established female convert is fit to marry a priest.
Rabbi Yohanan objects that the verse also includes a virgin from two peoples, so Rabbi Zakkai's limit is too narrow.
Asks what the two peoples are, and concludes it must mean an Ammonite man who married a Jewish woman.
Gives an alternative version: the verse includes a woman of mixed descent whose father is an Ammonite or Moabite convert.
Asks from where Rabbi Yohanan derives that such a daughter of an Egyptian convert is fit to marry a priest.
Answers that the case of a second-generation Egyptian man and woman proves the point, since their daughter is permitted.
Objects that the Egyptian case involves no transgression, unlike an Ammonite who married a Jewish woman.
Argues that the Ammonite case itself proves the point, so the argument goes back and forth without resolution.
Rav Yosef says he finally understood Rav Yehuda's lecture: an Ammonite convert's daughter from a Jewish woman is fit, per Rabbi Yohanan.
Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda reports Rabbi Zakkai's baraita: an Ammonite woman is fit, her son is unfit, and her daughter is fit.
Rabbi Yohanan rejects the baraita as unreliable and tells him to teach it outside the study hall.
Asks what the daughter's fitness in the baraita is meant to teach, since fitness for the congregation would be redundant.
Explains the baraita refers to fitness for marrying a priest, and that the daughter of an unlawful union is the case Rabbi Yohanan rejects.
Quotes the mishna: Egyptian and Edomite converts are barred only for three generations, but the question is what refutes Rabbi Shimon.
Asks what refutation the mishna refers to.
Rabba bar bar Hana says incest prohibitions show the common factor is irrelevant, since they reach daughters only up to three generations.
Rejects that proof: incest involves karet, while the mamzer prohibition applies to both sexes without karet.
Rejects the mamzer proof as well, since a mamzer is barred forever, while incest is barred only three generations.
Derives the halakha from a combination: the common factor is that the prohibition applies to both sexes, as with male and female Egyptian converts.
Objects that incest and mamzer share karet, which Egyptians lack, so the prohibition may apply to males only.
The Rabbis derive the female Egyptian prohibition from the ḥalal, a child of a union that involves a positive-mitzva transgression, per Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya'akov.
Asks what Rabbi Shimon meant by his response of not so.
Explains that Rabbi Shimon does not accept Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya'akov, and in any case relies on an inherited halakha.
A baraita cites Deuteronomy 23:9, the sons of the third generation, supporting Rabbi Shimon's view that only sons are barred.
Rabbi Yehuda reads born to them in the same verse as making the prohibition depend on birth, applying to daughters too.
Rabbi Yohanan argues that if Rabbi Yehuda did not hold this, he would contradict himself, since a convert congregation is called the Lord's congregation.

78a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks how a second-generation Egyptian convert could ever become pure enough for his offspring to enter the congregation.
Perhaps a case where he transgresses and marries a Jew, but the verse does not write such hypothetical cases.
Asks whether the mamzer halakha is a case of if that the Torah writes despite being a transgression.
Objects that remarrying a divorcee is written as an allowance, yet the Torah writes it, so the rule does not hold.
A baraita expounds the words sons and generations in Deuteronomy 23:9, counting generations from the converts and following the disqualified parent.
Explains why each to them and that are born is necessary, including the mamzer's lo, and why the fetus counts as its own generation.
Rabba bar bar Hana reports Rabbi Yohanan that a child of a second-generation Egyptian man and first-generation woman is third generation, assigned to the father.
Rav Yosef objects from the mishna on Rabbi Tarfon, where a mamzer's child by his maidservant follows the mother, not the father.
Replies that the slave case differs, since Exodus 21:4 says her children belong to her master, so they follow the mother.
Rava objects from the Minyamin baraita: if the child followed the father, the grandson would be permitted even from a first-generation wife.
Answers that Rabbi Yohanan taught the baraita to say Minyamin sought to marry his son to a first-generation Egyptian convert.
Rav Dimi reports that Rabbi Yohanan held the opposite, that such a child follows the mother and is second generation.
Abaye objects from Rabbi Yohanan's ruling on a pregnant sin-offering animal, which would be inconsistent if the fetus were not a part of the mother.
If a fetus is a separate creature attached to its mother, the case is like setting aside two sin-offerings as a guarantee.
Cites Rav Oshaya's ruling on two sin-offerings set aside as a guarantee, one of which is left to graze.
If the fetus is part of the mother, its young is a sin-offering that must die, so Abaye suggests the Egyptian case differs by the verse on birth.
Rav Dimi says he saw Abaye's head between the pillars when Rabbi Yohanan taught that the reason is the verse on birth.
The Gemara infers that the child is assigned to the Egyptian mother only because of the verse, while otherwise it follows the father.
Asks why a child of a pregnant gentile who converts needs no immersion, if the child is not assigned to its mother.
Considers that Rabbi Yitzchak's principle on interposition explains the matter, since the fetus is not particular about its covering.

ranges.en: Objection citing Rav Kahana that a partial covering does not interpose but a full covering does, even without intent.
A fetus is different because the womb is its natural place of growth, so it is treated as immersed.
Ravina reports Rabbi Yochanan's rule that among gentiles lineage follows the male, but after conversion the more flawed parent counts.
A baraita derives from Leviticus 25:45 that a son of a gentile and a Canaanite woman may be bought as a slave.
The baraita limits that verse to children begotten in your land, so a child born abroad to a Canaanite father is excluded.
Restating the rule that converts who married after conversion follow the more flawed lineage.
What case is meant if the convert couple is an Egyptian man and an Ammonite woman, since that yields no flaw?
Ammonite men are barred but Ammonite women are not, so the case must be an Ammonite man with an Egyptian woman.
The mishna teaches that mamzerim and Nethinim are forbidden permanently, for both males and females.
Reish Lakish holds that a female mamzer is permitted after ten generations.
A verbal analogy of the word tenth links mamzer to Ammonites and Moabites, whose females are permitted.
Objection: perhaps the females should be permitted immediately, just as the Ammonite and Moabite females are.
The verbal analogy only takes effect from the tenth generation onward, so the view stands.
Objection: the mishna teaches that mamzerim are forbidden permanently for both sexes, contradicting Reish Lakish.
No contradiction: the mishna follows a tanna who limits verbal analogies, while Reish Lakish follows one who extends them.
Students ask Rabbi Eliezer what the status is of a mamzeret after ten generations.
Rabbi Eliezer replies that he wishes he had a third-generation mamzer whom he could declare pure.
Inferring that Rabbi Eliezer holds mamzerim do not survive, and that Rav Huna said the same.
Objection: the mishna says mamzerim are forbidden permanently, which seems impossible if they never live to a third generation.
Rabbi Zeira explains that known mamzerim survive while unknown ones perish, and suspected ones survive only three generations.
A story of a man whom Rabbi Ami declared a mamzer and who was then told he would live.
Rav Hanna bar Adda states that David decreed the Gibeonites barred from the congregation.
Support from II Samuel 21:2, where the king says the Gibeonites are not of Israel but of the Amorites.
Why did David decree that the Gibeonites may not enter the congregation?
II Samuel 21:1 reports a three-year famine in David's time, year after year.
David sought the cause: first he suspected idolatry, citing Deuteronomy, then examined the people and found no sinners.
In the second year David suspected sexual transgression among the people as the cause of the drought.
Jeremiah 3:3 links withheld rain to licentious behavior, supporting David's second suspicion.
They examined the people again and found no such sinners.
In the third year David suspected that people pledge charity publicly but do not actually give.
Proverbs 25:14 compares a false boaster of a gift to clouds and wind without rain.
Once again they searched and found no such sinners.
David concluded that the matter depends on him alone and sought God.
What did David's seeking of the presence of the Lord actually consist of?
Reish Lakish says David inquired through the Urim VeTummim.
From where is it inferred that the seeking was through the Urim VeTummim?
Rabbi Elazar derives it from the repeated phrase presence of the Lord used in both places.
Numbers 27:21 says the high priest shall inquire by the judgment of the Urim before the Lord.
II Samuel 21:1 gives God's answer that the trouble is for Saul and his bloody house for killing the Gibeonites.
The Gemara explains the verse: for Saul means he was not properly eulogized, and bloody house means he killed the Gibeonites.
Where do we find that Saul killed the Gibeonites at all?
Saul killed the priests of Nob, who supplied the Gibeonites, so the verse credits him as if he killed them.
Why does God demand retribution twice, for not eulogizing Saul and for killing the Gibeonites?
Yes, both demands stand, as Reish Lakish explains.
Zephaniah 2:3 shows that where justice against a person is mentioned, his good deeds should be mentioned too.
David said that regarding the eulogy for Saul, the matter had already passed.

79a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mourning period for Saul has long passed, so it is no longer proper to eulogize him.
David proposes calling the Gibeonites and trying to appease them.
II Samuel 21:1-6 records David asking the Gibeonites what atonement they want, and their demand for seven of Saul's sons.
The Gibeonites were not appeased by David's other efforts.
The Jewish people have three distinguishing marks: they are merciful, shamefaced, and perform acts of kindness.
Three verses, Deuteronomy 13:18, Exodus 20:17 and Genesis 18:19, support each of the three marks.
Anyone who has these three marks is fit to join this nation; those lacking them are not.
II Samuel 21:8 names the seven descendants of Saul whom the king took, the sons of Rizpah and Michal.
What distinguished these particular sons, that they were chosen from all of Saul's descendants?
Rav Huna says the descendants were passed before the Ark, and whoever the Ark held back was condemned to death.
Objection from II Samuel 21:7: if the Ark decided their fate, how could the king's pity change Mephibosheth's sentence?
David did not pass Mephibosheth in vain: he passed him, the Ark held him, and David asked for mercy so he was released.
Objection: this is still favoritism, since David's mercy would have meant another must die in his place.
Objection from Deuteronomy 24:16 that fathers and children are not put to death for each other's sins.
Rabbi Yochanan holds it is better to uproot one mitzva than let God's name be desecrated publicly, so David's action is justified.
II Samuel 21:10 describes Rizpah guarding the bodies on the rock from harvest until rain, keeping birds and beasts away.
Objection from Deuteronomy 21:23 that a hanged body must not remain overnight, so leaving them exposed was forbidden.
Rabbi Yochanan, citing Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak, explains it is better to uproot one letter so that God's name is sanctified publicly.
Passersby would ask what these hanged men had done, and learned they were sons of kings who had harmed converts.
An a fortiori argument: if the sons of kings are treated so, then ordinary people and converts deserve even harsher treatment.
Immediately one hundred and fifty thousand converts joined the Jewish people.
I Kings 5:29 reports Solomon's seventy thousand burden bearers and eighty thousand hewers in the mountains.
Objection: perhaps these workers were Jews, which cannot be the case.
I Kings 9:22 says that Solomon made no slaves of the children of Israel, so these workers were converts.
Objection: perhaps the workers were merely hired employees in public service, not converts.
II Chronicles 2:16-17 counts the converts in Eretz Yisrael and assigns seventy and eighty thousand to burden bearing and hewing.
Was David the one who decreed that the Gibeonites may not enter the congregation, or was it Moses?
Deuteronomy 29:10 mentions hewers of wood and drawers of water already in Moses' time.
Moses decreed only for that generation, while David's decree applied to all generations.
Objection: still, Joshua decreed on them the same fate of hewing wood and drawing water.
Joshua 9:27 says Joshua made the Gibeonites hewers of wood and drawers of water for the congregation and the altar.
Joshua's decree applied while the Temple stands, indicated by the altar phrase; David's decree applied even when it does not.

ranges.en: In the days of Rabbi, the Sages sought to permit the Gibeonites to enter the congregation.
Rabbi objects: even if we free our share, who can release the altar's share, which belongs to the Temple?
The Gemara says this disagrees with a teaching of Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba.
Rabbi Yochanan teaches that the congregation's share of the Gibeonites is forever forbidden, while the altar's share is forbidden only when the Temple stands.
Mishna: Rabbi Yehoshua reports two rulings about eunuchs and halitza and levirate, but cannot explain them.
Rabbi Akiva explains: a eunuch made by man may perform halitza and levirate, having had an hour of fitness; a natural eunuch may not.
Rabbi Eliezer reverses this: a natural eunuch may perform them because he can be cured, and a man-made one may not.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Beteira testified that the brothers of ben Megusat, a man-made eunuch, performed levirate marriage to uphold Rabbi Akiva's view.
A sexually underdeveloped man or woman may neither perform halitza nor enter levirate marriage.
If such a person performed halitza, the woman is not disqualified for priesthood, but intercourse with them is licentious and does disqualify her.
Objection: Rabbi Akiva holds violators of prohibitions are like karet-liable, who cannot perform halitza, so why is this eunuch's halitza valid?
Rabbi Ami answers that the eunuch's brother married a convert, and Rabbi Akiva follows Rabbi Yosei that converts are not a congregation of the Lord.
If so, the eunuch should also be able to perform levirate marriage with a convert.
Yes, that is so; because Rabbi Yehoshua says halitza, Rabbi Akiva also says halitza, though levirate is in fact permitted.
The mishna's precise wording about ben Megusat shows that according to Rabbi Akiva even levirate marriage is permitted.
Rabba objects from a baraita listing crushed, severed, man-made eunuch and elderly men as able to perform halitza or levirate.
The baraita's rulings on brothers' acts with the wives of impaired men, plus its verse prohibiting them from the congregation, show it concerns Jews from birth.
Rabba resolves it: the case is where the impairment came on afterward, so the levirate mitzva applied first.
Abaye objects: then the prohibition for a crushed man should override the positive mitzva of levirate marriage.
Mishna of Rabban Gamliel: a minor sister's refusal annuls the marriage, so the wife's sister prohibition overrides levirate, showing prohibitions can override the mitzva.
Rav Yosef says this tanna follows Rabbi Akiva's school, where only offspring from incest prohibitions is a mamzer.
Rabbi Akiva's view: violators of ordinary prohibitions are not mamzerim, so they are not called mamzerim.
Deuteronomy 25:7 says the levirate is to establish a name for his brother in Israel.
Question: how does levirate apply to this eunuch, who can no longer father children and so cannot establish a name?
Rava: if one unable now to father children is exempt, no woman would be fit for a yavam, since every dying man loses fertility shortly before death.
Rabbi Eliezer's view refutes Rava's proof, since Rabbi Eliezer holds a man made impaired is not like a dying man.
Rabbi Eliezer's reply: a dying man's weakness only blocks relations, while his basic ability to father children remains intact.
What are the circumstances of a eunuch by natural causes?
Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef reports Rabbi Yochanan's definition of a natural eunuch; the passage is cut off here and continues on the next daf.

ranges.en: A person who was never capable of fathering children from birth, never having had an hour of fitness.
How do we know that someone was born this way and was never fertile?
Abaye: one who urinates without forming an arch, with urine dribbling straight down, never had sexual capacity.
From what does this defect arise, what is its cause?
It results from the mother baking bread at noon and drinking strong beer while pregnant, overheating the child.
Rav Yosef says this matches what Rabbi Ami said about one impaired from the mother's womb, which he had not understood until now.
Perhaps he was cured for a time in between, so he had an hour of fitness?
Since both the beginning and the end of his condition are impaired, we need not be concerned about an interim cure.
Rav Mari objects from a mishna of Rabbi Hanina ben Antigonus about examining a blemished firstborn three times.
The mishna says a single-organ blemish may be cured meanwhile, but a whole-body defect is not presumed cured.
Rabbi Eliezer's ruling as stated in the mishna, rejecting the view that a natural eunuch cannot perform halitza.
The Gemara offers a contradiction from another mishna.
The mishna in Nidda says a man or woman lacking two pubic hairs at twenty is established as impaired, and gives the Beit Hillel and Beit Shammai rulings.
Rabbi Eliezer's view: men follow Beit Hillel and women follow Beit Shammai, since women mature faster.
Rami bar Dikulei reports Shmuel's view that Rabbi Eliezer retracted his opinion.
Which of Rabbi Eliezer's statements did he retract?
A baraita says Rabbi Eliezer holds a natural eunuch may perform halitza, since such men are cured in Alexandria of Egypt.
Rabbi Elazar says Rabbi Eliezer never retracted, and the age ruling in that mishna concerns punishments, not halitza.
Amoraic dispute: a boy who ate forbidden fat, later showing impairment signs and then two hairs, is a eunuch retroactively per Rav, but a minor per Shmuel.
Rav Yosef objects: by Rav's view, a sexually underdeveloped woman by Rabbi Meir should be entitled to the rapist's fine.
Abaye replies that a sexually underdeveloped woman passes directly from minor to adult, so she gets no rapist's fine.
Rav Yosef praises the answer and wishes such fine points were attributed to him.
A baraita says an impaired man is not judged as a rebellious son, and an impaired betrothed woman is not judged as a betrothed young woman, corroborating Abaye.
Rabbi Abbahu: signs of impairment, or of an eighth-month child, are not acted on until the person reaches twenty.
Can a child born in the eighth month survive at all?
A baraita says an eighth-month child is like a stone, so it may not be moved on Shabbat, though its mother may nurse it.

80b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Because of the danger, in what case are we dealing here, with regard to the eighth-month baby?
We are dealing with a baby whose signs of viability are complete.
A baraita defines an eighth-month baby as one whose months are not complete, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi uses hair and nails as signs.
If hair and nails are fully developed, the child was fit for seven months but was delayed in the womb.
But if so, on what basis did Rava Tosfa'a rule on the case of the delayed child?
A woman whose husband went overseas carried her child for twelve months, and Rava Tosfa'a declared the child fit.
Whose opinion was that ruling based on, since it followed the view that a baby can be delayed?
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel also holds that a baby can be delayed, so Rava Tosfa'a followed the majority.
A baraita of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: a child who lives thirty days is not considered stillborn.
Sages taught the signs of a natural eunuch: no pubic hairs at twenty, a defective beard and hair, smooth skin, and urine that does not foam.
Other opinions list further signs: urine without an arch, semen failing to congeal, urine not fermenting, and no steam when bathing.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar: a defective voice that does not reveal whether one is a man or a woman.
Signs of a sexually underdeveloped woman: no pubic hairs at twenty, no breasts, and pain during intercourse.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: a woman lacking the lower abdominal flesh that other women have.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar: a thick voice that does not reveal whether a woman is a woman or a man.
Rav Huna requires all the signs of a eunuch to be present, while Rabbi Yochanan requires only one.
Where one has grown two beard hairs, all agree that all signs are needed; they disagree only when no hairs have grown.
If so, on which view did Rabba bar Avuh instruct the Sages to examine Rav Nachman, one with steam or with all signs?
No: Rav Nachman had wisps of a beard, so Rabba bar Avuh wanted to check whether he showed the other signs.
Mishna: a sexually underdeveloped man or woman neither performs halitza nor enters levirate marriage.
The Gemara infers that as a woman's impairment is from Heaven, a man's must be too, matching Rabbi Akiva's view.
Mishna: a eunuch who performed halitza with his yevama does not disqualify her from the priesthood.
The reason is that he is her yavam; intercourse with another man would be different and would not disqualify her.

ranges.en: Objection: does this not refute Rav Hamnuna, who held that a yavam's widow who was unfaithful is disqualified from marrying her yavam?
Rav Hamnuna's view: a waiting widow who committed adultery is disqualified from levirate marriage with her yavam.
No refutation: the same ruling holds even if she was with another man, and the tanna taught the rule about the yavam for both clauses.
Mishna: a sexually underdeveloped woman whose brothers-in-law performed halitza is not disqualified; intercourse with her disqualifies her.
The reason is that intercourse disqualifies her, so without intercourse she is not disqualified.
Whose opinion is this? It cannot be Rabbi Yehuda, who considers such a woman as one who had forbidden relations.
Mishna: a priest who is a natural eunuch who marries an Israelite woman enables her to eat teruma, and Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon say the same for a hermaphrodite.
Rabbi Yehuda on tumtum and hermaphrodite status for halitza and marriage, and Rabbi Eliezer's view on punishment by stoning.
Is this not obvious, since an impotent priest should evidently be able to enable his wife to eat teruma?
The ruling is needed in case one thinks the priest's ability to father children matters, based on the verse about those born in his house.
Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon hold that a hermaphrodite priest enables his wife to eat teruma.
Reish Lakish: such a priest enables teruma but not the breast and thigh of peace-offerings.
Rabbi Yochanan: such a priest enables even the breast and thigh of peace-offerings.
Why does Reish Lakish distinguish, since teruma and the breast and thigh are both by Torah law?
The distinction concerns teruma in the present, which is only by rabbinic law, while when the Temple stands the ruling differs.
Why did the tanna not teach the distinction within the teruma case itself?
The formulation would be that this applies only to rabbinic teruma, while Torah teruma is not covered.
Reish Lakish means that the permission covers present rabbinic teruma, but not the breast and thigh, lest she eat Torah teruma.
Rabbi Yochanan holds that the hermaphrodite priest even enables his wife to eat the breast and thigh of peace-offerings.
Yochanan asks Reish Lakish whether he holds that present-day teruma is only by rabbinic law.
Reish Lakish says yes, since a cake of figs is different: one cake among a hundred cakes is nullified.
Rabbi Yochanan objects: a piece of sin-offering among pieces is nullified, and only what is always sold by count is not nullified.
What is the mishna Rabbi Yochanan alludes to, about bundles of clover of forbidden mixtures that became mixed with others?

81b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Meir holds countable items make a mixture forbidden so it must all be burned; the Sages say only six items are unnullifiable, at one to two hundred.
Mishna: Rabbi Akiva lists seven items, including homeowner's loaves, and the prohibitions of orla and vineyard mixtures they carry.
Rabbi Yochanan reads the mishna as limited to items always sold by count, while Reish Lakish reads it as any item usually counted.
What is the case of a piece that Rabbi Yochanan refers to?
A baraita: an impure sin-offering piece nullifies among a hundred pure ones, but a pure piece does not nullify among ordinary meat; Rabbi Yehuda disagrees.
The first clause shows an impure piece can be nullified, which seems to contradict Reish Lakish's view of countable items.
Rabbi Hiyya bar Rav Huna: the baraita speaks of a piece that was crushed, and once it is no longer whole it can be nullified.
If the piece was crushed, what is the reason for Rabbi Yehuda's view that it is not nullified?

82a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yehuda follows his own principle that one kind of food mixed with its own kind cannot be nullified.
If the meat was not crushed, would it still not be nullified, and why not teach the distinction within the pure sacred case?
The tanna prefers to teach the novel case of pure items mixed with pure items, even though he could have distinguished within impurity.
What makes the first clause different from the latter clause, why is nullification possible for impure but not pure pieces?
Rav Sheisha bar Idi: the first clause concerns rabbinic impurity from liquids, while the latter concerns sacred food forbidden to non-priests by Torah law.
If the impurity came from a creeping animal, by Torah law, would the piece still be nullified, and why not distinguish within the case?
The tanna still prefers to teach the novel case of pure items mixed with pure items.
Rabba's alternative: the first clause risks a standard prohibition, while the latter risks a karet prohibition, so the piece is not nullified.
Objection: Rabba himself held that no difference exists between standard and karet prohibitions for nullification of Torah-forbidden items.
Rav Ashi's alternative: sacred meat is temporarily forbidden, and temporarily forbidden items cannot be nullified even at one in a thousand.
Rejection: Rav Ashi's teaching is a mistake, since the prohibition on sacred meat is for a priest permitted and for an Israelite always forbidden.
Does Rabbi Yochanan hold that present-day teruma is by Torah law?
A baraita about two baskets and two se'a vessels of teruma and non-sacred produce, where the mixture is permitted since each item fell into its own kind.
Reish Lakish requires the permitted produce to be greater in quantity, while Rabbi Yochanan permits even without that.
Reish Lakish's view makes sense if present-day teruma is rabbinic, but if Rabbi Yochanan holds it is Torah law, the permission is difficult.
Rabbi Yochanan can answer that the baraita follows the Rabbis, who hold present-day teruma is only rabbinic.

ranges.en: Rabbi Yochanan explains his view: it follows Rabbi Yosei, who holds that teruma nowadays is by Torah law.
A baraita in Seder Olam reads Deuteronomy 30:5 as showing two inheritances of the land, with no third.
Rabbi Yochanan identifies the tanna of Seder Olam as Rabbi Yosei, who holds the second sanctity never lapsed.
Objection: does Rabbi Yochanan not require a permitted majority even for rabbinic prohibitions?
Mikvaot 7:2: a mikveh of forty se'a remains fit after adding and removing a se'a of other liquid.
Rabbi Yochanan's view is that the mikveh remains fit up to the greater part, and the baskets case differs because each item is assumed to fall into its own kind.
The mishna says a hermaphrodite may marry a woman, which suggests ab initio, so the text should be emended to if he married.
But the mishna teaches he may marry a woman, and the next clause says he may not marry a man, so what does it mean?
May marry means ab initio, while may not be married means invalid even after the fact, so the difficulty against Reish Lakish remains.
Objection: the mishna's ruling that intercourse with a hermaphrodite is punished by stoning as with a male implies the first tanna is uncertain.
Both tannaim hold a hermaphrodite is a full male; they differ on whether intercourse in one or two places incurs stoning.
Rav said: the passage is cut off here and continues on the next daf.

83a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishna's ruling that a hermaphrodite priest enables teruma is not to be relied on against a contrary baraita.
A baraita of Rabbi Yosei: a hermaphrodite is a creature unto himself, and the Sages never decided if he is male or female.
Objection: on the contrary, the baraita should give way to the mishna, since baraitot are less authoritative.
Rabbi Yosei left his colleague Rabbi Shimon in the mishna, so he must have retracted his earlier view.
Shmuel says the reverse: the mishna is not to be relied on against the baraita.
Objection: on the contrary, Shmuel accepts a lone dissent in a baraita, so the mishna should give way.
Shmuel accepts a baraita only when it does not uproot the mishna; when it uproots it, he disregards it.
The school of Rav reports the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei on hermaphrodites and grafting; Shmuel says on protracted labor and proscription.
Clarification: the hermaphrodite halakha is as stated, and the grafting halakha is as learned in a mishna.
Shevi'it 2:6: one may not plant or graft within thirty days before the Sabbatical year, with differing periods given by Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon.
Rav Nachman explains the periods: the rooting time plus thirty days, and Rav rules like Rabbi Yosei.
Shmuel rules like Rabbi Yosei on protracted labor and proscription too.
What is the case of protracted labor?
Nidda 36b: tannaim dispute how long bleeding is attributed to protracted labor: forty or fifty days, a month, or two weeks; Shmuel follows Rabbi Yosei.
Kilayim 7:4: a vine overshadowing another's grain proscribes it and its owner bears responsibility, per Rabbi Meir, with Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon differing.

ranges.en: A person cannot make forbidden an item that does not belong to him.
A dilemma: what did Shmuel rule about the hermaphrodite case?
Come and hear: Shmuel told Rav Anan that a baraita does not override a mishna.
What did Shmuel rule on grafting?
Shmuel told Rav Anan to teach the view of the one who prohibits planning thirty-three days before the Sabbatical year, which suggests Rabbi Yehuda.
What did Rav rule about protracted labor, whether he follows Rabbi Yosei as Shmuel did?
Rav's ruling is unresolved, so the dilemma stands.
What did Rav rule on proscription?
Rav Yosef cites Rav Huna, who reports Rav's ruling that the halakha does not follow Rabbi Yosei.
Abaye objects: what did you see that made you rely on that source?
Rav Adda reports Rav's ruling that the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei, establishing Rav's acceptance of that view.
The school of Rav's teaching refers to Rav Huna, who ruled the halakha does not follow Rabbi Yosei, so Rav Adda's version is in error.
Mishna: Rabbi Yehuda rules that a tumtum torn open is treated as a eunuch and may not perform halitza.
Rabbi Ami objects: what would Rabbi Yehuda do with the tumtum who was torn open and later fathered seven children?
Rabbi Yehuda could have said to inquire about the children's origin, since he did not believe this man fathered them.
A baraita of Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda: a tumtum may not perform halitza, since he may be found to be a eunuch by nature.
Is it to say that every tumtum who is torn open is a male, when he could be a female?
Rabbi Yosei meant that he may be found female, who cannot perform halitza, or male but a eunuch by nature.
What is the practical difference between the views of Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei?
Rava: if other brothers exist, Rabbi Yosei disqualifies them via halitza, and without other brothers he must perform halitza.
A chain of transmission: Rav held that a hermaphrodite incurs stoning for intercourse in either of two places.
Objection from a baraita of Rabbi Eliezer: only intercourse through the male organ incurs stoning; through the female organ he is exempt.
Rav stated his view in accordance with the tanna of this baraita, that of Rabbi Simai.
Baraita: Rabbi Simai holds that intercourse with a hermaphrodite in either of two places incurs stoning.
What is the reasoning of Rabbi Simai?
Rava: Bar Hamedurei explained that the plural mishkevei isha in Leviticus 18:22 implies a hermaphrodite with two manners of lying.
The Rabbis counter that the verse also says with a male, so liability applies only to male-manner intercourse.
From where do the Rabbis derive that relations with an ordinary male are prohibited?
They derive it from the word woman, and from the inclusive and, which covers unnatural intercourse with a woman.
Rav Shezvi reports Rav Hisda: Rabbi Eliezer did not say a hermaphrodite is fully male in every respect.
Rabbi Eliezer's view: a hermaphrodite is a proper male.
Objection: if so, a hermaphrodite animal consecrated should become sacred.
From where do we know it does not become sacred?
A baraita lists prohibited birds, including tumtum and hermaphrodite birds, which if pinched render the killer and garments impure.
Rabbi Eliezer says pinching a tumtum or hermaphrodite bird does not render impure, since it is fit for the altar.
Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning: where male and female are stated, remove tumtum and hermaphrodite, but birds lack such terms, so they remain fit.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: we learned this explicitly in a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer says the same; the passage continues next daf.
