ranges.en: First riddle: a woman's half brother from her father is also her mother's husband, and she is his wife's daughter.
Rami bar Ḥama: this is possible only if it is not according to Rabbi Yehuda, since the Rabbis permit it.
Second riddle: a woman calls a man her brother and son, and herself his sister, whom she carries on her shoulders.
Solution: a gentile who had intercourse with his daughter, and she bore him a son who is both brother and son to her.
Third riddle: a woman greets a man as her son while calling herself the daughter of his sister.
Solution: a gentile who had intercourse with his daughter's daughter, producing a son whose mother is his sister's daughter.
Fourth riddle: a boy the woman carries is her son, and she is the daughter of his brother.
Solution: a gentile who had intercourse with his son's daughter, since their son is also her uncle.
Fifth riddle: a woman's father, husband, stepson and mother's husband are all one man, and she is the wife's daughter.
Solution: a gentile who had intercourse with his mother, bearing a daughter, then with her, and the old man as well.
Sixth riddle: a speaker says he and the addressee, and their parents, are all siblings.
Solution: a gentile who had intercourse with his mother, bearing two daughters, then one of them, bearing the son.
Seventh riddle: the same kinship, described as cousins instead of siblings, is said of a permitted family.
Solution: a permitted case, with Reuven's two daughters married to his brothers Shimon and Levi, and cousins from mothers' sides.
Mishnah: sons who converted with their mother are not subject to ḥalitza or levirate marriage for each other's wives, even if one was conceived before conversion.
The sons of Yudan the freed maidservant: Rav Aḥa bar Ya'akov permitted them to marry each other's wives after divorce.
Rava objects that Rav Sheshet prohibited this; Rav Aḥa replies that he prohibited it and he himself permits it.
Everyone agrees: half brothers from the father only are permitted, and half brothers from the mother only are prohibited.
The dispute concerns full brothers: Rav Aḥa follows the paternal line, while Rav Sheshet also uses the maternal line.
Another version: Rav Aḥa disputes even maternal half brothers, since a new convert is like a newborn, disregarding his past family.
Recites the mishnah on converted sons and their wives, not subject to ḥalitza or levirate marriage.
Asks whether the reason is that they are prohibited from marrying each other's wives.
No: the wives are not included in ḥalitza and levirate law, since they are unrelated, so each is permitted to others, and they to her.
Asks why the mishna says 'even' if they are permitted, since the first explanation with 'even' fits only a prohibition.
Even though both were born in sanctity, people may confuse them with born Jews, yet they are still permitted to marry each other's wives.
Another version: it is reasonable that they are permitted, since the mishna says 'even' if the mother converted while pregnant.
If permitted, 'even' fits: both were born in sanctity, and confusion with Jews from birth does not forbid them.
Asks what 'even' means on the alternative reading, if they are in fact prohibited.
The mishna's 'even' refers to the first son conceived outside sanctity, like two mothers' sons, and they are still prohibited.
A baraita: converted or freed twins, and their brothers' wives, are not liable for karet for intercourse, which shows the Rabbis' view.

98a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Gemara resolves that the baraita teaches only the absence of liability, since its first clause also shows there is none.
Rava: the rule that a gentile has no paternal lineage holds even when paternity is known, so there is no concern about it.
Identical twins from one drop have one father, yet they are not liable, which shows the Merciful One disowns a gentile's offspring (Ezekiel 23:20).
Come and hear: Rabbi Yosei relates that the convert Niftayim married his maternal half brother's wife, and the Sages ruled a convert's marriage is invalid.
The Gemara objects that the baraita should be read as saying there is no prohibition, since a convert cannot have betrothed a woman.
Asks what the baraita teaches if the brother married her as a gentile, since that is obviously permitted.
Lest one decree that a marriage while gentile is forbidden as if it occurred after conversion; the baraita teaches there is no such decree.
Come and hear: a convert married his maternal brother's wife, and Rabbi Akiva ruled that a convert may marry the former wife of his maternal half brother.
The baraita refers to a brother who married while still a gentile, and it teaches that no decree applies to such a case.
Questions the reliability of the convert who cited Rabbi Akiva, since the ruling benefited him personally, citing Rav's rule on timing.
The convert may be reliable: he taught the ruling before marrying, or he cited a case, or the cited teaching is an unrelated one.
Rabbi Akiva inferred that the Divine Presence spoke with Jonah only a second time, not a third.
II Kings 14:25 says Jonah prophesied for King Jeroboam, which contradicts that inference.
Ravina: Jonah had no third prophecy about Nineveh; Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak: the verse means Israel's fortune turned as Nineveh's did.
Come and hear: a convert born in sanctity but conceived outside it has maternal but not paternal kinship, with consequences for marriage.

98b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Baraita on half sisters: a father's maternal sister is maintained, a mother's maternal sister divorced; Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis differ on a mother's paternal sister.
Rabbi Meir's rule: any relative forbidden through the mother must be divorced, while one forbidden through the father may be kept.
Permitted: a maternal brother's wife, a paternal uncle's wife, and other forbidden relatives, with the father's wife included.
A man who married a woman and her daughter after conversion may keep one, not ab initio; after his wife dies he may keep the mother-in-law, per a dispute.
Asks whether the baraita is really about a brother who married her after conversion, since that would not be needed.
No, it concerns a brother who married her while still a gentile.
Asks what the baraita teaches if the marriage was as a gentile, since that is obviously permitted.
Lest one decree that such a marriage is forbidden; the baraita teaches there is no such decree.
The Master taught: a man who married a woman and her daughter after conversion may keep one, not ab initio.
Asks why it must be said that he should not marry ab initio, since he must divorce one anyway.
That ruling refers to the previous sentence: the wives the Sages allowed him to keep should not be married ab initio.
The two baraitot differ on the mother-in-law after the wife dies: one follows Rabbi Yishmael, the other Rabbi Akiva.
Rabbi Yishmael holds the mother-in-law stays forbidden, so the Sages decreed against a convert; Rabbi Akiva holds the prohibition weakens.
Mishnah: five women with mixed lineage; four unmixed brothers perform ḥalitza with one widow each, and one may perform levirate marriage.
Inference from the mishnah: ḥalitza is performed first, since levirate marriage first would breach the ban on a yevama with a stranger.
Asks why one brother who performed levirate marriage should not perform it with all the widows.
Each brother should perform levirate marriage with one widow, so that one may happen upon his own sister-in-law and the others still have the mitzva.
Baraita: among brothers, maternal brothers perform ḥalitza and those who are only paternal brothers perform levirate marriage.
Asks what the baraita means by this distinction.
Rav Safra: maternal brothers perform ḥalitza with all, since each may be a forbidden maternal sister-in-law; paternal brothers perform levirate marriage.
Baraita continues: priests perform ḥalitza and non-priests levirate marriage, and any mix with maternal brothers performs ḥalitza only.

99a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A baraita: one may perform ḥalitza with his mother, sister or daughter due to uncertainty, though no levirate bond can form with them.
Example: a mother and another woman bear mixed sons and daughters, so each son performs ḥalitza with both women due to uncertainty.
Example: a man performs ḥalitza with his half sister due to uncertainty, when mixed births produce paternal half siblings.
Example: a man performs ḥalitza with his daughter due to uncertainty, when his wife and another woman bear mixed daughters.
Rabbi Meir: a man and a woman can sometimes produce children of five nations, a different lineage category for each.
Illustration: a Jew's slave and maidservant produce a convert, a gentile, a slave, a mamzer, and a regular Jew through conversion and freeing.
Asks what the baraita is teaching with this example.
It teaches that the offspring of a gentile or slave with a Jewish woman is a mamzer.
A man may sell his father to collect his mother's marriage contract, if the father was a slave bequeathed to the son through the mother.
Asks what new point this baraita teaches.
Rabbi Meir's view: a slave is mortgaged for a marriage contract like movable property, or like real estate on all views.
Mishnah: a woman's offspring mixed with her daughter-in-law's; the certain sons of the daughter-in-law perform ḥalitza but not levirate marriage.
The certain sons of the elder woman perform either ḥalitza or levirate marriage, since the wife's status is uncertain.
If the dead were the sons of certain lineage, the mixed sons perform ḥalitza with the elder woman's widows, one ḥalitza and one levirate marriage.
A priestess whose offspring is mixed with her maidservant's may eat teruma, as both priest and priest's slave may eat it.

99b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishnah: the mixed sons may not become impure through a corpse, and may not marry women whether fit or unfit for the priesthood.
Once the mixed sons mature and free each other, they may marry women fit for priesthood, but not those unfit for it.
Mishnah: they may not eat teruma or become impure, and no one takes or gives them teruma, though their own produce is sold and kept.
Mishnah: they receive no consecrated offerings and are exempt from priestly gifts, while their firstling is kept until it gets a blemish.
Mishnah: if the sons of certain, unflawed lineage died, the mixed sons perform ḥalitza with the elder woman's widows but not levirate marriage.
Asks whether this implies the mixed sons are unfit merely because their lineage is unclear.
Rava Pappa: the correct wording is that the certain sons died, so the mixed sons are not described as unfit.
Mishnah: with the widows of the certain sons, one mixed son performs ḥalitza and the other levirate marriage, and ḥalitza is first.
Mishnah: a priestess whose offspring is mixed with her maidservant's receives one share of teruma in the granary.
Asks whether it is obvious they receive only one share, and proposes they receive a share together.
Tannaitic dispute: Rabbi Yehuda says teruma may be given to a slave only with his master; Rabbi Yosei allows it alone.
Background: in Rabbi Yehuda's place receiving teruma established presumptive priesthood, while in Rabbi Yosei's place it did not.
Baraita: Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok says a slave was almost promoted to presumptive priesthood on the basis of his one testimony.
Asks whether the Sages really promoted him, since God does not bring a stumbling block through the righteous.
Rabbi Elazar saw a man receive teruma in Rabbi Yosei's place and testified in Rabbi Yehuda's place, which nearly made him a priest.
Ten types of persons may not be given teruma in the granary, such as a deaf-mute and a slave, though it may be sent to their homes.
Asks why teruma may not be given to a deaf-mute, imbecile, and minor, and also not to a tumtum or hermaphrodite.

100a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Teruma is withheld from a slave, an uncircumcised man, an impure man, and one married to an unfit woman, for reasons of propriety and penalty.
Asks what the reason is that teruma is not distributed to a woman.
Rav Pappa and Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, give two reasons: a divorcee who may eat teruma, and concern about being alone in the granary.
Asks what practical difference there is between the two reasons.
The difference shows in a granary near town or one distant but frequented, depending on whether the divorce is known or the seclusion concern applies.
Baraita: teruma may be sent to the homes of all of them except an impure man and one married to an unfit woman.
Asks why an uncircumcised man may receive teruma while an impure man may not.
The uncircumcised man's state is entirely beyond his control, since circumcision is life-threatening, unlike the impure man's.
Baraita: teruma is not given to a slave or woman in the granary, but where it is distributed the woman is given first and released.
Asks how there can be a place where it is distributed, if it is not given to them at all.
The baraita refers to the poor man's tithe from the owner's house, and a woman goes first to spare her the shame of waiting with men.
Rava: he used to resolve a man's quarrel first, but after hearing this baraita he resolves the woman's first, out of shame.
Mishnah: if the mixed sons matured and freed each other, they may marry women fit for priesthood; freeing is not compelled.
Asks why they cannot marry a maidservant or a free woman, given their doubtful status.
Rava: say they are compelled to free each other, since they cannot otherwise fulfill the mitzva to be fruitful and multiply.
Mishnah: the mixed sons are subject to both the stringencies of priests and those of Israelites.
Asks with regard to what halakha the stringencies apply beyond those the mishnah cites.
Rav Pappa: the meal-offering's handful is taken like an Israelite's, but the rest is not eaten like a priest's, so each part is offered separately.
Asks how this can be done, since partly burned offerings may not have the rest burned as an offering.
Rabbi Yehuda son of Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi: the remainder is brought up only as wood, following Rabbi Elazar's ruling on sweet savor.
Asks what can be said according to the Rabbis, who disagree that the remainder may be burned as fuel.
The case follows Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon: the remainder is scattered over the ashes, and the Rabbis agree here.
Mishnah: a woman who remarried too soon and whose son's paternity is uncertain; brothers from both husbands perform ḥalitza but not levirate marriage.

100b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishnah: a son of two uncertain fathers, one Israelite and one priest, is restricted as a possible priest and a possible non-priest.
Mishnah: he may not eat teruma, is not given consecrated food, and is subject to both priestly and Israelite stringencies.
Mishnah: if both fathers were priests, mourning and burial rules apply to each, and inheritance runs only from him to them.
Mishnah: he is exempt from punishment for striking or cursing either father and serves in both priestly watches.
Gemara: the mishnah's half brothers from each father perform ḥalitza first and levirate marriage only afterward, to avoid a stranger's yevama.
Shmuel: if one of ten priests left the group and had a child, the child is shetuki, a child of unknown father.
Asks what shetuki means: if it means cut off from the father's property, that is obvious, since the father is unknown.
It means he is barred from priesthood, though his father is certainly a priest.
Asks what the reason is for barring him from priesthood.
Numbers 25:13: the priesthood is for his seed after him, so descendants must be traceable to a known lineage.
Rav Pappa objects: Genesis 17:7 uses the same phrase for Abraham, so the verse cannot mean an unknown parent bars a person.
It means God forbade Abraham a gentile woman or maidservant, since the child's status follows the mother's.
A baraita: a priest's levirate son by a brother's wife is fit to be High Priest, which seems to conflict with the lineage requirement.
The lineage requirement is rabbinic, with the verse as support; the decree barring the unknown-father child applies only to licentious unions.
Asks whether the Sages decreed anything for licentious unions, citing the mishnah on a woman who remarried within three months.
Asks what the phrase 'after separating from her husband' means.
If it means after the husband's death, the mishnah's mourning rules cannot apply, since the first husband is already dead.
If it means a divorcee, the burial rule is hard to explain for the first husband, who would be allowed to bury him.
Whichever is his father, one of the two would be permitted to become impure to bury him, so the divorce reading fails.
The mishnah refers to licentious intercourse with an unmarried woman, and the child is still a priest, refuting Shmuel's view.
Rav Shemaya: the mishnah concerns a minor girl who refused her husband, which nullifies the marriage without making her a divorcee.
Asks how a girl who refused her husband can give birth, given the rules on contraception.
Rav Beivai's baraita: minors, pregnant and nursing women may use contraception, per Rabbi Meir, with the age range defined.
The Rabbis say all women may have intercourse normally, relying on Heaven's mercy, citing Psalms 116:6.
Solution: a mistaken betrothal, where the marriage is nullified, so the woman may marry a priest and the child's father is uncertain.
Shmuel's view via Rabbi Yishmael: the extra word 'she' shows a woman with a mistaken betrothal who may return to her husband.

101a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Sages taught: when both uncertain fathers were priests, striking or cursing either one is capital; Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes simultaneous and successive acts.
Asks: isn't it taught that Rabbi Yehuda exempts even for simultaneous striking or cursing, contradicting this baraita?
These are two tanna'im, each stating an opinion in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda.
Asks what the reasoning is of the one who exempts the son from punishment.
Rabbi Ḥanina: blessing is used as a euphemism for cursing, so cursing applies only where paternity is certain, and striking is linked to cursing.
Mishnah: he ascends to Temple service with the watch of both uncertain fathers but receives no share of either.
Asks why he ascends at all, since he gains no share and would not want to perform a mitzva unfit for him.
The mishnah says he ascends in the present tense, so he is obligated to ascend even against his will.
Rabbi Yoḥanan: he is obligated due to the potential family flaw, lest people infer that both families are unfit for priesthood.
Mishnah: if both uncertain fathers were in one priestly watch, he receives one share.
Asks what distinguishes the case of two watches, where he gets no share, from one watch, where he does.
Rav Pappa: if both were in one watch and one patrilineal family, he receives one share, since he cannot be rejected.
Mishnah on ḥalitza: it is performed before three judges, and the shoe must be leather and suitably fit for the foot to be valid.
Asks why the mishnah mentions judges at all, if even three laymen are acceptable.
It teaches that the three must be able to recite the verses like judges, though they need not be expert adjudicators.
A baraita: ḥalitza is performed before three who know how to recite like judges; Rabbi Yehuda says five.
Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning: two elders and then one more for an odd court, giving five judges on his reading of the verses.
The Tanna Kamma's reasoning: the verses give two elders each, and an odd court gives three judges.
Asks what the first tanna does with the second use of the word 'elders'.
It includes even three laymen as judges, since two restrictive terms together widen the rule.
Asks from where Rabbi Yehuda derives that laymen may conduct ḥalitza.
Deuteronomy 25:9 'before the eyes' excludes the blind, implying that laymen are qualified judges for ḥalitza.
Asks why the blind need excluding if ḥalitza required judges fit for the Sanhedrin.
Rav Yosef's baraita: as a court must be clean in righteousness, it must also be free of physical blemish.

101b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Song of Songs 4:7: 'no blemish in you', used to show that only the blind are excluded from judging ḥalitza.
Asks what the first tanna does with the verse 'before the eyes of'.
It supports Rava's ruling that judges must see the spittle from the yevama's mouth during ḥalitza, per Deuteronomy 25:9.
Asks whether Rabbi Yehuda also needs 'before the eyes' for Rava's ruling.
Yes, Rabbi Yehuda reads 'before the eyes' that way, and so derives lay eligibility elsewhere.
Asks from where Rabbi Yehuda derives that laymen may serve as judges.
From 'in Israel' in Deuteronomy 25:10, which allows any Israelite, even a non-expert, to preside.
Asks what the first tanna does with the phrase 'in Israel'.
It teaches that the court must be of Israelites from birth, not of converts, as Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda taught.
Asks from where Rabbi Yehuda derives this halakha about converts.
'In Israel' appears again, and Rabbi Tarfon's practice shows witnesses must respond, derived from 'shall be called'.
If the plural 'elders' requires more judges, other plural verbs would also demand extra judges, giving nine or seven.
Those plural verbs teach that the court itself calls the yavam and advises him on suitability of age, avoiding strife.
Rava reports Rav Naḥman: ḥalitza is performed before three men, since an unattributed mishnah gives this rule.
Rava objects: then refusal, which is also before three judges, should follow the same rule as a baraita on refusal shows.
A baraita: Beit Shammai require an expert court for refusal, and both schools agree three are needed, unlike Rabbi Yosei's two.
Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Yosei validate refusal before two men.
Rav Yosef bar Minyumi: Rav Naḥman ruled in accordance with that pair, so he departs from the unattributed mishnah on ḥalitza.
The sources differ: refusal has one unattributed mishnah, while ḥalitza has several, so three suffices for ḥalitza.
Asks why the number of unattributed mishnayot matters, since each source is equally an unattributed mishnah.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak: the three-judge mishnah sits beside a dispute involving Rabbi Yehuda, which supports the ruling.
Mishnah in Sanhedrin: Rabbi Yehuda says five for ordination, but ḥalitza is three, showing he retracted his view on ḥalitza.
Rava: judges must set a fixed location for ḥalitza, as Deuteronomy 25:7 mentions the gate.
Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua used five judges only to publicize the matter, since Rabbi Yehuda had retracted.
Rav Ashi and Rav Kahana: Rav Yehuda had a reed bundle designated as the ḥalitza location, and five were gathered only to publicize.
Rav Yehuda sent Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda to join the five, and he objected that he was a convert, so the court must be of born Jews.
Rav Yehuda's answer seems to accept one witness, which contradicts the rule that two witnesses are required.
Rav Yehuda meant he would invalidate a bill of indebtedness based on the convert's claim that the debt was paid.
Asks whether one man's word can exact payment, given the requirement of two or three witnesses in Deuteronomy 19:15.
Rav Yehuda's intent was to invalidate a document based on the claim, not to exact payment from one witness.
Rava begins a further statement about converts and courts of ḥalitza.

102a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: By Torah law a convert may judge a fellow convert, since Deuteronomy 17:15 'from among your brothers' applies only to Jews by birth.
A convert whose mother was Israelite may judge civil cases, but for ḥalitza both parents must be Israelite, per Deuteronomy 25:10.
Rabba, citing Rav: if Elijah said a soft leather shoe may be used, they would accept it, but not for a sandal, which is customary.
Rav Yosef, citing Rav: if Elijah said a soft shoe may not be used, they would accept it, but not that a sandal may not be used.
Asks what the practical difference is between the two versions, since both seem to say the same thing.
The difference is whether ḥalitza with a soft leather shoe may be done ab initio, or only after the fact.
Asks whether, on the view that ab initio is allowed, the mishnah's wording that ḥalitza with a soft shoe is valid after the fact is problematic.
The mishnah's wording only reflects its later case, the cloth anpileya, which is disqualified even after the fact.
Rabbi Yosei relates that Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira's ḥalitza was performed with a shoe or sandal, asking an elder who had seen it.
The elder says a soft shoe is not permitted, and Rabbi Yosei notes that Rabbi Meir allowed ḥalitza with a soft shoe, showing a dispute.
Rabbi Ya'akov in Rabbi Meir's name permits a soft shoe ab initio, while others forbid it ab initio.
Asks what the reason is for the view that a soft shoe is not permitted ab initio.
Hypothesis: the shoe's upper and straps make it not on the foot, but that would make it invalid even after the fact, which the Torah does not say.
It is a rabbinic decree, lest a torn soft shoe or a half shoe be used, which there is no similar concern for with a sandal.
Rav: without seeing Rabbi Ḥiyya use a laced sandal, he would use only a tight sandal; the strap is tied to make ḥalitza of the highest standard.
A mnemonic: the release of a yevama is done with a sandal, the sandal being the means of release.
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav: a yevama is released to the public when most of the heel is removed from the shoe.
A baraita objects: if the shoe was untied or the yavam removed most of his foot, ḥalitza is invalid, which challenges the heel ruling.
The Gemara infers from the baraita that if the yevama removes most of the foot, the ḥalitza is valid, but not the heel alone.
Most of the foot is the same as most of the heel, since the leg's weight presses on the heel, so the heel suffices.
This baraita supports Rabbi Yannai, who requires both untying and removal by the parties for ḥalitza to be valid.
Asks whether ḥalitza requires removal of the shoe or exposure of the foot, when she tore the sandal instead or burned it.
Rabbi Neḥemya asks about two shoes, one on the other, and what the halakha is if the outer one is removed.
The case is where she tore the outer shoe and removed the inner one, leaving the outer one still on the foot.
Asks whether valid ḥalitza requires removal of the shoe, which occurred, or exposure of the foot, which did not occur here.

102b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether anyone actually wears one shoe on top of another.
Yes: the Sages saw Rav Yehuda go out to the market wearing five pairs of slipper-like shoes, one on top of another.
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav: an underage yevama raised among her yavamin is permitted to marry one of them, since we did not see her remove a sandal.
A baraita requires both parties to intend ḥalitza, which seems to conflict with Rav's ruling about the sandal.
Rav meant that even if one saw her remove a shoe, one need not fear the intention of ḥalitza was present.
Some reverse Rav's inference: an act of ḥalitza without intention still disqualifies her for the brothers, while intention matters only for a stranger.
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav: ḥalitza may not be performed with a sandal sewn with flax thread, since a shoe must be entirely of leather.
Ezekiel 16:10 'taḥash skin' is read to include all leather, since the word shoe appears many times in the Torah.
Asks whether, if shoes of any leather count, other materials would count too, and what the word taḥash adds.
Taḥash shows the shoe must be entirely of leather, but all types of leather count, while a shoe partly of goat hair is still a shoe.
Asks from where it is known that the word ḥalitza in Deuteronomy 25:9 means removal.
Leviticus 14:40 uses the same root for removing stones from their place, so ḥalitza means removal.
Asks whether the root could instead mean strengthening, as in the verse about arming men for war.
Even there the root means removal, taking people from their houses to go out to war.
Verses in Job, Psalms and Isaiah use the same root to mean deliverance or strengthening, which might suggest ḥalitza means strengthening.
Only one meaning fits here: had ḥalitza meant strengthening, the verse would say beraglo, so it means removal from the foot.
A heretic tells Rabban Gamliel that God performed ḥalitza with Israel, citing Hosea 5:6.
Rabban Gamliel replies that the verse says ḥalatz from them, meaning Israel abandoned God, which has no legal significance.
Asks whether the mishnah's reference to an anpileya means it is not a shoe at all.
The Shekalim mishnah shows an anpileya is not considered a shoe, since one may enter the Temple wearing it when a shoe is forbidden.
A baraita on Yom Kippur bans walking in an anpileya, which seems to treat it as a shoe, contradicting the prior source.
Abaye: the Yom Kippur case is a cushioned anpileya; Rava: leather anpileya counts as a shoe, cloth anpileya does not.
A baraita permits walking in an anpileya within the house on Yom Kippur, supporting the leather versus cloth distinction.
Conclusion: the leather anpileya is treated as a shoe, while the cloth anpileya is not.
A baraita in accordance with Rava lists which footwear is valid for ḥalitza, including opened seams, cork, prosthetics and leather anpileya.

103a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Halitza is valid whether the yavam stands, sits or leans, and a blind woman may perform it; invalid with a torn shoe, broken sandal or cloth soft shoe.
Asks which tanna holds that an amputee's prosthetic counts as a shoe.
Cites a Shabbat mishna: Rabbi Meir lets an amputee go out with a wooden leg as a shoe, while Rabbi Yosei forbids it.
Objects that the baraita would then follow the Rabbis, who would disqualify any non-leather shoe.
Abaye resolves by reading the first clause as the Rabbis' view, limited to a prosthetic covered in leather.
Rava objects that Abaye's reading leaves the case unstated; the baraita should have specified the leather-covered prosthetic.
Rava reconciles both clauses under Rabbi Meir: protective footwear is required, not leather, and a cloth soft shoe does not protect.
Ameimar holds that the one performing halitza must press his foot to the ground so the shoe can be removed.
Rav Ashi objects that the baraita allows standing, sitting or leaning, so pressing down cannot be required.
Ameimar replies that the baraita means only when the foot is pressed down, which is harder while leaning.
Ameimar holds that a person who walks on the backs of his feet cannot perform halitza.
Rav Ashi objects to Ameimar, citing a baraita on leg supports.
The baraita says leg supports may be used if given to another person with normal feet who wears them for halitza.
Rav Ashi argues that Ameimar's view would bar bar Uva and bar Kipof, who had crooked feet, from halitza.
The mishna's ruling that halitza is valid when the leg is amputated from the knee down.
Raises a contradiction: a baraita says the word regalim excludes people with prosthetic legs from the pilgrimage.
Distinguishes halitza: the verse says from on his foot, which reaches the part of the leg above the foot.
Objects that by the same logic a leg amputated above the knee should also qualify.
Rav Pappa infers that the heel bone reaches the ground where it joins the foot.
Rav Ashi explains that anything attached to the sole counts as foot, so the calf is above the foot but the knee limits it.
The mishna's ruling that halitza is invalid when the leg is amputated from the knee upward.
Rav Kahana objects from the verse about the afterbirth between her legs, suggesting regel includes the thigh.
Abaye explains that a woman crouching to give birth plants her heels against her thighs, so the phrase means between her feet.
Brings a verse on dressing his feet, read as pubic hair, to suggest regel covers the thigh area.
Brings a verse on covering the feet, read as urination, as another proof that regel includes the thigh.
Brings the Eglon verse about covering the feet in the cool chamber as further proof.
Explains that the Eglon verse also uses feet as a euphemism.
Says the phrase between her legs is also a euphemism, so it does not prove regel includes the thigh.
Rabbi Yoḥanan states that Sisera had intercourse with Yael seven times that day.
Supports this with the verse from Judges describing Sisera sinking and falling at her feet.
Asks how Yael could derive pleasure from a sinful act with a gentile.
Rabbi Yoḥanan, citing Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai, answers that the wicked receive all their benefit at the cost of their own good.

103b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A benefit from the wicked is a harm to the righteous.
Cites Laban's warning to Jacob to speak neither good nor bad, as the source for the principle.
Asks why the verse forbids good speech too, and concludes the wicked's benefit harms the righteous.
Asks how Yael's intercourse with Sisera can be harmful, if it was not a reminder of idolatry.
The serpent implanted filth in Eve, which Israel at Sinai removed but gentiles kept; Yael was repulsed by it.
The mishna rules that halitza performed in a shoe that is not the yavam's own is valid.
A baraita derives from the repeated word shoe that any person's shoe may be used for halitza.
The baraita reads his shoe as excluding oversized, undersized and heelless sandals.
Abaye, standing before Rav Yosef, gave the yavam his left sandal for the halitza.
Rav Yosef asks whether the Sages permitted a left shoe only after the fact, or ab initio too.
Abaye asks whether the same applies to a sandal that is not the yavam's own.
Rav Yosef clarifies: give the sandal as a gift so the yavam owns it, making the halitza ideal.
The mishna states that halitza is valid when the yavam wears a wooden sandal.
Asks which tanna permits a wooden sandal; Shmuel says it is Rabbi Meir.
Cites the Shabbat mishna where Rabbi Meir lets an amputee go out with a wooden leg, Rabbi Yosei forbidding.
Shmuel's father explains the mishna refers to a wooden sandal covered in leather, which all agree is valid.
Rav Pappi, in Rava's name, rules halitza with a quarantined sandal is invalid ab initio but valid after the fact.
A confirmed leprous sandal may not be used, and halitza with it is invalid.
Rav Pappa, in Rava's name, rules that both sandal types may not be used ab initio, but halitza with them is valid.
Objects from a mishna in Negaim that a quarantined house and a confirmed house both impart impurity by entering.
If a leprous item is considered crushed, the verse requiring a house would not apply, which is a problem.
The verse says the house is demolished, and even during demolition it is still called a house.
Brings a baraita on a cloth three by three, which becomes impure only when most of it enters a house, to test the sandal case.
Suggests reading the latter clause of the baraita as a quarantined item with several olives, cutting against the sandal case.
If the item is confirmed leprous, why is it compared to a corpse; if quarantined, why is it compared to a corpse?
The verse says the garment is burned, and even burning leaves it called a garment; impurity is not derived from prohibition.
Rava rules: quarantined sandal, confirmed sandal and an idolater's sandal may not be used; halitza with them is valid after the fact, and a sacrificial item of idolatry is treated the same.

104a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A sandal of an idolatrous city or an elder's burial sandal may not be used for halitza; if used, halitza is invalid.
Ravina asks Rav Ashi what distinguishes an elder's burial sandal, since the court's halitza sandal also is not worn for walking.
Rav Ashi replies that a court messenger may walk in the court's sandal, but a burial sandal is never used for walking.
Mishna: halitza at night is valid, though Rabbi Elazar disqualifies it; left-foot halitza is invalid, though Rabbi Elazar validates it.
Proposes that the tannaim dispute whether monetary laws, including halitza, are compared to leprosy cases decided only by day.
Rejects that reading: all agree monetary cases are not compared to leprosy, so the dispute must be elsewhere.
The Sages disagree whether halitza is like the start of a judgment or like its conclusion.
Rabbah bar Ḥiyya performed a halitza case alone, at night, and in a hidden place.
Shmuel objects that Rav's ruling would then be an individual opinion.
Asks what the difficulty is if the baraita is unspecified about location or time, and whether only the individual case is problematic.
Asks how a single yavam can perform halitza when the mishna requires two or three witnesses and disqualifies one related or invalid witness.
Cites Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yoḥanan the cobbler validating such halitza, and a case where Rabbi Akiva validated it.
Rav Yosef bar Maniumi, in Rav Nachman's name, rules that the halakha is not like that pair of rulings.
Alternatively, all these cases teach individual halitza as an individual act, not a rule for the pair.
A baraita reports Rabbi Yishmael bar Yose saw Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha perform halitza alone, at night, on the left foot.
Asks what reason the Rabbis give for requiring the right foot.
Ulla says the Rabbis derive regel from the leper's rite, where the right foot is singled out.
Rabbi Elazar does not derive regel from the leper's rite.
A baraita from Rabbi Eliezer derives the right side from the piercing of the ear, and Rabbi Elazar's method is then questioned.
Rav Yitzḥak bar Yosef says Rabbi Yoḥanan reversed the inference, so the derivation is switched.
Rava says the comparison cannot be reversed, since foot cannot be compared to ear; the leper's rite involves cedar, hyssop and crimson wool.
Mishna: halitza performed with spitting but not recitation is valid; recitation with spitting but no halitza is invalid; halitza with recitation but no spitting is invalid.
Rabbi Elazar says that halitza with recitation but no spitting is invalid, while Rabbi Akiva validates it.

104b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Elazar cites the verse thus shall it be done to derive that every act in halitza is indispensable.
Rabbi Akiva objects: the verse only requires acts performed on the man's body, so spitting is not indispensable.
Mishna: halitza by a deaf-mute, by a woman with a minor, or before a disqualified judge is invalid; a minor's halitza must be repeated.
Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yoḥanan the Cobbler validate halitza before two or three judges when one is disqualified.
Cites a case of halitza in prison, performed privately, that Rabbi Akiva validated.
Rava rules that recitation is not indispensable, so a mute man or woman's halitza is valid.
Objects from the mishna: halitza by a deaf-mute or with a minor is invalid, which suggests recitation is indispensable.
Asks what the reason is for invalidity, if not inability to recite.
The reason is that deaf-mutes lack intellectual capacity, so their acts carry no halakhic weight.
Asks: if so, a mute man and woman should also lack capacity.
Rava replies that mutes do have intellect; the pain is in their mouths, so they cannot speak.
Objects that the school of Rabbi Yannai says the ruling applies because the mute cannot speak, and was said of the latter clause.
Restates the mishna: a deaf-mute's halitza and a minor's halitza are invalid.
Rava now holds recitation is indispensable, so mute halitza is invalid.
The mishna follows Rabbi Zeira: if the act can be performed in the proper way, the deficiency is indispensable; if not, it is not.
Asks whether a yavama who spat in halitza may proceed, and whether that implies a disqualification by the brothers.
Objects to the reasoning of Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Elazar, since two permitting acts cannot be combined without one another.
Cites a baraita on the sacrifice of the Festival of Weeks, where the sacrifice must be slaughtered and sprinkled for its own sake.
Asks whether Rabbi Akiva ruled that a wafer does not disqualify, citing a baraita where halitza is performed but not completed.

105a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna continues: spitting without recitation or halitza is valid; recitation without spitting or halitza is invalid, as is halitza without the other acts.
Asks whose opinion this is, since there is no room for doubt here.
Asks whether this is Rabbi Eliezer's view, where halitza without spitting or recitation is valid.
Objects: Rabbi Eliezer holds every act in halitza is indispensable, so the ruling must be obvious.
Cites the mishna as Rabbi Akiva's view, which invalidates halitza done without spitting, recitation or the act.
Asks whom the mishna follows: if it applies generally, it is obvious; so it must be about the brothers.
Asks what distinguishes spitting from recitation for Rabbi Akiva.
Recitation is not confused whether before or after, but spitting before halitza is absent, so it may be confused and permit the halitza to brothers.
Some say a yavama who spat may perform halitza without spitting again.
Narrates a case before Rabbi Ami where Rabbi Abba bar Memel had a woman spit before halitza.
Rabbi Ami rules that she may perform halitza and is permitted to the brothers.
Rabbi Abba objects that spitting must be repeated, which would bring a dangerous consequence.
Explains the danger: if spitting must be repeated, people would argue the first spitting has no effect and permit halitza to the brothers.
Objects that the order of the acts must be kept, and that Rabbi Akiva's view is order is not indispensable.
A baraita holds that whether halitza or spitting came first, what was done stands.
Asks whether an amputated hand disqualifies a yavama who spat blood.
Cites the verse in Daniel that a written truth is distinct from writing that is untrue.
Asks whether the text says 'with the hand' or 'spat', to judge the act of halitza.
Quotes the verse about writing that is true, to argue there is no untrue writing.
Reconciles the case: where the sentence carries an oath it does not tear, and where it has no oath it may tear.
Cites Rabbi Yonatan: from the verse in Samuel that a sentence carrying an oath does not tear, since the oath stands.
Rabbah holds sacrifices and meal offerings do not atone, but matters of Torah do atone.
Abaye holds sacrifices and meal offerings do not atone, but acts of kindness do atone.
Narrates that Rabbah, who studied Torah, lived forty years, while Abaye, who studied Torah and did kindness, lived sixty years.
A baraita: a family in Jerusalem, from the house of Eli, kept dying at about eighteen years old.
They told Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai, who asked whether they were of Eli's house, citing the Samuel verse on the house of Eli.
He told them to study Torah and live, and the family was called after Yoḥanan.
Rav Shmuel bar Oniya, in Rav's name: a communal sentence not yet sealed is not sealed; a sealed one may be torn.
Objects from Jeremiah: even with soap your iniquity remains stained before Me, so a sentence once sealed cannot be undone.
Explains that the Jeremiah verse applies to an individual, while the communal sentence can be torn.
Rav Naḥman says Rabbah bar Abuha taught that the ten days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur permit halitza of a yavama who spat blood.
The reason: blood cannot come out without some spitting.
Objects from a baraita: blood from the mouth and from the vessel is impure, but blood from the mouth and vessel is pure, from the verse on flux.
Resolves the baraita: one case is about sucking, the other about flowing.
Begins the mishna on a deaf-mute who performed halitza.

105b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Yehuda, in Rav's name: Rabbi Meir holds a male minor's halitza has effect, while the Sages hold it has no effect at all.
Mishna: a minor girl who performed halitza must perform it again once she matures.
Rabbi Meir's reasoning: the Torah writes man, and a woman is compared to a man, so she must be an adult too.
The Sages reason from the word man, and conclude the woman's halitza is valid whether she is adult or minor.
Asks who the Sages are, and identifies them with Rabbi Yose, Rabbi Ḥiyya and Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi.
Rabbi Yose, Rabbi Ḥiyya and Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi were sitting together, and one opened a discussion about prayer.
One holds the one who prays should lower his eyes; the other holds he should raise his eyes, each citing a verse.
Rabbi Yishmael bar Yose came and asked what they were discussing; they told him, prayer.
Abba explains: one should lower his eyes and lift his heart so that both verses are fulfilled.
Rabbi came to the study house; while the group was seated, Rabbi Yishmael bar Yose walked past them, honored, stepping over heads.
Abbedan asks who this is who steps on the heads of the holy people.
Rabbi Yishmael identifies himself as the son of Rabbi Yose who came to learn Torah from Rabbi.
Abbedan rebukes him: are you fit to learn from Rabbi, as Moses did not learn from the Almighty; your teacher is God.
Narrates that a yavama came before Rabbi, who sent Abbedan out to examine her; after he left, Rabbi Yishmael gave his father's teaching.
Rabbi Yishmael cites his father: the verse says man, but the woman is both adult and minor.
Rabbi replies that the elder has already ruled, so Abbedan is not needed; Abbedan then came back.
Rabbi Yishmael bar Yose objects: how can one step on the heads of the holy people when one who needs them and one who does not need them both do so.
Rabbi tells Abbedan to stand in his place; at that hour Abbedan was struck with leprosy, and two of his sons drowned and two daughters-in-law died.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak blesses the Merciful for having paid Abbedan his reward in this world.
Rabbi Ami says from Rabbi's teaching that a minor girl may perform halitza with infants.
Rava says it must be until she brings two pubic hairs; the halakha is that she needs two hairs.
Mishna: halitza performed before two is valid.
Rav Yosef bar Maniumi, in Rav Naḥman's name: the halakha is not like that pair of rulings.
Objects: Rav Naḥman once said that Rav Yosef bar Maniumi, in Rav Naḥman's name, requires three for halitza.
Reconciles: the first ruling applies ab initio, and after the fact even two suffice, so the halakha follows the first tanna.
Recounts a case of halitza performed between the two, and Rav Yehuda, in Shmuel's name, says witnesses see the act from outside.
Asks whether the case of halitza between the two was in a hidden place or in prison, and before whom it came.
Rav Yehuda, in Rav's name, says the case took place in prison and came to the court in prison.

106a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A mistaken halitza is valid; Resh Lakish says it is a yavam who is told the halitza is his marriage to her.
Rabbi Yoḥanan objects: halitza is invalid unless both intend a proper halitza, yet you validate one where he intends to marry her.
Rather, a mistaken halitza is one where the yavam is told to perform halitza on condition she pays two hundred zuz.
A baraita holds a mistaken halitza is valid, including one performed on condition of payment of two hundred zuz.
Recounts a case where a woman fell before an unsuitable yavam, who was told to perform halitza on condition of two hundred zuz.
The case came before Rabbi Ḥiyya, who validated the halitza.
Another case came before Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba.
Rabbi Ḥiyya's dialogue with the woman about her stance and whether she wished to be married to him.
The woman said no; the yavam was told to perform halitza, and he would then marry her.
Rabbi Ḥiyya explains that now she is disqualified because of you, and halitza is better so she is permitted to others.
A case of the daughter-in-law of Rav Pappa fell before an unsuitable yavam and came before Abaye, who ruled the halitza valid.
Rav Pappa asks Abaye whether he does not hold Rabbi Yoḥanan's view.
Abaye answers: then how should I tell him; she made halitza on condition of payment, and only afterward got her payment.
Abaye explains that she was joking with him, and the baraita on a man fleeing prison similarly deals with a joke.
A baraita about a man fleeing prison, who paid a dinar to be taken across, teaches that he only receives his wage.
Narrates the joke: asks where the father and mother are, and they answer that the parents are in town and the woman lowered her eyes and slept.
A baraita: a mistaken halitza is valid, while a mistaken get is invalid.
A coerced halitza is invalid, while a coerced get is valid.
Asks what the case is: if she says she wishes it, even halitza; if not, even the get is not valid, as the baraita says.
A mistaken halitza is always valid, a mistaken get is always invalid; a coerced halitza or coerced get is sometimes valid, sometimes invalid.
The difference: one where she says she wishes, and one where she does not say she wishes.
A baraita reads the verse 'he shall offer it' to show that the husband is compelled until he says he wishes to comply.
Rava, in Rav's name: a merchant or sale matter.
Rav Huna: halitza is accepted even when the parties are not known; refusal is accepted only when they are known.
Therefore one does not write a halitza document unless the parties are known, because of the risk that the court errs.
Rava holds halitza is performed only if known, and refusal only if known; therefore a get is written, because the court may err.
Halitza is accepted even when unknown, and a refusal document is written even when unknown, since we do not fear the court erring.

106b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mitzva of halitza: the parties come to court, and the court advises the yavam whether to perform levirate marriage or halitza.
Cites the verse that the elders of the city shall call him and speak to him.
If they decide on halitza, she declares her refusal, he states he does not wish to take her, and she performs the shoe removal and spitting in Hebrew.
Rabbi Hyrkanus prompted the participants under the ela tree to recite the whole passage, which became the custom.
The mitzva of saying the house of him who had his shoe removed applies to the judges, not the students; Rabbi Yehuda says it applies to all present.
Rav Yehuda: the mitzva is that she reads, he reads, she removes the shoe, spits, and she reads again.
Asks what the mishna teaches by this, if it is the same as the mitzva procedure and does not matter otherwise.
A baraita holds that whether the shoe removal or the spitting came first, what was done stands.
Abaye analyzes the wording: the verse does not allow a split reading, so the text must be read whole, as the yavam did not refuse or wish.
Rava says splitting a statement is permitted, and there is no objection to it.
Rav Ashi found Rav Kahana distressed and read to him; Rav Kahana held that without the yavam's refusal, Rava also agrees.
Abaye proposes how the halitza document should read: the yavam's refusal and his statement of not wishing to take her.
Mar Zutra writes out the whole passage in the document.
Mar bar Idi objects that the text cannot be written this way.
The halakha follows Mar Zutra's view.
Abaye: if she spat and the wind carried the spittle away, it counts for nothing, since spitting before him is required.
Abaye continues: if he is tall and she is short, and the wind carried the spit, it is valid only when it reaches his face.
Rava: if she spat with food in her mouth, or a gruel, it counts for nothing, since spitting must come from her own mouth.
Rava explains that judges must see the spittle come from the yavama's mouth, as the verse says before the elders.
The house of him who had his shoe removed is a mitzva for the judges, not for the students.
Rabbi Yehuda recounts that when they sat before Rabbi Tarfon and a yavama came to perform halitza, he told them all to say the shoe removal.
The closing line of the chapter: the mitzva of halitza.

107a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: a minor's father has died, and her mother or brothers may marry her off; the Sages dispute whether she may refuse, Beit Shammai limiting it to betrothed girls.
Beit Shammai hold refusal is directed only at her husband, not her yavam; Beit Hillel allow either.
Beit Shammai require refusal in the husband's presence and in court; Beit Hillel allow either.
Beit Hillel say she may refuse repeatedly while a minor; Beit Shammai reply she refuses once and waits until majority.
Beit Shammai hold the daughters of Israel must not be passed from one man to another.
Rav Yehuda, in Shmuel's name, states the reason for Beit Shammai's ruling.
Asks what the reason of Beit Shammai is, since there are no conditions in marriage that could be cancelled.
Asks what else can be said if the father delivered his daughter to the husband's agents before the wedding.
The Sages did not distinguish cases, so no marriage is conditional.
Beit Hillel know that the marriage of a minor is by rabbinic law.
Rabba and Rav Yosef both say Beit Shammai's reason is that a marriage is not like illicit relations.
Asks what can be said if she entered the canopy but was not consummated; it is not desired to be a forbidden canopy.
Since there are kiddushin and a ketubah, the marriage is not taken to be an illicit union.
Rav Pappa says Beit Shammai's reason concerns fruits: if she could refuse, the husband would eat the produce, since eventually she leaves.
Beit Hillel's reasoning: they favor the refusal being announced, lest her relatives marry her off and take her away.
Rava says Beit Shammai's reason is that a man does not trouble himself over a feast only to lose it; both schools want the news of marriage to spread.
Beit Shammai say the refusal is directed at the husband.
Rabbi Oshaya: she may refuse his declaration, but not the bond of levirate marriage.
Rav Ḥisda explains: a declaration made from her own will can uproot the levirate bond, but a bond imposed against her will cannot uproot it.

107b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The reasoning: she can nullify the consummation and betrothal the yavam performs, but not the levirate bond the Merciful One imposes.
Ulla says she may refuse even the levirate bond.
Asks what the reason is, since the first marriage's bond is the one being undone.
Rava objects to Ulla: a co-wife who could refuse but did not is not released by ḥalitza and cannot be married by levirate, so the bond is not undone.
Rava's distinction: a baraita on Rami bar Yeḥezkel shows that at the time of falling, the co-wife is seen as the daughter-in-law.
Rav holds that a refusal made concerning one is forbidden to the other, like a divorcee cannot be married by her husband's brother.
Shmuel holds that a refusal concerning one is permitted to the other, unlike a divorcee.
Rav Asi holds that refusal concerning one permits her even to him.
Asks whether this follows Rabbi Oshaya's view that she may not refuse the bond with one yavam; here the case concerns two yavamim.
Explains that there is no refusal for half of a bond.
Ravin, in Rabbi Yoḥanan's name: refusal concerning one permits her to the brothers; Abaye and Rav Rava give the attributions.
Beit Shammai say the refusal is in the husband's presence, and a baraita reports the dispute.
A baraita: Beit Hillel cite a case of a man who refused his wife not in his presence, and the halakha follows the case of Pishon the camel.
Objects: it is obvious she is married, yet Beit Shammai hold a married woman cannot refuse.
Beit Shammai say the refusal is before the court.
Asks which tanna holds that halitza and refusals require three judges.
Rabbah says it is Beit Shammai; Abaye says even according to Beit Hillel, who only do not require experts but do require three.
A baraita: Beit Shammai say before the court, and Beit Hillel say before or not before the court, and all agree three are needed.
Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda and Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon validate with two; Rav Yosef bar Maniumi, in Rav Naḥman's name, rules the halakha follows that pair.
Beit Shammai say she refuses.
Objects: she refused once, and Shmuel said she must reach majority and say she wishes to continue the earlier refusal.
Ulla says the Mishnah teaches two options; if Shmuel's view applies, the Mishnah should say until she grows up and says she wishes, which is problematic.
Mishna: which minor needs a refusal: one whom her mother and brothers married off without her consent.
Rabbi Ḥanina ben Antigonus: a girl who cannot guard her betrothal does not need a refusal.
Rabbi Elazar: a minor's act is nothing, except as one seduced: a daughter of Israel to a priest may not eat terumah.
Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov: any impediment from the man makes her his wife, and any impediment not from the man makes her not his wife.
Rav Yehuda, and others say, in the Tannaitic statement: in earlier times they wrote a refusal document, and the woman does not wish to marry him.
Explains the practice changed because they saw the talk about it spreading.

108a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Institutes that the refusal document be written with the day, and that the woman refuses her named husband.
The Sages taught what counts as refusal: she states she does not want her husband, even seated in a litter, as Rabbi Yehuda holds.
Rabbi Yehuda holds refusal counts even when guests are reclining in the house and she serves them, declaring she does not want her husband.
Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda holds refusal counts even when her husband sends her to a shopkeeper and she declares she does not want him; this is greater refusal.
Rabbi Ḥanina ben Antigonus says a girl who cannot guard her betrothal does not need refusal.
Rav Yehuda, in Shmuel's name, holds the halakha follows Rabbi Ḥanina ben Antigonus, and cites the case of Rabbi Yehuda ben Batira.
Asks whether refusal applies to a minor who did not refuse and stood, then was betrothed.
Asks whether the Sages disagree with Rabbi Yehuda ben Batira in betrothal or in marriage, and whether the halakha follows him.
Objects: if the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda ben Batira, it implies a dispute, and the question remains whether she was married first or betrothed.
Cites the case of the daughter-in-law of Abdan, sent by Rabbi to examine the halakha; the rule that refusal of marriage is greater than betrothal.
Rabbi Elazar says the rule as well.
Rav Yehuda, in Shmuel's name: Shmuel found no one whose view matches Rabbi Elazar, who made the minor like one walking with him in the courtyard.
A baraita: Rabbi Eliezer holds a minor's act is nothing; her husband has no claim on her find or vows, and she needs refusal.
Rabbi Yehoshua holds the husband has claim on her find and her acts, and she is his wife in all respects, leaving through refusal.
Rabbi Eliezer's view appears to be the view of Rabbi Yehoshua, since Rabbi Eliezer equalized the minor's status.
Asks whether a get is needed for Rabbi Eliezer too; if she is not his wife, refusal is not needed.
Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says the rule.
Explains the cases of an impediment from the man versus one not from the man, with Shmuel's case of a woman whose relatives married her off.
Abaye bar Avin and Rav Ḥanina bar Avin both say: if he gave her a get, he is forbidden to her relatives and she is forbidden to his, and she is disqualified from priesthood.
A woman who refused her husband is an impediment from the man: he is forbidden to her relatives and she to his, and she is disqualified.
Explains the mishna's case: the refusal does not disqualify when the impediment is not from the man.
Mishna: a woman who refused her husband: he is permitted to her relatives and she to his, and she is not disqualified.
Mishna: if he gave her a get, he is forbidden to her relatives and she to his, and she is disqualified.
Mishna: if he gave her a get and she then refused him and married another and was widowed or divorced, she may return to him.
Mishna: if she refused him and he gave her a get, she married another and was widowed or divorced, she is forbidden to return to him.

108b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The general rule: after a get, a refusal makes her forbidden to return; after a refusal, a get makes her permitted to return.
Restates the rule: if she is taken out by a get she is forbidden to return; if by a refusal she is permitted to return.
Infers from this that a refusal comes and nullifies the other's get.

ranges.en: She may remain with him on a dilemma: acquired or not, the deaf-mute case is resolved either way.

ranges.en: If the first wife was consummated, the yavam's later intercourse with a second deaf-mute does not disqualify her.

If the wife herself reports that a war occurred and that her husband died in it, is she suspected of lying?
