ranges.en: Sides of the dilemma: she would not lie by claiming peace, so does her war claim lose the presumption of why she would lie?
Baraita: a woman whose house was set on fire, and who says her husband died while she was saved, is not believed.
Distinguished: in the fire case one may say a miracle saved the husband too, unlike the gentile attack case.
Baraita: a woman whose husband died in an attack by gentiles or bandits, and she was saved, is believed.
Rav Idi: a woman's weapons are upon her, since thieves would more likely assault than kill her, so her account is credible.
Story: a groom died in a fire at his wedding, and his bride saw a burnt man and a hand lying there.
Rav Ḥiyya bar Avin proposes the burning case is like the smoke-filled house, so her claim is not relied upon.
Rava objects: she did not say look at my husband, and the body and palm were there, so the cases differ.
Rav Ḥiyya bar Avin: a fallen burnt man is not proof, since another might have rescued him and he could have fled alive.
A dilemma: is one witness believed about a husband's death during war, and what is the reason for that rule?
Rami bar Ḥama's resolution: Rabbi Akiva reports Neḥemya of Beit D'li citing Rabban Gamliel that one witness suffices, though the land is riddled with troops.
Does the troops remark mean the war does not stop the rule that one witness suffices?
Rava: if so, why does he name this country rather than any place with troops?
Rava: Neḥemya meant he cannot leave his household to testify before the Sages because of danger.
Baraita: two scholars drowned in a boat with Abba Yosei ben Simai, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi allowed their wives to remarry on women's testimony.
Objection: water is like war, and even a hundred women count as one witness, so one witness should not suffice in war.
Reply: the women testified only that the boat sank in endless water, so the case is that they were brought up before them.

115b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Reply: the women's testimony is not relied on by itself, but the distinguishing marks they gave are.
Case: a man deposited sesame plants with a friend, who later claims they were already returned, and the amounts match.
Rav Ḥisda: this is like the drowned scholars identified by marks, so the sesame plants can be relied upon.
Rava objects that the cases differ, since the sesame plants have no distinguishing marks and matching amount may be chance.
Mar Kashisha asks Rav Ashi: are we concerned that the guardian moved the plants from their place?
Mishna of Ma'aser Sheni: a vessel marked with a letter is designated accordingly, with no concern that the contents were moved.
Ravina objects: the mishna's latter clause, citing Rabbi Yosei, shows that moving the contents is a concern.
Rabbi Yosei: a barrel marked teruma is non-sacred, since someone may have replaced the teruma.
Both sides agree one is concerned about moving contents; the disagreement is whether the marking would be erased or left to preserve the produce.
Story: Yitzḥak the Exilarch, son of the sister of Rav Beivai, died on a journey, and the report named him without further detail.
Are we concerned that another man named Yitzḥak with the same name might be meant?
Abaye says we are concerned; Rava says we are not concerned.
Abaye's proof: a bill of divorce found in Neharde'a named a man who might be another person of the same name, prompting an examination.
Rava: the story proves nothing, since if concern was justified the whole world would have to be examined.
Rava: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia's instruction was out of respect for Shmuel's father, not a real concern.
Rava's proof: two promissory notes naming common creditors were collected without concern for namesakes.
An objection: but these names are very common in Meḥoza, so how does Abaye answer this proof?

116a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Should we be concerned that the note fell and was found by a namesake, or that it was deposited with the bailee?
If the owner transferred the note to the namesake, the holder may collect, since letters of credit are acquired by transfer.
Case: a bill of divorce found in Sura names Anan bar Ḥiyya of Neharde'a, but witnesses say a namesake from Ḥagra was in Neharde'a.
Abaye: even by his view that namesakes are a concern, here the witnesses place the other man in Neharde'a, so no concern.
Rava: where the namesake is established, concern applies; the witnesses' location is explained by a flying camel or a shortcut.
Rav and Rav Huna instructed scribes to write the place of the instruction, supporting Rava's explanation about writing by instruction.
Sesame plants: Rav Yeimar says no concern, Ravina says concern, and the halakha is that we are concerned about replacement.
What are the circumstances of a quarrel between a husband and wife, in which her testimony of his death is not accepted?
Rav Yehuda said Shmuel: it is when she tells her husband to divorce her in anger.
Objection: all women say this in anger, so it does not prove an unresolved quarrel.
Rather, a quarrel exists when she says he already divorced her.
If she claims he divorced her, why not believe her by Rav Hamnuna's rule that a woman would not lie before her husband?
A quarrel exists when she says he divorced her before witnesses, and the witnesses deny it, so her claim is not accepted.
What is the reason the court does not accept her testimony in a quarrel?
Rav Ḥanina: she lies; Rav Shimi bar Ashi: she speaks from imagination, examining less when she is glad to be rid of him.
What is the practical difference between these two explanations?

116b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If she was the one who started the quarrel she would not lie about his death, but she may be careless in checking.
A dilemma: is one witness believed about a husband's death when there was a quarrel, and why is one witness trusted?
Rabbi Yehuda: a wife is never believed unless she comes crying with torn clothes; a baraita introduces this dispute.
The Rabbis object: a crafty woman would fake grief and be permitted, while a simple woman would not, which is unfair.
Story: at Rabbi Yehuda's court, a woman was told to mourn publicly, since they followed the Rabbis but wanted Rabbi Yehuda to also permit her.
Mishna: Beit Hillel say a woman's testimony of death is accepted only from the grain harvest, in the same country, in a similar incident.
Beit Shammai object: the same applies to any harvest, and even to moving between countries, since the grain harvest was only the example.
Beit Hillel retracted and taught in accordance with Beit Shammai.
Baraita: Beit Shammai argue that Beit Hillel's rule, if limited to the wheat harvest, must extend to other harvests and crops.
Beit Shammai conclude that the incident was only an example, and the rule applies to all such circumstances.
Beit Hillel reply: in the same country people move around, so she fears exposure; between countries they do not, so she is not deterred.
What was the incident that occurred?
Shmuel: at the end of the wheat harvest a snake killed one of ten harvesters, and the court verified the wife's account, so she was permitted to remarry.
Do Rabbi Ḥananya ben Akiva and the Rabbis disagree on the same issue as Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel?
Baraita on the red heifer's ashes: one may not carry them across the Jordan by boat, nor on a rider, but may use a bridge.
Rabbi Ḥananya ben Akiva: the prohibition applies only to the Jordan and a boat, in the circumstances of the incident.
Shall we say the Rabbis hold like Beit Shammai that a decree extends to similar cases, while Ben Akiva holds like Beit Hillel?
The Rabbis reply that Beit Hillel's rule for near and far places differs, and Beit Hillel's concern was local danger of exposure.
Ben Akiva replies that Beit Shammai's concern is only the woman's own care, so the decree stays with the actual incident.
The incident: a man carrying the ashes on the Jordan by boat, where an olive-bulk of a corpse was found under the boat.
Mishna: Beit Shammai say the widow may remarry and take her marriage contract; Beit Hillel say she may remarry but not take the contract.

117a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Evidently a woman's testimony is accepted for forbidden relations but not for monetary inheritance matters.
Beit Shammai: the marriage contract's wording, if you remarry, take what is written, shows her money depends on remarriage eligibility.
Rav Ḥisda: a yavam who consummates on her testimony also inherits, by the same homiletic logic applied to the Torah.
The verse he shall succeed in the name of his brother shows the yavam takes his brother's inheritance too.
Rav Naḥman: a widow who asks permission to remarry is permitted and paid her contract, but one who asks only for the contract is refused.
If she asks both for permission and for her contract, does mentioning the money show she came for the money?
She may have mentioned the contract first only because she thought it part of the process, so the question stays unresolved.
Mishna: all are credible to testify on a husband's death except her mother-in-law, her mother-in-law's daughter, her rival, her yavam's wife, and her stepdaughter.
Is the daughter of her father-in-law, not her mother-in-law's daughter, credible, or is she suspect like the mother-in-law's daughter?
Baraita: all are credible except five women, which seems to exclude the father-in-law's daughter differently.
Rejected: the five are the same disqualification, since both women hate her for eating food in their own house.
Contradiction: a baraita lists seven untrustworthy women, so the father-in-law's daughter is a separate category; Rabbi Yehuda adds a father's wife and daughter-in-law.
Rabbi Yehuda's reply: the hatred of each category has a different reason, so each is counted separately.
What is the reason Rabbi Yehuda adds these two categories?
Each hates for a different reason: a daughter-in-law reports to her son, a father's wife reports to her father; the Rabbis cite Proverbs, and Rabbi Yehuda says it refers to Torah.
Rav Aḥa bar Avya's dilemma: must a mother-in-law's testimony be discounted for a future daughter-in-law she will later host?

117b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Baraita: if she said my husband died and then my father-in-law died, she may remarry, but her mother-in-law may not.
Why is the mother-in-law forbidden, if not because her husband may not really have died and she is still his wife?
She reasons that later the husbands return, so she would not trouble herself by lying about her future daughter-in-law.
Rejected: the daughter-in-law had earlier dealings with the mother-in-law, so the same suspicion does not carry over.
Mishna: one witness that the husband died, then another witness that he did not: she need not leave a new husband, but two against one requires her to leave.
Ulla holds that one witness equals two, so why may she not remarry even before marrying if a second witness contradicts?
The mishna speaks of a woman already permitted by one witness, who stays permitted even if a later witness contradicts.
Is it not obvious that one witness cannot override two, so why is the mishna needed?
It is needed for witnesses disqualified from testimony, in line with Rabbi Neḥemya.
Baraita of Rabbi Neḥemya: where the Torah accepts one witness, follow the majority even if they are disqualified; two women count as two men against one.
Another reading: a qualified witness first testifying cannot be overridden by many women, and Rabbi Neḥemya's rule applies to two women against one man equally.
Mishna: two witnesses say he died and one says he did not, so even if she has not yet married she may marry.
What does this case teach, if it simply repeats the disqualified-witness case under Rabbi Neḥemya's majority rule?
It is needed lest the majority rule apply only to stringency and not to leniency; the mishna says it applies both ways.
Mishna: of two wives, one says he died and may remarry with her contract; the other may not. Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon dispute the case where he was killed.

118a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: if one wife says he died and the other says he did not, the one who denies death may not remarry.
Does the mishna imply that if the second wife stayed silent she could remarry, though one rival cannot testify for another?
No: the mishna needed to say he did not die, since she may be trying to harm her rival, even at her own expense.
Mishna: if one wife says he died and one says he was killed, a dispute on whether they may remarry.
Should Rabbi Meir also disagree in the first clause, where one witness says he died and another says he did not?
Rabbi Elazar: this is a tannaitic dispute; Rabbi Yoḥanan: even Rabbi Meir concedes that a denial is no contradiction for remarriage.
Objection: the anonymous mishna follows Rabbi Meir, which Rabbi Yoḥanan's view cannot easily support.
Mishna: a wife returns from overseas and says her husband died; her rival may not remarry and may still eat teruma. Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva dispute the case of a mother-in-law too.
Both cases are needed: the jealousy in a rival case is physical, while a mother-in-law's grievance is verbal, so the two cases must be distinguished.
Rav Yehuda said Shmuel: the halakha follows Rabbi Tarfon, so a woman suspected of ill will is entirely rejected regarding her rival.
Abaye: a mishna on 118b shows the court is concerned only about the woman's own statement, not her rival's testimony.
The mishna continues that the court is concerned about her statement only, and the Gemara concludes from this that a rival's statement is disregarded.

118b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: a man betrothed one of five women and does not know which; Rabbi Tarfon has him divorce all and leave the contract, while Rabbi Akiva requires paying each.
The parallel case of theft from one of five people: Tarfon leaves the money among them, Akiva requires paying each one.
Since the mishna teaches betrothal and theft but not intercourse and purchase, whose view is it, if neither the first tanna nor Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar?
Baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar: Tarfon and Akiva agree on betrothal and purchase, and dispute only intercourse for betrothal and theft.
From Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's remark, it follows that the first tanna holds they dispute the betrothal and purchase cases.
If the mishna follows the first tanna, why teach theft and intercourse, and if Shimon ben Elazar, why teach betrothal and purchase?
The mishna follows Shimon ben Elazar: betrothal means by intercourse, teaching Akiva's stringency, and theft teaches Tarfon's leniency.
Mishna: a woman goes overseas with husband and son; if she says her husband died and then her son, she is believed and may remarry without levirate.
Further mishna cases: a childless couple abroad, a yavam born abroad, and a woman or man who falsely claims a death to remarry is not believed.
Rava asks Rav Naḥman: if a husband sends a bill of divorce to his wife with a potential yavam, is it divorced upon delivery to an agent, or only when received?
Rav Naḥman: the mishna shows that her statement is considered in either case, so levirate status is uncertain and no ruling follows.
Ravina asks the same of a bill sent through an agent during a quarrel: is it for her benefit or is physical comfort preferable?
Reish Lakish: women say it is better to sit as two than to sit lonely as a widow, so a bill is not for her benefit.
Sayings on wives' contentment: Abaye's, Rav Pappa's and Rav Ashi's popular idioms about women who value marriage whatever their husbands' status.
A Sage taught that all these women commit adultery and attribute children to their husbands, showing their keenness to remain married.
Chapter-closing formula marking the end of the chapter that begins with the woman who went overseas.

119a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna rules the widow may not remarry or do yibum until she knows whether the rival wife is pregnant
Mishna's second case: with a mother-in-law abroad, she must wait if the mother-in-law was pregnant
Rabbi Yehoshua dissents and says she need not be concerned at all
Why does the Mishna say she, when the rival wife is the obvious subject
The word teaches that only the rival wife's pregnancy is a concern, not a pregnancy of another wife
Gemara restates the Mishna's ruling that she may neither remarry nor perform yibum
Why may she not remarry at all, given yibum is only a doubt and majority of women bear children
Proposal that the Mishna follows Rabbi Meir, who is concerned about a minority
Rejection: the Rabbis follow majorities only when visible, such as stores or the Sanhedrin, not statistical ones
Objection: minor boys and girls are decided by a non-visible majority, which the Rabbis accept
Baraita of Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis on minors, the Rabbis answering that the verse parallels man and woman
Asks the reason minors may not perform yibum if the Torah text does not specify adulthood
Rabbi Meir replies that a minor may turn out a sexually underdeveloped man or woman
The Rabbis hold that most minors are not underdeveloped, so majority is followed even here
Conclusion: the Mishna must be following Rabbi Meir, who is concerned about the minority
How can the Mishna follow Rabbi Meir, and why not be concerned in the latter clause
Explanation: half of births are male, so the minority who miscarry leaves males as the minority
If Rabbi Meir is followed, why not worry that a yavam may have been born
Resolution: since the widow is presumed permitted to the public, the concern is only for the first clause
Rav Naḥman, citing Rabba bar Avuh, explains that the severe karet prohibition warrants the minority concern
Rava objects: both prohibitions are Torah law, so the severity distinction makes no difference
Rava rejects this contention and offers an alternative resolution, continued on the next daf

119b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains the first clause: presumption of yibum and majority of births balance once miscarriages are counted, so she waits
Latter clause: presumption favors remarriage, and a minority of a minority is disregarded even by Rabbi Meir
Restates the Mishna that she may neither remarry nor perform yibum until knowing whether the rival wife is pregnant
Ze'eiri's view: she waits three months for herself and nine months for the rival wife, then performs halitza
Rabbi Ḥanina's view: for her own concern she waits three months, but for the rival wife's pregnancy she waits indefinitely
Objection to Rabbi Ḥanina: she should perform halitza either way, since after nine months it is certainly permitted
Abaye bar Avin and Rabbi Ḥanina bar Avin explain: a rabbinic decree lest a viable child was born to the other wife
Objection: the decree leads to an unnecessary halitza and then an announcement that she is permitted to a priest
Why not require the announcement anyway if a viable offspring is later found
Answer: some present at the halitza may not hear the announcement, and would think a halutza may marry a priest
Mishna cited: a woman claiming a son died before her husband is not credible, so she performs halitza but may not marry
Objection: witnesses may later confirm her sequence, so the announcement concern should be raised here too
Rav Pappa: the Mishna refers only to a divorcee, who is already forbidden to a priest
Rav Ḥiyya bar Huna: the case is one where she and her husband and son were alone in a cave, so no witnesses come
Mishna: two sisters-in-law each claim husband died; each is prohibited, since sisters-in-law are not credible about each other
Mishna continues: with witnesses or children, one may be permitted while the other, lacking them, remains prohibited
Mishna: if the yevamin died childless after yibum, the women are prohibited from marrying anyone
Rabbi Elazar says they are permitted to any man, since they were permitted to the living yevamin
Baraita: a woman with witnesses and children and one with neither are both permitted, supporting the Mishna's reasoning
Mishna: when yibum was performed and the yevamin died, the women are prohibited from marrying
Rabbi Elazar again: since they were permitted to the yevamin, they are permitted to any man
Rava asks the basis of Rabbi Elazar: general testimony of rival wives, or that she would not harm herself, and the practical difference

120a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Practical difference: whether the rival wife may remarry before the widow does, depending on the reason for Rabbi Elazar's view
Asks what the basis of Rabbi Elazar's ruling is and proposes checking it against the baraita
Baraita: Rabbi Elazar says that since they were permitted to the yevamin, they are permitted to any man
Tests the two possible reasons; concludes Rabbi Elazar's reason is that she has already remarried and would not harm herself
Rejects that conclusion: Rabbi Elazar spoke to the Rabbis' view, and even they accept remarriage after actual marriage
Rabbis cite the verse Let me die with the Philistines, and a baraita where the rival wife is forbidden until certainty
Rabbi Elazar says that since she is permitted to marry, her rival wife is permitted too
Reinterprets Rabbi Elazar's reason: she was permitted and has actually married
If she would not harm herself, why could the rival wife be permitted, given the possibility of a divorce document
Validates the concern for a divorcee who married an Israelite, but a priest's marriage shows she was a widow
Mishna: a death may be testified to only by seeing the face with the nose, and only within three days of death
Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava says no general rule fits all people, places, or hours, since decomposition varies
Baraita: testimony requires seeing both forehead and face with the nose, not one without the other
Abaye, or Rav Kahana, asks which verse teaches that one must see the face to testify
Verse Isaiah 3:9 is cited, and an anecdote of Abba bar Marta disguising his forehead shows how faces change
Asks whether distinguishing marks are only rabbinic, since the Mishna requires stricter Torah standards for death testimony
Contradiction: a bill of divorce found tied to a purse or ring is valid, suggesting marks suffice by Torah law
Abaye: the baraita follows Rabbi Eliezer ben Mahavai, while the Mishna follows the Rabbis
Baraita on a mole: Rabbi Eliezer ben Mahavai permits testimony based on a mole, the Rabbis do not
Abaye's explanation: the dispute is whether distinguishing marks are Torah-based or rabbinic
Rava: all agree marks are Torah-based; the dispute is whether such a mole is common among similar people
Alternative version: the dispute is whether a mole changes in appearance after death
Another version of Rava: all agree marks are rabbinic, and the Mishna refers to ordinary marks, unusual ones suffice

120b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rava's version: the sides disagree on whether a mole is an unambiguous mark that a corpse can be identified by
Asks whether the mishna's denial of mark-based identification conflicts with Rava's view that marks are Torah-valid
Mishna refers to weak general body marks, and not marks on belongings, since belongings may have been borrowed
If borrowing is a concern, how can a donkey be returned based on marks on its saddle
People do not normally lend a saddle, since it must fit the donkey exactly and would bruise it
Raises the baraita: how can a divorce document tied to a purse or ring be returned if these may have been lent
A signet ring is not lent for fear of forgery, purses are not lent as a bad omen, and marks may be only general
Mishna: one may not testify to death even if the man was cut open and severely wounded
Asks whether a person cut open can still live for a long time afterward
Contradiction with a mishna in Oholot: a corpse conveys impurity only once the soul departs, even if cut open
Abaye: the Mishna follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, while the Oholot mishna follows the Rabbis
Baraita: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says cutting open may be cauterized, so one may not testify to death
Challenges the resolution: the latter clause suggests a cut-open man is dead, which contradicts Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
Incident at Asya: a man lowered into the sea and cut from the knee up is assumed dead, cited as the Sages ruling
Water aggravates the wound, so a leg cut in water certainly leads to death
Rabba bar bar Ḥanna saw a camel cut open with a sword die instantly, suggesting cut-open beings cannot survive
Abaye: that camel was emaciated and weak, so a healthy camel would not have died so quickly
Rava: the Mishna refers to cutting with a white-hot knife, which cauterizes, so all agree no testimony
Mishna: one may not testify to death even if a wild animal was eating parts of him
Shmuel: this applies only where the animal eats a non-fatal part, but if the eaten part is fatal one may testify
Shmuel: if someone cut the two passageways and the man fled, one may testify to his death
Objects: Shmuel also held that the maimed man who gestured a divorce is alive, so he is not yet dead
He is still alive now but will eventually die, so he may appoint an agent but later can be declared dead
If such a wound is fatal, an unintentional wounder should be exiled, yet a baraita says he is not exiled
Rav Hoshaya: the wind may have aggravated the wound, or the maimed man himself may have worsened it

121a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks what the practical difference is between the wind hastening death and the victim himself hastening it
Practical difference: a victim cut inside a closed marble house convulses, while one cut outside in wind does not
Mishna's teaching of Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava: no general rule fits all persons, places, or hours
Dilemma: did Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava dissent to be more lenient or more stringent than the Rabbis
Cases brought as a solution: a drowned man found after three days and another seen after five days, both permitted
If he dissented to be lenient, those Sages acted by his view; if stringent, by whose view did they act
Water is different, since it contracts the body and prevents its shape from changing
Objects that water was said to aggravate a wound, so how can it preserve the body
That applies when there is a wound; without one water contracts the body, but only if viewed immediately
Mishna: if a man fell into water, with or without a visible end, his wife is prohibited from remarrying
Rabbi Meir cites an incident of a man who fell into a great cistern and emerged after three days
Rabbi Yosei cites a blind man who vanished into a cave and the Asya incident of the leg cut from the knee
Baraita: Rabbi Meir says the wife is prohibited in any case, while the Sages distinguish visible-end from endless water
What are the circumstances defining a body of water with a visible end
Abaye: a body of water is visible-ended if one standing in place can see the shore in all four directions
Account of a man drowned in the Samkei lake, whose wife Rav Sheila permitted to remarry; Rav asks to excommunicate him
Shmuel's counsel: send a query asking whether, in an endless body of water, the wife is forbidden or permitted
The reply: the wife is forbidden
Is the Samkei lake a body of water with a visible end or an endless one
The reply: it is an endless body of water, since its shore cannot be seen on every side
If so, what was the reason the Master acted that way and permitted the wife to remarry
Rav Sheila: I erred, thinking stagnant waters have a visible end; the waves may have carried him out unseen
Shmuel and Rav praise each other with verses from Proverbs about the righteous and about counsel
Baraita: a man entered a fish cave, was thought drowned, and returned; Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi praises the Sages' distinction
If so, even in visible-end water one should worry about a fish cave where the man may still be alive
A cave containing a fish pond is not common in a body of water with a visible end
Rav Ashi: the endless-water prohibition applies only to ordinary people, not a Torah scholar who would be publicized
Rejection: no difference between an ordinary man and a scholar; after the fact she stays, but ab initio she may not remarry
Baraita: Rabban Gamliel saw a boat sink, thought Rabbi Akiva died, but Rabbi Akiva survived clinging to a plank
Lesson that the wicked should be placated by bending the head; Rabban Gamliel repeats the endless-water ruling
Baraita: Rabbi Akiva recounts a boat sinking, with Rabbi Meir surviving by the waves, as he affirms the same ruling
Sages: one may not testify about a man who fell into a lions' den, but may for a pit of snakes and scorpions
Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira: even for a pit of snakes and scorpions, one may not testify, since we are concerned

121b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The first tanna disregards the possibility he is a snake charmer, since his falling body would still injure him
Baraita on who may be declared dead by fire, wine, or oil, with Rabbi Aha's distinction between oil and wine
Rabbi Meir repeats the incident of a man who fell into the Great Cistern and emerged after three days
Baraita: they told Rabbi Meir that miracles are not cited to teach general halakha
What was the miraculous element if he neither ate nor drank, given the verse in Esther permitting fasting
The miracle is that he did not sleep for three days, as Rabbi Yoḥanan's oath-based ruling implies
According to Rabbi Meir, what is the reason this was not considered a miraculous incident
Rav Kahana: he held onto arches while sleeping, while Rabbi Meir deems it implausible he never grasped one
Baraita on Neḥunya the well digger's daughter, rescued from a cistern through Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa's prayer and a ram
Rabbi Abba: the son of Neḥunya still died of thirst, citing the verse that God is exacting with those around Him
Rabbi Ḥanina derives the same idea from a verse that God is most feared by those nearest to Him
Mishna: testimony of death may rely on women's reports, on children's reports, and on mention by anyone regardless of intent
Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava: a Jew's report counts even if intended as testimony, but a gentile's counts only if not intended
Perhaps the children did not go, and the person did not in fact die
Rav Yehuda said Shmuel: the case is children saying they are coming from eulogizing and burying a named man
Perhaps the children were merely playing with a grasshopper they called by that man's name
Answer: the children name rabbis and eulogizers present, so it is clear a real event occurred
Mishna: a gentile's testimony is invalid if he intended to testify
Rav Yehuda said Shmuel: this applies only if the gentile intended to permit remarriage, not merely to testify about death
How do we know whether a gentile intended to permit remarriage or only to testify
Rav Yosef: if he comes to court asking to permit the wife to remarry, that is intent to permit; a bare report is testimony
Reish Lakish: the same distinction, as taught by others among the amora'im
Rabbi Yoḥanan objects with Rabbi Oshaya's ruling on gentile testimony, which the Rabbis did not accept
If so, what is the mishna's implication that an offhand gentile statement may be relied upon, and how is such a case found
Offhand statements: a gentile repeatedly announcing the death of the house of Ḥivvai and a horseman, on which Rav Yosef allowed remarriage
A gentile announces that Ḥasa drowned; Rav Naḥman says the fish ate him, and Ḥasa's wife remarries without a ruling
Rav Ashi: the endless-water prohibition applies ab initio, so if she already married, she is not removed from him
Some say Rav Naḥman issued an actual ruling, reasoning that a great man's survival would have been publicized
Rejection: it makes no difference whether he is great; after the fact she stays, but ab initio she may not remarry
Narrative: a gentile threatened a Jew that he killed another Jew, and the widow brings the matter before Abaye

ranges.en: Rav Adda bar Ahava sends the woman to Rav Yosef, whose keen insight can settle her case after three festivals of uncertainty
Rav Yosef resolves the case from a baraita: a gentile's claims about fruit are not credible, since he may just want a higher price
Abba Yudan's case: a gentile reports a Jew with him on the road died and was buried, and the Sages allowed remarriage
Further cases of gentile reports about a group of collared prisoners and sixty travelers, both accepted as grounds for remarriage
Mishna: witnesses may testify by candlelight or moonlight, and a disembodied voice or unverified reports may permit remarriage
Rabba bar Shmuel: a baraita says Beit Shammai reject a disembodied voice while Beit Hillel accept it
What is Rabba bar Shmuel teaching, since the mishna already gives the decisive ruling of Beit Hillel
Such an anonymous ruling rejecting a voice reflects Beit Shammai's opinion and is not the accepted halakha
The mishna's case: they heard a voice, went to the spot, and found no person there
Perhaps it was a demon
Rav Yehuda said Rav: he had the form of a person and a shadow, which demons do not have in the same way
Demons also have a shadow, so perhaps they also have a shadow of a shadow
Rabbi Ḥanina cites Yonatan the demon expert: demons have a shadow but not a shadow of a shadow
Perhaps it was a rival wife or enemy who cried out the husband was dead to trick her
The school of Rabbi Yishmael: in a period of danger, a bill of divorce is written without knowing witnesses, since suspicion is not raised
Mishna: Rabbi Akiva recounts Neḥemya of Beit D'li's tradition from Rabban Gamliel the Elder that a single witness may permit remarriage
Rabban Gamliel the Elder's protocol is confirmed, and after the Tel Arza murders he allowed remarriage on one witness
Mishna: from then on, remarriage was permitted on hearsay, a slave's, a woman's, or a maidservant's testimony
Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua: the court may not permit remarriage on the testimony of one witness
Rabbi Akiva: the court may not permit remarriage on the testimony of a woman, slave, maidservant, or close relatives
Does Rabbi Akiva really hold that a woman's testimony is not accepted for another woman's remarriage
Baraita in Rabbi Akiva's name: a woman may bring her own bill of divorce, so she should be credible about her husband's death
Resolution: Rabbi Akiva's view applied before the protocol was established, and his lenient view applies after it
Mishna: Levites left a sick man at an inn, and the innkeeper woman testified he died, so the wife remarried
Rabbi Akiva: a woman is credible only when as convincing as the innkeeper, who produced his staff, bag, and Torah scroll as support

ranges.en: What was unfavorable about the innkeeper that made her less trustworthy than an ordinary woman
Rav Kahana: she was a gentile innkeeper speaking offhandedly, so her report of death and burial is credible
But they asked her where their friend was, which seems to show she was answering a question
She cried upon seeing them, so her crying began the account and she is treated as speaking offhandedly
Baraita: Rabbi Tarfon questions a witness about a man who tore an olive branch to scare off soldiers, asking how he knows
The witness recounts that the man called himself Arye, sickened and died, and Rabbi Tarfon permitted the wife to remarry
But didn't Rabbi Tarfon require inquiry and interrogation of the witness
Baraita version: the same story with a fig branch, where the witness reports the lion's name and death
In this version Rabbi Tarfon cross-examines the witness repeatedly, showing mere report is not sufficient
Explanation: a tannaitic dispute, where Rabbi Akiva says witnesses are not examined by inquiry, and Rabbi Tarfon says they are
Rabbi Ḥanina: by Torah law monetary and capital cases both need scrutiny, based on the verse of one law
Reason monetary cases are exempt: so as not to lock the door against potential lenders
With what do the tannaim disagree in the case of testimony that permits a woman to remarry
Rabbi Akiva treats it as monetary law due to the marriage contract; Rabbi Tarfon treats it as capital law due to adultery
Rabbi Elazar, citing Rabbi Ḥanina: Torah scholars increase peace in the world, based on the verse about children taught of the Lord
Closing colophon: the chapter ends and the tractate Yevamot is concluded
